News.title: Man, 76, arrested for ‘covering face amid mask ban’ at Portsmouth anti-migrant protest
News.content:
A MAN has been arrested for covering his face at an anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth.

Hampshire Police had warned anyone “concealing their identity” would be arrested at the protest – which saw thousands descend on the city.



Cops were forced to intervene as anti-migrant protesters were met with Stand Up to Racism campaigners on the south coast.

Hundreds of officers formed a barrier to separate both groups to each side of the popular Guildhall Square.



A man in the area, wearing what appeared to be black scarves tied across his face and head, was pictured in handcuffs this afternoon.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary later said a pensioner, 76, was arrested on suspicion of wearing an item to conceal identity at a protest.

The force confirmed it would use its new powers to ban masks in a designated area within a 24-hour window.

Today’s face-covering arrest is the first to be made using these powers, which are enforced under the Crime and Policing Act.



Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood demanded police chiefs make “full use” of new powers allowing them to ban face coverings at protests.

Across the UK, Nottingham has become the first city to confirm a ban on face coverings, with the rules set to come into play on Tuesday.

It means cops can ask people to remove face coverings if they “reasonably believe” it is being used to commit a crime or antisocial behaviour.

Refusal to remove it may result in a £70 on-the-spot fine or potential prosecution – with a maximum penalty of £1,000.

However, this does not include face coverings for “legitimate reasons” including religious, cultural, health or personal reasons.



Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has backed a ban on face coverings, describing them as “a menace”.

He told The Telegraph: “Facial coverings, quite frankly, are not the British way. Let’s ban them in public once and for all.”

A 33-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder.



Both arrests are in relation to chaotic scenes last Sunday, it is understood.

Police yesterday said they will not tolerate protesters “whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence”.

Protesters initially gathered at All Saints Church in the city centre just after midday, as chants of “stop the boats” rang out.



A man with a megaphone addressing the crowd said the protesters were reportedly against “illegal men invading the shores”.

Opposing demonstrators held Stand Up to Racism and Refugees Welcome banners, with signs including “RNLI are heroes, no-one is illegal”.

Protests and counter-protests have also descended on other UK cities including Newcastle and Glasgow.

Speaking near the demonstration, Dennis Wills, 82, said he wanted to “stop the boats” but said he was upset about the anti-RNLI sentiment.

Mr Wills, who has lived in Portsmouth his whole life, told The Sun: “I want to stop the boats but the RNLI are getting a horrid time.



“They are just called in to save life, when the boats come in. Remember, they are volunteers, I have supported them for decades.

“People need to realise they are just saving life, with no questions asked.

“I don’t like the growing anger against them, especially after their involvement on Sunday at Eastney Marina.

“That said, we must stop the boats. We can’t have these people just arriving in the country. Personally, they don’t give a fig for our counter.”

Today’s demonstration comes days after hundreds of anti-migrant protesters clashed with police last Sunday.



Chaotic scenes were sparked when 140 Channel migrants were brought ashore by the RNLI at Portsmouth’s Eastney Marina.

Demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying the migrants from leaving the city on Sunday night.

Vehicles were damaged and a small number of officers injured following the disorder which the government branded “thuggish”.

RNLI volunteers have since been warned not to wear charity-branded clothing following “unacceptable abuse” from anti-migrant protesters.

As the brave lifeboat crews returned to shore, they were branded “traitors” and met with abuse from the balaclava-clad crowd.



One shouted: “Look at these guys absolute traitors to this country. Look at the state of you.”

Protests have also been held at sites belonging to the charity, including an anti-migrant gathering outside the RNLI College in Poole, Dorset.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The RNLI has now issued security advice for its hardworking staff in the wake of protests in Portsmouth and Dover.

The protesters have also been accused of launching rocks and bricks at cops who were “caught off guard” during the clashes on Sunday.

News.title: Mum fights off vicious coyote with a flip-flop after it attacks four-year-old daughter then bites her face
News.content:
MOTHER’S INSTINCT Mum fights off vicious coyote with a flip-flop after it attacks four-year-old daughter then bites her face

A BRAVE mother has battled a savage coyote with just a flip-flop after the animal attacked her four-year-old daughter.

Brittany Cardinal, 36, has been left with serious injuries after the crazed canine clamped its jaws on her face as she was out flying a kite with her young child.



The nightmare unfolded in Surprise, Arizona, on September 6 when Brittany suddenly heard her child’s piercing scream.

She instantly spun around and – to her horror – saw a coyote attacking her defenceless child.



Acting fast, she swiped the flip-flop from her foot and began swinging it at the beast, while screaming at the top of her lungs.

She told WWNY-TV: “There was no hesitation at all.



“I don’t even think I thought about anything.

“I think you, like a mom, try to protect your kid.”



Amidst the chaos the brave mother fell to the ground and while she was finally able to free her child, the coyote then turned its fury to her.

The savage animal sank its jaws into the felled mothers face but even though she was wounded her commitment to battling the beast continued.

She continued: “I always hear people say, ‘You don’t feel the pain when trauma like that happens,’ and I mean, I really didn’t feel any pain.

“I just felt like the pressure of it.”

In a moment of reprieve, Brittany and her daughter were finally able to make a run for their home and help.



The mother suffered severe lacerations and puncture wounds to her face but thanks to her heroism her daughter came from the ordeal unharmed.

Arizona Game and Fish officials told the outlet the bizarre attack was the first recorded coyote attack on a person in the Phoenix area since December 2023, and they don’t know what triggered it.

Wildlife officials have since removed several coyotes from the area and are testing them for rabies.

Alex Flickinger, public affairs community liaison for Arizona Game and Fish said the mother took exemplary action.

He said: “You fight back, you yell at the animal, be loud with it, throw rocks, whatever you have to do to get that animal to just run off.”



The mother said she will now carry pepper spray with her at all times.

It comes following another terrifying incident where a three-year-old boy was pounced on by a coyote in Los Angeles, California.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shocking footage shows a dangerous predator ambushing an unsuspecting toddler and violently biting him outside his home before his family managed to chase the animal away.

He was rushed to hospital with non-life threatening puncture wounds to his leg and torso.

News.title: Man dies after 2-bed flat on 17th floor of tower block goes up in flames as woman and child flee blaze
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BLAZE TRAGEDY Man dies after 2-bed flat on 17th floor of tower block goes up in flames as woman and child flee blaze

A MAN has died after a two-bedroom flat on the 17th floor of a tower block went up in flames, as a woman and child manged to flee.

Some 50 other residents of the block in Poplar, east London, also managed to escape before firefighters were at the scene at around 4.35am today, September 12.



An investigation into the fire has already been launched.

Initially, London Fire Brigade (LFB) said a woman and child had been rescued from the burning apartment.



Then in an update this afternoon, they announced a man had died in the blaze.

Around 70 firefighters tackled the fire on Blackwall Way, across the Thames form the 02, and were able to get the blaze under control by 6.41am.

Half of the property in the 22-storey residential block was damaged, LFB said.

An LFB spokesperson said: “Ten fire engines and around 70 firefighters were called to a flat fire on Blackwall Way in Poplar.



“A two-room flat and balcony on the 17th floor of a 22-storey residential block of flats was damaged by fire.

“Two adults and one child were rescued by firefighters wearing breathing apparatus.

“Sadly, a man was declared dead at the scene.

“A further 50 people left the building before the Brigade arrived on scene and are currently at a rest centre.”

Crews from across east London were sent to help tackle the blaze.



The LFB added: “A range of factors are being investigated regarding the cause of the fire.”

News.title: Man arrested after allegedly holding bus driver hostage with knife in Tyrone and leading cops on high-speed chase
News.content:
BUS HORROR Man arrested after allegedly holding bus driver hostage with knife in Tyrone and leading cops on high-speed chase

A MAN has been arrested following the alleged hijacking of a bus after a police chase in Co Tyrone today.

It’s alleged that the passengers were allowed to leave the bus but the driver was kept on board while it was pursued during the incident which began in Omagh.



Police said they received a number of reports of collisions involving the stolen bus.

Cops received a report that a bus had been allegedly hijacked in the Beltany Road area of Omagh shortly before 1pm.



It is understood the driver of the bus was allegedly threatened at knifepoint by a man while being chased by a PSNI patrol car.

The man in his 30s who allegedly hijacked the bus made off in the direction of Newtownstewart and a pursuit ensued along the A5 through Victoria Bridge and Sion Mills. And it lasted nearly 20 miles.

A PSNI spokesperson said: “The man, believed to be armed with a knife, allowed the passengers to leave the bus, however, kept the driver on board before making off in the direction of Newtownstewart.

“A pursuit ensued along the A5 through Victoria Bridge and Sion Mills.

“The bus was eventually stopped in the Head of the Town area of Strabane and the man, aged in his 30s, was removed from the bus and subsequently arrested.”

The suspect remains in police custody.



One man has been taken to hospital for treatment for his injuries.

The PSNI added: “The Fountain Street and Drumrallagh areas in Strabane remain closed at this time and the public are asked to avoid the area.

“A number of reports of collisions involving the stolen bus and other vehicles, including a police car and damage to property have been received at this time and officers are appealing to anyone involved in a collision or to anyone with footage that could assist with inquiries to contact detectives on 101, quoting reference number 624 12/09/26.”

Sinn Fein councillor Brian Barney Harte said that the garden wall of a house had been damaged during the pursuit.

And he added that people are “understandably shocked and distressed at the reckless behaviour of the individual involved”.



He said: “I spoke to the driver who understandably has been pretty shook up by the entire ordeal.

“From what I heard he was able to tell him to slow down at points along the way, which may have prevented a major incident.

“My thoughts are with the passengers and driver, who have come through a terrifying experience.

“How there has not been a fatality is only by a miracle.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Cllr Barney claimed that a number of cars and properties had also been allegedly damaged, adding the bus came to stop beside a children’s playground.



A spokesperson for Translink NI said the public transport operator is assisting the PSNI with their investigation.

News.title: Andy Burnham could get a cat for No10 North because Larry is such a hit in Downing Street
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

Larry the Cat, 19, has been the chief mouser of No10 Downing Street for 15 years

Manc's Cat Andy Burnham could get a cat for No10 North because Larry is such a hit in Downing Street

ANDY Burnham is considering getting a cat for No10 North – as Downing Street’s Larry the Cat is so popular.

Aides to the PM are lobbying for a chief mouser to be installed in the government’s new Manchester outpost.



Suggested names include “Gary” and “Barry” – in tribute to No10’s Larry.

A senior sources told The Sun on Sunday: “Everyone loves Larry the cat.



“Now there is a concerted lobbying effort to get a cat for No10 North.

“But the building is owned by GCHQ, so they would have to get permission from them to do it.”



Larry was adopted by then PM David Cameron from Battersea Dogs and Cats home in 2011.

The chief mouser, who is 19 years-old, and is now onto his seventh PM.

He is a huge hit with the public and politicians from all over the world. He has met Barack and Michelle Obama and Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron.

Mr Burnham has a pet dog called Axel, but decided not to move him from Manchester to Downing Street as “he wouldn’t get on with Larry”.



Larry proved such a hit that other Whitehall departments adopted their own cats.

The Treasury adopted black cat Gladstone in 2016, names after former Liberal Chancellor William Gladstone.

The Foreign Office adopted the black and white cat Palmerston – named after the famous 19th Century Foreign Secretary Lord Palmerston.

Mr Burnham opened No10 North in Manchester in July, just weeks after becoming PM.



It is designed to turbocharge economic growth and devolution across the North.

News.title: Andy Burnham’s class war posturing will hold back working class kids and harm school standards
News.content:
Tory former Education Secretary savages the PM and Education Secretary over their school reforms that he says will trash standards and harm working kids the most

IN LIFE it shouldn’t matter where you come from – it’s where you’re going.

And in politics we shouldn’t be trying to put people in boxes and keep them there, but liberate them to decide their own future.

That was the lesson of the Eighties, when Mrs Thatcher believed that people shouldn’t be prisoners of a rigid class system but should be helped to earn more, own their own property, aspire to a richer life and leave their children a better future.



She was battling against the assumptions on the Left of the Know Your Place Tendency.



Those in the Labour Party, and beyond, who thought that working people should have their lives set by others – whether as council tenants, or trade union members, or minorities to be patronised.

It was Maggie’s great achievement to help working people buy their own homes, free themselves from the trade union barons, aspire to more choice in their lives and be accorded the dignity of sovereign individuals.

It was that spirit that inspired me into politics, to be on the side of the liberators.



That’s why I was so proud to have Maggie’s old job, as Education Secretary under a Conservative Prime Minister.

I believed that we could extend the horizons of future generations by making our schools powerful engines of social mobility – giving every child the chance to become author of their own life story.

And I was pleased that I could work with Blairite Labour folk, and even Lib Dems, who also believed we should be breaking down the old class barriers of the past.



This week I was delighted that the evidence was now in that we did indeed make opportunity more equal.

English schools have risen up international league tables.

Our children are in the top ten globally for reading, writing and science. In Europe only tiny Estonia does better.

The improvement in our education system, and in children’s opportunities, came as a result of hard work by teachers and students but also our decision to embed ambition into everything schools did.

We gave heads more powers, especially over discipline, by making it easier to exclude unruly students, allowing teachers to teach and pupils to learn.



We made the curriculum more aspirational, rigorous and stretching.

We toughened up exams to deal with grade inflation. We recruited talented people from outside teaching to bring additional expertise and excellence into the classroom.

Together, these policies have transformed opportunities for thousands.

And it has been children from traditionally disadvantaged backgrounds who have been helped most of all.

New “free” schools which we set up in poorer parts of the country, in the teeth of Labour and trade union opposition, have had amazing results.



Schools like Michaela in Wembley and Mercia in Sheffield have sent pupils from the poorest homes on to places at our best universities.

And all by embracing the freedom from bureaucracy we gave them and the ambitious academic standards we believed in.

But that progress is now at risk. Under Keir Starmer, Labour tried to turn back the clock on the changes we made, curbing the freedom of schools to set higher standards for poorer pupils.

And I fear, under Andy Burnham, the situation could become even worse.

His new Education Secretary Lucy Powell has said that we had an “over-focus on academic outcomes”.



In other words – working class kids, know your place, curb your ambition, don’t get above yourself by thinking you can rise through education.

Both Burnham and Powell have said that the universities they attended – Cambridge and Oxford – were not really for them, and unwelcoming places for working class students.

The message again, even if unintended, is clear – don’t aspire, don’t aim for the top.

Burnham and Powell’s policies will have a direct impact on the children, grandchildren and kids to be of Sun on Sunday readers.



Alongside their drive to make almost every new home a council house – and thus restrict home ownership, they’ve also set up a new unit in Government to entrench class thinking and set social groups against each other.

This reads like the Old Labour, pre-Blair, playbook – stereotyping people by class background instead of treating each individual with respect.

The irony is that both Andy Burnham and Lucy Powell, like Bridget Phillipson and others in the Labour Cabinet, are role models.

Individuals from what were thought of as working class backgrounds who, thanks to loving parents, strong support at home, hard work, a commitment to education, and good personal values, have gone on to scale the professional summit.

As the adopted child of a mum and dad who both left school at 15 I admire them and their professed desire to help individuals from every background.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

But if they really want to succeed in spreading opportunity, and help the country succeed in the future, they should ditch the class war posturing, celebrate ambition and aspiration and demand that every school in the country meets the standard of the best.

That’s the way to make us all proud, whatever our roots.

News.title: How did Brit hols favourite become a massacre hotspot? Gun hell in Thailand – where owning a weapon is easier than a car
News.content:
ON October 6, 2022, a former Thai cop drove his pick-up truck to a nursery armed with a pistol, shotgun and knife.

Panya Khamrab, a lifelong drug abuser, attacked children and staff before shooting and ramming pedestrians as he drove home, killing 37 people. More than half of his victims were toddlers.



It was Thailand’s worst-ever mass killing by a single attacker and sparked calls for an aggressive crackdown on guns.

But four years on, the country has still not escaped the cycle.

Public policy expert Dr. Boonwara Sumano told The Sun: “Gun violence happens almost every day in Thailand, unfortunately.”



Two weeks ago, a Bangkok suburb was confronted by another nightmare when a 14-year-old boy shot eight people dead after storming his school.

He murdered his grandparents, five teachers and a 12-year-old girl.

The perpetrator, Patchata Yimruang, had displayed a number of red flags leading up to the mass shooting, but was still able to access his grandad’s gun cabinet and fatally wield a legally-owned semi-automatic pistol.



Sumano said: “We’re one of the countries with very high gun-related crimes, and I think this is due to many factors, and most of them are structural ones.”

Thailand’s gun laws are, on paper, relatively strict, but relaxed enforcement on ownership has created gaps in the system.

One of the most glaring is that a licence to own a gun is effectively granted for life.

Sumano said: “In Thailand you have to renew your driving licence every five years, and you actually need a health screen by the doctor to ensure you are still fit to drive.

“But for a gun permit, it’s not in that way.”



The crisis has led Brits to get caught up in deadly incidents and concerned holidaymakers may now opt for safer destination.

In August 2025, a British tourist from Dundee was shot by a cannabis dealer during a road rage incident outside a hotel in Mae Hong Son.

Another was killed when he shot himself in the head during a game of Russian Roulette while high on a cocktail of drugs.

In 2013, 22-year-old Brit Stephen Ashton was killed in a gang shooting on Koh Phangan, a popular destination for tourists famous for its Full Moon parties.

The Siam Paragon Mall shooting in 2023 led the Foreign Office to warn Brtis about illegal firearm accessibility in Thailand and the potential risks in crowded nightlife areas.



In light of recent tragedies and a worsening reputation for gun violence, the government is now considering requiring permits to be renewed every three or five years.

But Sumano says that would only address part of the problem.

Thailand’s estimated civilian arsenal is larger than that of the other nine Asean (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) countries combined, according to a 2017 review by the Small Arms Survey.



More than 10 million privately-owned guns are currently in circulation among its 71 million population, according to the Geneva-based Small Arms Survey.

That means there are 15 firearms per every 100 people, which dwarfs the rate of its regional neighbours.

Indonesia, a country nearly four times the population of Thailand, has only 82,000 civilian firearms in circulation.



What’s more, around 40 per cent of civilian-owned guns in the country are not legally registered.

The problem is that many of those unregistered weapons may have originated through legal channels.

For decades, Thailand has operated a gun welfare scheme under which public-sector workers could buy firearms at discounted prices.

After five years, those guns can be legally transferred to new owners.

The scheme was originally introduced to protect civil servants working in remote areas, but it has long since been abused.



Sumano said: “The development of this scheme, expansion of coverage of this scheme has been so large.”

Even after the 2022 nursery massacre, the scheme was suspended rather than scrapped, then resumed.

Following the latest school shooting, the government again moved to suspend it.



But Sumano argues that temporary suspensions do not go far enough.

She said: “If the government is serious about responding to this gun control crisis, the least they could do is to reduce the coverage of those who could participate in the gun welfare scheme.

“Why would we need even more guns?”

The distinction between legal and illegal firearms in Thailand is not always as straightforward as it appears.

For years, much of the country’s gun-licensing system relied on separate paper permits to buy, possess and carry a firearm.



The lack of a centralised database makes it difficult to track whether someone who has been allowed to buy a gun has actually registered it.

Sumano said: “There’s no linkage of the data. So, I would say a lot of unregistered guns came from the legal channel ones.”

The government is now moving to modernise and scrap the confusing, paper-heavy system.

Experts say that regulators must also track how responsible licensed gun owners are after getting their hands on a lethal weapon.

Professor Trynh Phoraksa, a prominent criminologist and gun control advocate, told The Sun: “Gun regulation should not end when the licence is issued.”



That means looking at how guns are stored, who can access them and whether owners should have to renew their licences periodically.

Another problem, as in the case of the most recent shooting, is addressing how firearms are stored in the home to prevent them getting into the wrong hands.

Sumano said: “There’s no monitor about safe storage of one’s gun.”



She acknowledged that enforcing safe storage inside private homes would be tricky, but argued more could be done to minimise the risk.

For example, prospective gun owners should have to prove that they have appropriate storage.

In the case of the 14-year-old, the gun was legally owned by his grandfather.

Phoraksa said: “Legal ownership does not automatically mean safe accessibility.”

The distinction is important because a gun can be legally registered to one person while still being accessible to somebody else in the same home.



Phoraksa said the shooting showed why the question should not simply be who owns a gun, but who can get their hands on it.

Regulation is not the only issue Thailand faces.

The country has a tendency to associate guns with power and status, originating from a decades-long military culture.

Sumano said: “There are two norms that would look like conflicting ones but that, in the end, they work together in the same way.



“One is the culture of worshipping power. Guns and firearms are seen as tools to make you look more powerful and make your social status higher.

“The other is the norm of non-confrontation. Many Asian countries have the same norm of trying to stay polite and not having conflict discussed openly.

“Therefore people will not tell you directly that they are unhappy and all of these disagreements can build up and explode one day.”

Criminologist Dr. Piyaporn Tunneekul believes the problem also goes beyond guns themselves, pointing to rising social and economic pressures, and what she describes as a lack of emotional support within some families.



She said these pressures can affect children’s emotional development and contribute to violent behaviour.

She also warned that public concern tends to spike after a mass shooting before gradually fading.

Thailand’s gun laws are outdated, having been enacted in 1947, and Tunneekul says they urgently need modernising.

Among her proposals are regular licence renewals rather than lifetime permits, tighter controls on welfare gun schemes, stricter ammunition sales and requiring applicants to prove they have secure storage.

The issue of preventing violence before it happens is also becoming increasingly important.



Following the latest attack, some Thai schools have introduced measures including active-shooter drills, metal-detector screening and bag checks.

But Phoraksa said security measures alone cannot address the warning signs that may come before an attack.

He said: “By the time a child enters a school carrying a firearm, several opportunities for prevention may already have been missed.”

Schools also need better ways of identifying and reporting concerning behaviour before it escalates into violence.

Phoraksa explained: “We should stop asking what a school shooter looks like and start asking what a pathway toward violence looks like.”



The challenge now is whether Thailand can turn the public anger that follows each mass shooting into lasting reform.

Phoraksa said: “Thailand needs to move from event-driven to system-driven gun control.”

If it wants to keep its booming tourist industry – especially among Brits – Thailand will need to get a grip on the problem before it spins out of control.

News.title: How DIY criminals convert fake pistols into lethal firearms from grannies’ garages in terrifying national epidemic
News.content:
COWBOY CRIMS How DIY criminals convert fake pistols into lethal firearms from grannies’ garages in terrifying national epidemic

GANGSTER Daniel Wren’s elderly grandparents must have thought he had an obsession with cars.

He spent hours tinkering away in the garage of their Nottingham home but behind the shuttered doors Wren was running a gun factory that converted blank pistols to live firearms.



When cops raided his home they found five revolvers, ammunition, two 3D printers and even a hand grenade.

The 27-year-old has now been jailed six years for running his illicit workshop while his half brother was also caged for converting guns.



The Sun can today reveal Britain’s streets are being flooded with replica guns which can easily be modified into the real thing.

Almost 2000 fakes were discovered in the 12 months to March this year – equating to 38 percent of all gun crime.

It’s almost double the 20 per cent recorded in the first year of the pandemic in 2019.

One expert told us how organised crime is turning to replicas to save cash.



Ex-Sussex detective Martyn Underhill said: “They sell for about half the price of real weapons so they are not that expensive.”

The retired DCI, who worked on the high-profile murder inquiry of eight-year-old Sarah Payne in 200, said: “These imitations achieve the desired outcome because the public or the victim believe they are real.

“The expression flooding in is a good one to describe what’s happening.

“The stats are going up.

“Any firearm increase is worrying but if the imitations are coming in more, you have to ask why and I imagine that is because of cost.”



Martyn, who was the police and crime commissioner for Dorest for almost a decade, said while some criminals rely on fakes, gang warfare involves real weapons.

He said: “They don’t use imitations because they want to kill each other.”

More than a third of all recorded gun crime now involves fake weapons – almost double the 20percent during the pandemic.



Figures from the Office of National Statistics show that 38percent of guns used last year are phony equating to 1,957 cases – compared to 20percent in 2019/20.

Daniel Wren, 27, was the head of a gang converting guns from his grandparents’home in Bakersfield, east Nottingham.

The city’s crown court heard how the gang took blank-firing pistols that had their barrels constricted and made them into lethal weapons.

When the gun factory was raided in October last year, cops found guns, ammunition and tools.

They went on to bust Wren’s home in St Ann’s, Nottingham, where they found other guns as well as a 3D printer and hand grenade.



It’s known that such printers are used to produce 3D replicas.

A search of his half-brother Kerrigan Wright’s home also found blank pistols and ammunition.

The 35- year-old was jailed two years after being found guilty of converting an imitation firearm.

Other associates were also given jail time.

Sean Bates, 36, of Netherfield, Nottinghamshire, was given four-and-a-half years for converting a gun and an unrelated charge of being concerned in the supply of cocaine.



Quisar Iqbal, 33, of Mapperley, Notts, was also given four-and-a-half years for modifying a gun.

He has a previous conviction for possessing a disguised firearm from 2016.

Many replica guns are shipped into Britain from Eastern Europe.



In 2022, cops uncovered a conversion workshop being run from the kitchen of a house in Huddersfield where handguns were being modified.

It supplied criminals across the north of England.

Thomas Robinson, 38, and Junaid Ali, 24, were sent replica weapons from Eastern Europe.

Robinson was jailed for 13 years and six months and Ali was jailed for eight years and three months after they admitted their roles in the operation.

Dale Bates, 29, was given five years for his involvement as a customer.



Martyn Underhill said criminals with fake guns were gambling with their own lives as armed police have no idea if weapons are real or not.

He said: ““It’s a bit of a fool’s errand really because it increases the risk of them being shot by armed police, so it doesn’t really do them any favours does it?

“The police officer is going to draw and shoot, not knowing whether that’s a real weapon.”

In 2019, Hull man Andrejs Saveljevs was shot in the shoulder by officers after brandishing a replica handgun in the street.



The 35-year-old food factory worker was later jailed two-and-a-half years after pleading guilty to possessing an imitation 9mm calibre Beretta pistol.

One undercover cop told how he was forced to drive into a thug as he pointed a fake gun at his partner.

Jack Dawe, who has written a book about his role called Hard Stop, said he was forced to ram his car into the suspect, who went flying into the air “like a ragdoll” before smashing through the windscreen.

Jack said: “These replicas are designed to look real and if someone ever pointed one at you, you have a split second to decide, fight or flight.



“I chose to fight.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“People are too quick to judge the actions of the police with no understanding of violence.

“ There is a large proportion of society who have never faced physical violence in their lives and have no idea what strength it takes to make an arrest using proportionate force against an uncooperative suspect, some of whom are on drugs and possess an almost superhuman strength.”

News.title: Manchester incident live: Cordon in place with major emergency response
News.content:
A police cordon is in place by the Arndale shopping centre in Manchester city centre after a boy in his mid-teens had an "unknown substance" thrown at him

A teenager has suffered a "potentially life-changing" injury after an "unknown substance" was thrown at him in Manchester city centre.

Police, fire crews and colleagues from the North West Ambulance service are outside the Arndale shopping centre opposite the Printworks with a large cordon in place.

Officers rushed to the scene at 6.10pm where they established a substance which has not yet been identified was thrown following an argument.

A statement from Greater Manchester Police read: "The victim, a male in his mid-teens has received an injury that has been described as not life-threatening but potentially life-changing. A 19-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of assault and remains in custody."

News.title: Seven-hour RNLI sea drama as six people rescued from yacht in gale-force winds
News.content:
Seven-hour RNLI sea drama as six people rescued from yacht in gale-force winds

Crew from Red Bay RNLI rushed to the rescue of a 46ft yacht that got into difficulty off the coast of Cushendall, Northern Ireland, in harsh weather conditions

View Image The dramatic rescue of six people from the yacht (Image: RNLI)

Six people were rescued from a yacht after a dramatic seven-hour rescue operation by the RNLI in brutal gale-force conditions at sea.

‌



The crew of Red Bay RNLI launched after the crew of a 46ft yacht got into difficulty off the coast of Cushendall, Northern Ireland, and sent out a Mayday while on a passenger from Oban in Scotland to Portugal.

‌



Belfast Coastguard received the emergency message from the stricken vessel which had lost all power and steering after making contact with a fish farm in Red Bay in 60-knot winds, becoming trapped..

‌



The RNLI lifeboat under Coxswain Paddy McLaughlin and with five crew members onboard, launched at 3.22am this morning and made its way the short distance to the scene. The inshore lifeboat from Red Bay RNLI also launched to assist.

UK temperatures to soar to 25C on Monday as another heatwave on the cards READ MORE :

NATO military aircraft scrambled over Europe as urgent warning issued in Poland READ MORE :

Weather conditions were difficult throughout the call-out, with force nine gusting winds, driving rain, and the darkness of night.

‌



Once on scene, the RNLI crew found that all onboard were safe but trapped due to the yacht having got entangled on the fish cages, reported BelfastLive.

Given the difficult weather and sea conditions, the Coxswain made the decision that the safest course of action was for the sailors to remain onboard the yacht and for the lifeboat to stand by until daylight broke at 7:30am.

At 9:30am, the lifeboat crew successfully freed the yacht from the fish farm and brought the sailors safely to Glenarm, where they arrived at 10am and were assisted by Larne Coastguard.

Article continues below

Speaking following the call out, Mr McLaughlin said: "This was a challenging call out in difficult weather conditions, but we were delighted to bring the sailors to safety, and we would like to wish them well.

"We would also like to commend our colleagues in the Coastguard and thank our crew who responded quickly in the middle of the night, launched our lifeboats in darkness and made their way to the scene in what were gale force conditions, and for then spending seven hours at sea.

"This shout was a great example of the selfless and dedicated efforts of volunteers who used their skills and training to bring six people to safety in what was a challenging operation."

News.title: Mum died after nine-month wait for cancer results as NHS department 'overwhelmed'
News.content:
Mum died after nine-month wait for cancer results as NHS department 'overwhelmed'

Sarah Daniels underwent surgery, chemotherapy and private treatment after finally getting her diagnosis, but an inquest heard the long wait had reduced her chances of successful treatment

View 3 Images The mum-of-three fought through 10 rounds of chemotherapy (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

A mum-of-three died after waiting nine months for cancer test results, an inquest has heard.

‌



Sarah Daniels, 43, faced what a consultant later described as an “unacceptable” delay after a cyst removed from her ovary was sent for testing. The mass was later found to be an aggressive and rare form of appendix cancer which had spread to her ovary.

‌



But by the time Sarah, from Porth, south Wales, received the results, her condition was terminal and she was told she had around 12 months to live. The inquest heard she had first gone to her GP in October 2021 with “gynaecological symptoms of concern”.

‌



View 3 Images Sarah died in April 2025 (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Sarah was offered two surgical options and chose a less invasive procedure rather than a total hysterectomy. The cyst was removed in February the following year and sent for testing, but Sarah then waited nine months for the results. The cancer, known as signet ring adenocarcinoma, had metastasised and spread to the ovary.

The inquest heard the pathology department at Cwm Taf Morgannwg health board had been “completely overwhelmed by demand” after being hit by a Covid “backlog” and “deluge” of work.

‌



Biomedical scientist Martin Ludlam said the department’s workload had risen significantly after routine appointments were put on hold during the pandemic. Mr Ludlam said: “This case has highlighted the case that we can never go back to a position where we have a routine back log again.”

In a statement, Sarah’s husband Ben said she was told her cancer was terminal when the results finally came back. But he said she remained determined to get better and underwent private treatment at the Christie cancer treatment centre in Manchester to have her appendix removed.

Sarah later received treatment at Velindre Cancer Centre in Cardiff, including 10 rounds of chemotherapy and scans. The inquest heard she was eventually given the all clear, before scans showed the cancer had returned just months later.

‌



View 3 Images The inquest heard the pathology department had been "completely overwhelmed by demand" (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Ben Daniels said his wife “never gave up” fighting the disease, but her condition had become “progressively worse” by January last year. She died three months later in April 2025.

Consultant Mohamed Khalifa, who leads gynaecological cancer multidisciplinary team meetings for the health board, said earlier treatment could have made a difference.

‌



He said: “When she died might have been different if the chemotherapy or other treatment had been started sooner. The delay of nine months between surgery and histology was unacceptable.”

He added that Sarah’s Risk of Malignancy Index had been “incorrectly reassuring” to her and her family. Her medical cause of death was recorded as “metastatic signet ring adenocarcinoma of the appendix”.

Coroner Rachel Knight recorded a narrative conclusion, finding Sarah’s death was “naturally occurring” but that the delay had reduced her chance of chemotherapy being successful. She said the wait for test results was also likely to have affected when Sarah died and her quality of life.

Article continues below

Addressing Ben at the inquest in Pontypridd, south Wales, Ms Knight said: “I’m sorry you lost Sarah in the way you did. You have shown great dignity throughout the proceedings. What you went though must have been horrendous It is clear how loved Sarah was and how missed she is”.

The coroner said the pathology department had since begun outsourcing its backlog.

News.title: Heartbroken dad of daughter who died after Turkey op urges Brits to avoid surgery abroad
News.content:
Heartbroken dad of daughter who died after Turkey op urges Brits to avoid surgery abroad

EXCLUSIVE: Morgan travelled to Turkey for life-changing surgery, but came home in a coffin. Her grieving dad speaks out to deter others from taking the same risk

My daughter passed away from gastric sleeve complications

Broken by grief, Ricardo Ribeiro has a question for anyone thinking of cut-price surgery abroad.

‌



“Is it worth taking a risk to possibly come back in a brown box?”, he asks.

‌



He was speaking just days after an inquest heard how his beloved daughter Morgan died aged just 20 after jetting to Turkey for a weight loss operation.

‌



Having struggled with her weight from a young age, she could barely wait to jet to Turkey for gastric sleeve surgery.

The nursery worker had counted the days until her surgery, hoping it would change her life. Instead, it ended it.

Just three days after going under the knife in January 2024, Morgan collapsed on a flight back to the UK, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing in the Serbian capital Belgrade.

‌



View 6 Images Morgan was excited about having gastric sleeve surgery (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

Turkey surgeon still dodging questions over British woman who died after gastric band operation READ MORE :

She died in a hospital there five days later. Last week an inquest concluded Morgan perished as a result of ­complications from the op.

Today, her heartbroken dad, Ricardo, is sharing his precious girl’s story in a bid to deter others from travelling abroad for cosmetic procedures.

‌



Speaking to people considering surgery overseas, he said: “You’re putting your life in the hands of someone you can’t guarantee will do the job correctly.

“Yes, 80% may come out with a perfect result, and everyone says ‘it’s my body, my choice,’ but you’ve still got family who’ve got to deal with the agony if you pass away – you have to realise the effect is wider than that.

“Part of me died that day – it’s a gut punch I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemy. I don’t want any other family to suffer what I’ve suffered.”

‌



View 6 Images Ricardo says part of him died the day Morgan passed away (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

A post mortem examination found Morgan’s intestinal wall had ruptured during the procedure, which triggered deadly peritonitis.

Ricardo, 46, told how Morgan spent hours choosing a reputable-looking surgeon with glowing reviews.

‌



But when she arrived in Istanbul on January 5, 2024, the hospital replaced her chosen doctor with someone else.

He fears the new medic may have lacked experience and proper checks were not conducted.

Ricardo said: “If they have to replace a surgeon with somebody else, they should ensure they’re capable of doing the job.

‌



“It feels like many doctors there [in Turkey] are not held to the same high standards as British surgeons. It doesn’t make sense.”

View 6 Images Morgan was bullied for her weight at school (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

Morgan, from Croydon, South London, was scheduled to stay in hospital for two nights, but she was kept in for an extra day because of swelling, stomach pains and a fever.

‌



Yet in discharge notes obtained by the coroner, hospital staff claim Morgan was recovering and signed her off as medically fit to fly.

Ricardo said: “You cannot have kept her in for an extra day due to concerns, and on the discharge sheet have no concerns written ­whatsoever – it’s rubbish.

“It was blatantly just a form that you reuse and change the pieces to suit your needs. All they’ve done is cover ­themselves. To me, it just doesn’t ring true.”

‌



View 6 Images Morgan fell unconscious on her way back to the UK

In 2024, the Mirror tracked down Morgan’s surgeon, who was named by the coroner as Dr Serkan Bayil, and he denied any wrongdoing, claiming that Ms Ribeiro died of an embolism. But the coroner couldn’t get hold of him, and the hospital in Istanbul, ­Medivita Incirli Hastanesi, is listed online as permanently closed.

Ricardo says Global Medical Care – the firm that organised the trip and introduced Morgan to the hospital – also has ­questions to answer.

‌



He said: “They put the [team] together, so some of that ­responsibility has to lie with them.

“If you’re going to provide a service to someone, you make sure that their best interests are at the forefront.”

Ricardo thinks Global Medical Care and other similar companies should be barred from plugging surgery through social media ads. He added: “These companies are targeting the British public with ­fairytales – no matter what social media you go on, you’re bombarded with everything from gastric bands to Turkey teeth.

‌



“The UK government should be banning [the ads].

“If people were more aware they probably wouldn’t go, because who is going to risk their life for a BBL, breast implant or a gastric sleeve? It feels like money is more motivational to these ­companies than human life.”

View 6 Images Morgan's surgeon Dr Serjan Bayil denies any wrongdoing (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

‌



For Ricardo, most agonising of all is just how much his girl had to live for. “Morgan did have a stage where she was crying out for help,” her dad said. “She was dealing with bullying due to her weight, and she wasn’t in the best of places. But at the time of her death, she was blossoming.

“She knew she wanted to work with young people, because she ­understood what it was like to get bullied.

“She’d overcome all those problems, and wanted to help others do the same.

‌



“She went from trying to do so much good to having her life end in the blink of an eye.” And he has vowed never to give up on his fight for justice.

View 6 Images Morgan was counting down the days until her surgery

He said: “Someone, somewhere, has got to take accountability for what happened. Because if that doesn’t happen, how many more people are going to be burying their children?” Global Medical Care Turkey said: “We were saddened by Morgan’s death. We understand why her father is asking these questions.

Article continues below

“When a patient approaches us, we present more than one doctor and hospital option. The patient makes their own choice. Before a patient travels, a live consultation is arranged directly between the patient and the treating doctor, in which... the risks are explained and set out in writing.

“The decision to proceed remains the patient’s. The ­clinical assessment, consent process, the surgery and post-operative care are carried out by the hospital

A UK government spokesperson said: “We would urge anyone ­considering medical procedures abroad to review guidance from the NHS and other bodies.”

News.title: Putin makes chilling warning of 'war' over peacekeeping force in Ukraine
News.content:
Putin makes chilling warning of 'war' over peacekeeping force in Ukraine

Vladimir Putin made it clear that Russia would see the sending of a peacekeeping force to Ukraine as meaning war, with some European leaders pledging their commitment to the plan

View 2 Images Vladimir Putin has threatened Europe with war over a peacekeeping force (Image: Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik K)

Vladimir Putin made a chilling warning to Europe of "war" over a peacekeeping force as Russian strikes killed eight people and injured dozens more in Ukraine.

‌



The Russian leader did not mince his words when speaking at a summit of the BRICS group of emerging economies in India, when asked about the involvement of western European countries in Ukraine.

‌



He said: “Now they’re talking about how they’re considering sending troops into Ukraine. That means a war with Russia."

‌



Some European leaders have pledged their commitment to a potential peacekeeping force, a prospect that Moscow has repeatedly described as unacceptable.

View 2 Images Putin with the Russian delegation at the BRICS summit (Image: Kristina Solovyova/Pool Sputnik)

UK temperatures to soar to 25C on Monday as another heatwave on the cards READ MORE :

NATO military aircraft scrambled over Europe as urgent warning issued in Poland READ MORE :

At the same time, Putin also denied Russia posed any threat to Europe, saying “there is no such threat and never has been. We do not threaten, nor do we intend to threaten, European countries."

‌



Overnight Russian strikes killed eight civilians and wounded dozens of other people in Ukraine, local officials said today.

Ukraine is under mounting pressure from Russia’s intensifying air campaign that uses ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce defences. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralise civilians.

Two people were killed and one wounded when Russian drones struck a residential area in the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional head Ivan Fedorov said. One person also died and three others were wounded in strikes on Kryvyi Rih.

‌



In the Black Sea port of Odesa and the surrounding area, 35 people were wounded overnight in what regional head Oleh Kiper called a “massive attack.” Among the buildings hit was a residential high-rise, whose upper floors were completely destroyed.

Three people were killed on Saturday when cars were hit by drones in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s partially occupied Donetsk region, along with a further two people in a Russian attack on a grocery store in the Zhytomyr region, local officials said.

Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces struck two chemical industry facilities in Russia, one in Samara and one in Perm. The governors of the regions did not immediately comment, but Russian independent online news outlet Astra reported drone attacks on chemical plants in both regions.

‌



Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said that two incidents along Ukraine’s borders with Poland and Moldova this week were a preview of potential intensified Russian provocations at Ukraine’s border crossing points with Europe.

Two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday night, while a “direct threat” to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point on Wednesday night was only avoided thanks to cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, he said.

In an interview with Deutsche Welle today, Zelensky said he would meet Putin if both leaders were invited to the Group of 20 summit of rich and developing nations in December in Miami.

Article continues below

Putin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, said the possibility of Putin attending the summit had not yet been discussed. The Kremlin in the past has said that Zelenskyy can come to Moscow if he wants a meeting with Putin, a proposal Kyiv has rejected.

“If he really wants to meet with Putin, Putin has already said that he could fly to Moscow,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Saturday. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov affirmed Saturday that Russia is “ready for negotiations,” but that the so-called “special military operation,” as Moscow refers to its war in Ukraine, “will not be suspended during this period of negotiations.”

News.title: Professor Tim Spector's 'harmless daily habit' warning - eat these 6 things instead
News.content:
Professor Tim Spector's 'harmless daily habit' warning - eat these 6 things instead

Professor Tim Spector, co-founder of the Zoe app and well-known for his TV appearances on the BBC and ITV, has warned against the seemingly 'harmless daily habit'

View 2 Images Professor Tim Spector (Image: ITV)

A UK professor has issued a warning over a 'harmless daily habit'. Professor Tim Spector, co-founder of the Zoe app, and Professor of Genetic Epidemiology at King's College London and Honorary Consultant Physician at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, is a familiar face on BBC and ITV.

‌



He also regularly features on the Zoe health podcast. In a recent Instagram post, he revealed he had decided to "have a closer look at some of the world's most popular snack bars."

‌



The clip shows him adding ingredients to a jar relating to an unnamed snack. He said: "I don't know about you, but seeing all the ingredients laid out like this doesn't make me want to reach for one."

‌



He admitted that during his time as a hospital doctor, he would routinely reach for a chocolate bar or chocolate digestive most afternoons. He added: "I thought it was a harmless daily habit, but in the short-term, snacks like these will leave you hungrier due to spikes and crashes in blood sugar, and in the long-term, can lead to problems like inflammation."

View 2 Images The professor says fruit is a much better simple snack than the snack he examined (Image: fcafotodigital via Getty Images)

He then went on to list six healthier alternatives, saying: "Nuts, fruit, vegetables, yoghurt, cheese or a couple squares of dark chocolate are all simple snacks that can keep you satisfied and support your health. If you get into the habit of reaching for basic whole foods, you really can't go wrong."

‌



His followers were quick to respond, though not everyone was ready to ditch their favourite treats. One commented: "I'm sticking to all things in moderation I think - some a bit more moderate than others."

Another asked: "But healthy eating IS eating a treat and not denying and restricting any food. Is this post saying not to eat any treats?"

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



In the video, he adds a series of ingredients to the jar, starting with oats before including others.

"Let's see what's in the UK's leading snack bar," he says. The other ingredients are sunflower oil, sugar, honey, molasses, sunflower lecithin and sodium bicarbonate.

He concludes: "So there you have it. That's what's in your average healthy snack bar. Now the oats might have some health benefits. The rest of the ingredients none at all."

‌



NHS advice on what to eat each day for a healthy diet

The NHS website encourages people to look at The Eatwell Guide. It shows that to have a healthy, balanced diet, people should try to:

drink at least 6 to 8 glasses of fluids a day – this can include tap and bottled water, tea, coffee and fruit juice.

eat some beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other protein.

have some dairy or dairy alternatives (such as soya drinks).

eat at least 5 portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables every day (see 5 A Day).

base meals on higher-fibre starchy foods like potatoes, bread, rice or pasta.

choose unsaturated oils and spreads, and eat them in small amounts.

The NHS says: "If you're having foods and drinks that are high in fat, salt and sugar, have these less often and in small amounts. Try to choose a variety of different foods from the 5 main food groups to get a wide range of nutrients."

Article continues below

The site warns that most people in t Britons are consuming far too many calories, along with excessive amounts of saturated fat, sugar and salt, while falling short on fruit, vegetables, oily fish and fibre, according to the health service.

It does point out, however, that The Eatwell Guide does not apply to children under the age of 2, as they have distinct nutritional requirements. The NHS advises that once children reach the age of 2, they should gradually transition to eating the same foods as the rest of the family, in the proportions outlined in the Eatwell Guide.

You can find out more about the Zoe science and nutrition podcast here.

News.title: Nigel Farage accused of failing to declare donors from fundraising events in the Middle East
News.content:
Nigel Farage accused of failing to declare donors from fundraising events in the Middle East

EXCLUSIVE: The Electoral Commission has confirmed it will look into hospitality heaped on Nigel Farage and senior party figures in Dubai last January by mega-rich supporters

View 2 Images Nigel Farage could be facing another investigation (Image: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Nigel Farage faces being embroiled in another investigation after Reform was accused of failing to declare donors who paid for glitzy fundraising events in the Middle East.

‌



The Electoral Commission has confirmed it had received a complaint over hospitality heaped on Mr Farage and senior party figures in Dubai last January by mega-rich supporters.

‌



Fresh scrutiny over Reform’s finances come after Scotland Yard confirmed this week that it was investigating separate allegations the party broke foreign funding laws.

‌



The latest furore centres on whether Mr Farage should have declared lavish hospitality he received during a two-day trip in May 2025, according to an investigation by Babelfish.

One event was a reception hosted by the Binghatti family, who are among the largest property tycoons in the emirate. Hussain Binghatti Aljbori is ranked by Forbes as one of the richest men in the Middle East, with a £1.8billion fortune. The other was a lunch reportedly paid for by Indian billionaire businessman Sunny Varkey, according to Bloomberg News. There is no suggestion of wrongdoing from the Binghatti family, or Mr Varkey.

Nigel Farage may be wishing Binface won as he faces bad vibes in every direction READ MORE :

View 2 Images Nigel Farage faces questions over donations (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Founder of Babelfish, Dale Vince, said: “Nigel Farage has put democracy in Britain up for sale to the highest bidder - he clearly does not care where the money comes from - but we should. Ultimately all of this just reinforces the case for a total ban on donations to political parties in Britain."

Neither the party nor Mr Farage have declared donations covering the cost of these events. The Electoral Commission has confirmed it will review the evidence after a complaint from Labour MP Phil Brickell.

UK political parties must check whether any donation worth over £500 is from a “permissible” donor - including UK voters and companies - and must declare any donations worth more than £11,180.

‌



After Labour MP Phil Brickell wrote to the Electoral Commission calling for a probe into the trip, the commission has now confirmed that it will review the evidence.

In his letter, the Bolton West MP said: “These reports appear to raise a straightforward question of electoral law: were goods, services or hospitality provided to Reform UK in connection with these fundraising events, and if so, were they donations which were properly recorded and reported to the Commission?”

He told us: “We need to understand if this is just a case of a couple of bad apples - albeit ones that haven’t fallen very far from the tree - or if there is a systemic culture of obfuscation, secrecy and, essentially, cheating, within Reform UK.”

Article continues below

An Electoral Commission spokesperson said: “We can confirm we have received a letter from Phil Brickell MP regarding Reform and fundraising in Dubai. The Commission reviews all information it receives and is considering this matter under its regulatory remit.”

Reform was approached for comment.

News.title: Nuns swindled after two men flee their guesthouse without paying four-figure bill
News.content:
Nuns swindled after two men flee their guesthouse without paying four-figure bill

Two nuns who have been left short of a four-figure sum have been trying to work out what happened after two men allegedly left their guesthouse without paying their bill

View 3 Images Nuns swindled after two men flee their guesthouse

Two nuns were left over €1,000 out of pocket after two men allegedly fled their guesthouse without paying. Said nuns, the Discalced Franciscan Poor Clare sisters of the Convent of La Purisimia Conception, ran the business out of the village of Marchena, located south east of the Spanish city of Seville.

‌



According to reports, two men checked in to the venue situated next to the Church of Santa Maria on Wednesday September 2nd, before leaving a week later. The bill was due to be paid just before the end of their stay on Monday, September 7th.

‌



However, the two men, who claimed they worked for a company based in the Vega del Guadalquivir region, a claim later found to be false, were nowhere to be found. The nuns went upstairs the next day to find the room empty of both the men and their belongings.

‌



Furthermore, it has also been alleged that as well as taking their own belongings, the two men took the keys to their room, and the keys to the entrance gate and main door.

View 3 Images The two men allegedly left without paying (Image: Facebook)

According to the nuns the two men, who were staying at the guesthouse for the first time, had paid for a room as well as dinner and lunch, costing them €913 plus 10 percent VAT to bring their total to €1,004.30 (£861.89).

‌



Following the occurrence, the religious community has reported the incident to the local police in a bid to find the men. It has since been reported that the guesthouse where the two men stayed had CCTV fitted and shows them in the area at 11.30am on the Monday.

In a further twist, a quick search of the company they claimed to work for revealed it was actually located in Almeria.

ABC Sevilla reported that the two men had given the nuns their supervisor's contact details, whom they claimed would not only settle the bill, but also stay at the guesthouse for two nights.

‌



View 3 Images The guesthouse is near the city of Seville (stock) (Image: Getty)

Attempting to get the bill paid, the convent's superior, Sister Susana, called the number, but said the man hung up when he realised it was the convent calling about the bill.

As a result, they have not received any form of response. The venue the nuns run is not a large business, and helps to serve a low income community.

Article continues below

The pair also produce Christmas carol albums and prepare takeaway food whilst trying to maintain their life at the venue.

On the website for the Santa Maria Inn, the 13 rooms are described as being “comfortable” and suitable places “for rest, prayer, and study”.

Furthermore, alongside the air-conditioned rooms, there is a “multi-purpose hall available for various cultural events with a capacity of 80 people” and “a dining room”.

News.title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
News.content:
Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a Â£5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.

Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.

The party is also facing scrutiny after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations.

The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.

The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by Tice.

Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage".

"A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.

Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.

Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field". He said in April he was moving back to Britain from Hong Kong.

Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

However, the Labour government has introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.

There were nine donations of Â£1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was Â£9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.

Labour had five donations of Â£1m or more - totalling nearly Â£10m - and the Conservatives had three of Â£1m each.

Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.

Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal".

She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."

Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of Â£500,000.

She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding: "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for the government to introduce emergency legislation to cap donations.

She said: "These are eye-watering amounts of money. This is real emergency for our democracy. It presents a very clear and present threat."

Labour MP Stella Creasy and other backbenchers had proposed an amendment to the Government's Representation of the People Bill that would stop donors giving parties over Â£100,000 a year.

But the amendment was never debated in the Commons after the government said it would set up a task force to investigate the issue. The bill will be debated in the House of Lords on Monday.

Duncan Hames, Director of Policy and Programmes at campaigning charity Transparency International UK, said: "This is a watershed moment, with two billionaires pledging Â£72m to one political party in less than 48 hours.

"This situation is now completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast."

News.title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations
News.content:
Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer.

Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donations putting it back in the headlines today.

For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that initial Â£36m gift to Nigel Farage's party alone is like something from a different political universe.

"It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me.

That was even before another Reform donor pledged to match that astonishing sum with another Â£36m, saying the first donation had provoked his "competitive spirit".

But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values".

A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way.

The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence.

News.title: Céline Dion fans prepare for comeback concert in Paris
News.content:
CÃ©line Dion greeted fans today as she left her hotel, hours before she kicked off her comeback concert in Paris.

The Canadian singer returns to the stage on Saturday for her first full concert in six years, to open a sell-out Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder put a pause in her career.

Some fans arrived as early as 06:00 to get a spot in front of LeRoyal Monceau hotel to catch a glimpse of the star before she left.

She is one of the best-selling music artists of all time and is due to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months.

News.title: Three arrests at Portsmouth protests including man, 76, suspected of concealing identity
News.content:
The new powers came into effect at 10:00 BST. Participants on both sides were not seen to be wearing any face coverings when the marches started.

The city centre protests follow disorder on 6 September, when police attended Eastney Marina as hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

On Saturday, up to 500 anti-migrant protesters held Union and St George flags while some wearing Portsmouth Patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road shortly before midday on Saturday.

The crowd chanted "stop the boats" as they marched to Guidhall Square.

About 300 people joined the counter-protest.

Both sets of demonstrators were kept apart by police when they arrived at the square.

Speaking before the march, Simon Magorian, of Stand up to Racism Portsmouth, described the demonstrations in Eastney as a "horrible spectacle".

He said: "Portsmouth is actually a good functioning multi-cultural city.

"We are now organising to have the broadest possible opposition to what we see as a fascist street movement and we're not going to allow them to get a grip on Portsmouth or any other town - this is quite terrifying."

Among the anti-migration protesters, Pete Davies, from Portsmouth, said he had also taken part in the demonstrations at Eastney.

"They should be having them turned back to France again. It's a safe country, there's no war in France.

"They want to stop the benefits, stop the free housing... they don't give nothing back to the people of the country."

Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones said: "I'm pleased that today's protests in Portsmouth took place without major issue.

"Thankfully, we didn't see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people's property."

She thanked the officers for their work and their impartial use of the power to ask people to remove face coverings.

News.title: Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
News.content:
Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.

This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.

Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.

They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".

Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.

While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.

Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".

One conference speaker, Grindr CEO George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".

He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology.

"It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said.

"Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"

Anthropic was valued at $965bn (Â£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.

The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements.

In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".

News.title: I never got to experience my baby's scan, but blind parents like me can now feel them
News.content:
When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat.

But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby.

Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme.

At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment.

Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did".

But he said the 20-week scan was more positive.

"The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says.

News.title: Hardened activists are changing tactics and mobilising the anti-migrant vote
News.content:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normandy in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."
