World.title: Chelsea draw with Hull, Liverpool held by Fulham and Villa remain winless
World.content:
Hull nearly claim Premier League win at Chelsea, while Liverpool and Fulham fire blanks, and Aston Villa lose again.

Share Chelsea draw with Hull, Liverpool held by Fulham and Villa remain winless on social media

Hull held free-scoring Chelsea to a 2-2 draw at Stamford Bridge to go third in the Premier League on Saturday as Liverpool failed to find a way past struggling Fulham in a 0-0 draw.

It was a familiar tale for Chelsea as the front three of Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer dazzled, but the Blues were undone by their inability to defend.

In five games against top-flight opposition since Xabi Alonso took charge, Chelsea have scored 16 times and conceded 12.

Hull were the last side in the Premier League to concede, but after three clean sheets, they were finally breached when Rogers drilled in at the near post on seven minutes.

Mohamed Belloumi took advantage of Chelsea’s slackness at the back to blast home on the volley after Jorrel Hato got caught under a cross to the back post.

The Algerian winger then put Hull in front with a deflected strike after Emi Martinez failed to deal with a corner.

Pedro drilled a Palmer cross into the top corner to bring Chelsea level just after the hour mark.

But the home side could not find a winner as Hull’s honeymoon back in the Premier League goes on, with only defending champions Arsenal and Manchester City above them in the table.

Liverpool held as Fulham fight for former Real Madrid boss

Liverpool remain unbeaten under Andoni Iraola, but there were boos at Anfield after Fulham picked up their first point under Alvaro Arbeloa.

Former Liverpool defender Arbeloa was reportedly fighting for his job after losing his first three league matches since arriving in west London from Real Madrid.



Yet a Liverpool forward line featuring three 100 million pounds ($135m) players in Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak failed to click against the Cottagers’ leaky defence.

Indeed, it was Fulham who had the better chances to take all three points as Gonzalo Garcia missed a glorious opportunity in the first half and Alisson Becker produced a brilliant save to deny Josh King the winner.

Liverpool climb to sixth but could find themselves already six points off the top should Arsenal win at Sunderland later on Saturday.

Aston Villa are rooted in the relegation zone after Nottingham Forest exacted revenge with a 2-1 win at Villa Park.

Villa beat their Midlands rivals in the Europa League semifinals last season on their way to lifting a first trophy in 30 years.

Many eyebrows were raised at the reported 45 million pounds ($61m) club record Forest paid Chelsea for Liam Delap after failing to make the grade at Stamford Bridge.

But the striker proved his worth with a long-range shot into the bottom corner to open the scoring.

Alysson levelled with Villa’s first league goal of the season, but Igor Jesus secured Oliver Glasner’s first win as Forest boss.

His old club Crystal Palace’s poor start to the campaign continued with a 3-2 home defeat to Ipswich.

The visitors were aided by Axel Disasi’s first half red card as Zian Flemming’s first goal for the Tractor Boys snatched all three points in stoppage time.

Brentford remain unbeaten, thanks to Kevin Schade’s double in a 2-2 draw at Bournemouth.

The Cherries, by contrast, are yet to win in the Premier League under Marco Rose, despite leading in all four games.

Tottenham are aiming to kick-start their league season with a first goal and win at home to Everton later.

Manchester United host local rivals City in the pick of Sunday’s action.

World.title: Will the Houthi attacks activate the Mecca Pact?
World.content:
If there is a Saudi request, Pakistan and Turkiye will intervene, but direct involvement in the Yemen war is unlikely.

Yemen’s Houthi rebels have captured Mocha port and now threaten to control the main waterway of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. They have also attacked several cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding about 70 people, including women and children.

The repeated attacks against Saudi energy, civil, and defence facilities, combined with the maritime blockage by Iran and its Yemeni partner the Houthis, directly raise the question of the Mecca Pact’s operationalisation between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan.

The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia can activate the mutual defence agreement. If that happens, what could a Pakistani and Turkish intervention look like?

The answer to this question necessitates some crucial background first.

The US – the main security partner of the Gulf states – has signalled for a while now that it expects regional countries to take primary responsibility for their own defence and deterrence, with US help remaining critical but limited.

That posture is already visible on the ground. Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the US has not been able to provide comprehensive defence for its regional partners. On several occasions, it has even failed to stop attacks on its own bases in the Gulf.

With US presence receding and Washington emphasising regional burden-sharing, Gulf states have had to look into a new defence architecture. In September 2025, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed their first mutual defence agreement, which expanded in August this year to include Turkiye and became the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.



The three countries have since established a joint secretariat, with its headquarters in Riyadh, with Pakistan taking the chairmanship for an initial three-year term.

The pact remains in a gestation period. It does not publicly identify the thresholds or scenarios under which a member would move to direct military intervention. Its organisational and institutional structure, including rules of engagement, mechanisms of consultation, and collective defence and deterrence, are yet to be formally developed.

Now, back to the question of how the pact will be operational if a member state is attacked.

Earlier this week, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said that an unprovoked aggression against Saudi Arabia, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into the kingdom, would make the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement operational, adding that “there should be no doubt in this.”

Asif, however, did not share specific details on what shape that operationalisation would take. Last month, Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan clarified that the Mecca Pact would work the same way as NATO: If a member state is attacked, it must actively request and define the specific type of help it needs.

NATO’s Article 4 allows for a member to call alliance consultations and exchange of information. Article 5 requires mutual assistance from allies, but it leaves each state to decide the nature of that assistance.

In 2012, after Syria shot down a Turkish warplane, Ankara invoked Article 4 for consultation and requested specific defence assistance. Instead of demanding direct military intervention, the Turkish government explicitly asked for Patriot missile defence batteries. NATO approved the request and deployed the systems to protect Turkish airspace.

In this context, if the Mecca Pact is to be operationalised, it would have to be Saudi Arabia that defines the type of military assistance and involvement that it needs. If, for example, Riyadh makes an actual request for Pakistani direct military intervention, beyond materiel and intelligence support, Islamabad would be obliged to comply. But the request, and the scale of the response, would still likely need to be defined and agreed in a consultation meeting.

For now, none of this has been tested as Riyadh has not invoked the pact with either Pakistan or Turkiye.

In the meantime, diplomatic efforts have intensified, with Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud talking to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.



Islamabad has also publicly urged Iran to rein in the Houthis from attacking Saudi Arabia and threatening the Bab al-Mandeb, and has reminded Tehran of Pakistan’s commitment to Riyadh’s defence through the pact. Ankara would likely play its own part in diplomatically restraining the Houthis and Iran.

If diplomacy fails and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia or the Bab al-Mandeb continue, Turkiye and Pakistan would likely expand the air and technological support they already provide. Islamabad already has an air squadron of about 16 JF-17 Thunder multirole aircraft, defence systems, and thousands of troops deployed in Saudi Arabia.

But a direct military operation by Pakistani forces inside Yemen remains unlikely at the moment. Given the disastrous and lasting impacts of its participation in the Afghan war against the Soviet Union on behalf of the US, Pakistan would be far more wary of joining a war against Iran and its allies, for fear of spillover into its western border provinces’ economy, domestic security, sectarian balance, and societal harmony. Pakistani leaders would find it hard to build domestic consensus for direct attacks on the Houthis or a fight with Iran.

The likely scenario is that Pakistan would increase joint diplomatic pressure on Iran to restrain the Houthis, further augment its support for Saudi defence, and push for a multinational naval coalition to secure the Bab al-Mandeb. Adopting this restraint would still keep the essence of the Mecca Pact intact, while putting more weight behind regional de-escalation.

The new security architecture that agreements like the Mecca Pact are setting up will take years to mature. Until the mechanisms and rules of collective response develop, Pakistan’s existing bilateral defence relationships with Saudi Arabia and other Arab partners will continue to focus on defence needs.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: DR Congo’s worst Ebola epidemic ever passes 7,000 cases
World.content:
DRC detected the outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo virus in mid-May; nearly 3,400 people have since died.

More than 7,000 Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s (DRC) worst outbreak of the deadly disease, according to figures from Congolese authorities.

The DRC officially detected the latest outbreak in mid-May, but experts suspect it had been spreading under the radar for weeks before.

Of the 7,022 registered cases, 3,398 people have died, according to DRC authorities. Currently, 837 people are in isolation or receiving treatment.

The outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo virus, DRC’s 17th Ebola epidemic, began in the northeastern Ituri province.

It has since spread across conflict-plagued, remote eastern and northern regions where armed groups have roamed for decades, the presence of the state is weak and health infrastructure is largely lacking.

Earlier this week, one case of the disease was confirmed in a seventh province, South-Ubangi, which is in the northwest of the country bordering the Central African Republic and Congo-Brazzaville.

Most of the recorded cases remain in Ituri, where Ebola has been detected in schools in the days after the post-summer holiday return to classes, causing alarm among parents and health workers.

“We are very worried because we don’t know which child comes from which family or what the health status of the members of that family is,” Angele Magani, a mother of a schoolboy in Bunia, Ituri’s provincial capital, told the AFP news agency.

“We are so scared, even though the school authorities reassure us about the health measures that have been put in place,” she added.

Bunia school official Roger Mungimbo told AFP that “there is a mandatory hand-washing system with soap, and we have also done everything possible to have a maximum of 30 pupils per classroom”.



“We regularly make the children aware that they must not touch each other, must not greet each other and must wash their hands regularly,” he added.

Ebola, which has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the last 50 years, is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and can cause severe internal and external bleeding and organ failure.

The world’s deadliest outbreak in West Africa in 2014-2016 was the Zaire Ebola virus. That epidemic killed more than 11,325 people, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

The Bundibugyo strain currently seen in DRC has no approved vaccine or treatment currently, although several potential treatments and vaccines are being tested.

World.title: In Doonbeg, Trump’s Irish Open Visit Prompts Protests and Praise
World.content:
Festive bunting was strung between shops along the tiny main street in Doonbeg, a village on the west coast of Ireland. Temporary signs pointed the way down freshly paved roads toward the nearby Trump International golf resort, where the Irish Open is underway this week. The smell of paint hung in the air.

“If you stood still in the village long enough over the last two months, you would have been painted yourself,” Rita McInerney, a local councilor and lifelong resident, said with a laugh, speaking proudly about Doonbeg’s spruce-up ahead of the tournament. “It’s given us a great opportunity, I suppose, to get a lot done.”

President Trump is attending the tournament on Saturday and Sunday, a moment that will briefly cast the village of around 200 people into the international spotlight.

World.title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down
World.content:
The head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored.

In an essay on Saturday, Dario Amodei said developing AI was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious" and companies and governments must be given time to address them.

Amodei proposed a three-point plan that includes independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation.

There have been growing concerns recently about the technology's potential risks, the most serious of which suggested there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Anthropic previously said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.

But the starkest warning came from two employees from Anthropic's safety team who have resigned in the last two weeks saying humanity may not survive, external the race among AI companies to develop machines that are smarter than humans.

As Amodei's proposal made the rounds, even competitors voiced support for the idea of third-party monitors who could evaluate the safety of models as they are developed.

"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," wrote OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on X. He called independent evaluators "a great idea."

In a new interview with Fortune Magazine, Altman had sounded similar safety concerns, saying standards were "not at a place" to push AI capabilities much further.

He added that he believed AI beyond human control is "absolutely" possible.

Elon Musk meanwhile said the Anthropic boss was "right".

The warnings have prompted calls to action, but US President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".

Some observers have also suggested that Amodei's post may be less about safety than about consolidating control over AI technology.

Cyber-security concerns have grown as new models have exhibited more and more powerful hacking capabilities.

Anthropic withheld its Mythos model from public use when it was announced in April that it could independently escape the testing environment, known as the sandbox.

In the run-up to the release of its most recent Astra model, OpenAI cited cybersecurity concerns as it explained it had paused certain aspects of the model's development.

Safety has also taken centrestage in the rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Amodei, who had previously worked as a vice president at OpenAI, has said he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 so he could build safer and more trusted AI models.

World.title: Saudi Arabia shuts key oil pipeline after drone attack launched from Iraq
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was attacked by drones launched from Iraq, as conflict in the Middle East widens.

Iraq said it had fired a military commander and launched an investigation after admitting the drone attack on its neighbour's East-West pipeline had originated in one of its provinces bordering Iran. Saudi Arabia has previously accused Iran-backed militia in Iraq of targeting its oil facilities.

The 1,200km (745 mile) pipeline has helped Saudi Arabia - the world's largest crude oil exporter - bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

The incident comes amid a major advance by the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, putting more pressure on global oil shipping routes as the US-Iran war stretches into its seventh month.

On Friday, Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the strategic coastal city of Mokha, a day after the Houthis seized control of the entire Red Sea coast.

Riyadh on Friday said it had shut the pipeline as a precaution, as satellite images of scorched ground and smoke near the site emerged.

The foreign ministry said the attack resulted in some injuries and damage, which was still being assessed.

The Saudi pipeline has been moving 4% to 5% of global oil supply, news agency Reuters has reported, citing ship tracking companies and analysts.

Saudi Arabia has chosen not to retaliate at this stage, its foreign ministry says, following a call from Iraq's prime minister.

It said the kingdom would "support the efforts of the Iraqi government" to "prevent attacks" launched from the country against neighbouring states.

World.title: A united Ireland would be 'fantastic' says Trump during Irish visit
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) during a visit in Dublin.

Trump is on a two-day visit to the country where earlier he had a courtesy call with the Irish President Catherine Connolly at the Ãras an UachtarÃ¡in - the official residence of the Irish president.

He attended meetings in Dublin, before travelling to County Clare for the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament.

Trump said a united Ireland would happen eventually and that the Taoiseach was "the right man over here to get it moving".

Meanwhile, more than 10,000 people marched through Dublin to show their opposition to the US president.

During his meeting with MicheÃ¡l Martin at Farmleigh House, in Phoenix Park, Trump said a united Ireland would be a "fantastic thing", and added: "now the UK would have something to say about it obviously but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?"

A spokesperson for Number 10 referred to Prime Minister Andy Burnham's words on Wednesday in the House of Commons that he "will stick to it (the Good Friday Agreement) 100%".

On Wednesday, Burnham added that "the question of a border poll" was for the Northern Ireland secretary "when there is clear consensus in the country - when public opinion has changed to the point at which the call has to be considered".

A spokesperson for Martin said Trump's comments should "come as a surprise to no one" and the US president has been "consistent in his view that he sees unity in Ireland as the optimal outcome".

World.title: French officials investigate if malicious act caused train derailment
World.content:
Officials in northern France are investigating whether the derailment of a passenger train on Friday evening was the result of a malicious act.

"At this stage, the leading theory is that a piece of rail was present on one of the tracks, potentially causing the derailment. The reason for its presence is unknown," prosecutor SÃ©bastien Gallois said on Saturday.

Local media say 186 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.

Forty-four people were treated for injuries, including an 18-year-old woman who was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.

"The train's 'black box' has been seized. Several interviews are scheduled, and a court-appointed expert has been called in," prosecutor Gallois said in a press release.

"The main victim is still in hospital but her life is no longer in danger. The other victims have received care and treatment; they have either been discharged or are about to be."

The Rouen prosecutor's office earlier said the train driver had tested negative for drugs and alcohol.

The train derailed near ClÃ©on, just south of Rouen, shortly before 20:00 (18:00 GMT), and some 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were immediately deployed to the crash scene.

"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, a passenger on the train, told ICI Normandie radio.

"I couldn't stay in my seat anymore. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I'm still shaking," he added.

World.title: Ukraine faces 'toughest winter' since Russia's full-scale invasion, UN official tells BBC
World.content:
De Croo, a former prime minister of Belgium, told the BBC: "This winter is going to be the toughest one since the war".

He said Ukraine started "from a very weak base going into this winter". He added the UN were "very, very worried... about what this winter could become."

The concerns are driven by what De Croo said was Russia's "very systematic" targeting of civilian and energy infrastructure.

"This is petrol stations, it's shopping malls, it's business centres, but it's especially energy infrastructure, energy transmission lines, and so on. There is absolutely no justification for that," he said.

This could lead a "worst-case scenario" where people struggled to access energy to run heating, and water and sewage systems stopped working.

"With the temperatures that you would get here that would lead to circumstances which would be really close to humanitarian catastrophe," De Croo said.

Winter temperatures in Ukraine can drop to -20C.

If power supplies and critical infrastructure were severely damaged it could lead to "quite some human suffering", De Croo said.

Under efforts to prepare Ukraine for winter the UN Development Programme is helping to rebuild parts of its energy system that were damaged last winter. It is also establishing more sustainable and decentralised energy plants, which are less vulnerable to attack.

De Croo said completing the difficult and dangerous work was "almost an impossible task".

"They are reconstructing these sites under constant, constant air alarms. And they know that they are working at a site which is a target," he said. "So you try to reconstruct, but part of your day you can't work because it's just too dangerous."

World.title: Uganda's King Oyo buried amid calls for unity over his successor
World.content:
Uganda's King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, once the world's youngest reigning monarch, was buried on Saturday, days after a row broke out over who would succeed him.

Oyo, 34, who had ruled the traditional kingdom of Tooro in western Uganda since the age of three, died last month while undergoing cancer treatment in the US.

Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. They were abolished in 1967 but restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.

Thousands of mourners lined the streets as the king's casket was transported to the royal tombs in Fort Portal where a private ceremony took place.

Oyo was just a toddler when he was named as Tooro's king and, according to Guinness World Records, was the world's youngest monarch while he reigned.

TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, who was named as the next monarch by clan elders, reportedly cast nine coffee beans into Oyo's grave, a ritual signifying the end of one reign and the start of another.

But days earlier, Oyo's family rejected Kijanangoma, the late monarch's cousin, as Tooro's new king.

Oyo's sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will, written in 2022, naming his young son as his successor.

The boy's identity has never been disclosed.

Meanwhile, his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, said royal guards had been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed. This, she said, restricted the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing it as "house arrest".

On Saturday, the Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kazimba Mugalu, urged unity.

"Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict. It can even destroy the legacy of the king we are mourning," he told mourners.

Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni also called for the matter to be resolved "and to favour unity over division".

The clan overseeing the succession defended its choice of Kijanangoma.

Omusuuga Charles Karumasi, head of the Babiito royal clan, said: "We have done everything in observance of the culture and traditions of Tooro. We must all preserve peace and serenity."

World.title: 'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
World.content:
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.

Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.

"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.

"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.

In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.

She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.

"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.

In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.

Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.

Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.

Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.

He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.

The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.

The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.

Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.

Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.

The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.

World.title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire rises to 76, with more still missing
World.content:
The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 41 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 76.

More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.

The coast guard said on Saturday the number of survivors remained 43, with many receiving treatment in hospital, but 13 people remain unaccounted for.

Recovery of bodies had been hampered due to toxic fumes and lingering heat, which meant authorities were unable to board until Friday.

Geronimo Tuvilla, an official for the Philippine Coast Guard, said the priority was identifying victims and determining the cause of the blaze.

Kristine Ablana, a tourism official in Coron, said relatives were being asked to help identify family members through personal items and DNA testing.

"Once someone is able to verify that this photo or these belongings are indeed those of their relative, they will be asked to provide a DNA sample," she said.

Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the fire began in a cargo hold before spreading.

She said survivors had described hearing a loud explosion, "the appearance of smoke and then fire. It spread very quickly". She added that those who had made it off the ship did not have time to put on lifejackets.

A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.

The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.

Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full co-operation with the inquiry.

World.title: BRICS Summit: Shettima meets with Okonjo-Iweala, reaffirms Nigeria’s support for WTO, multilateralism
World.content:
Nigeria has reaffirmed its commitment to the World Trade Organisation and the multilateral trading system, saying no country can prosper in isolation from the global community.

Specifically, Vice President Kashim Shettima, who restated the nation’s position, assured that Nigeria would continue to support the WTO in strengthening multilateralism and promoting a global system built on cooperation rather than isolation.

Mr Shettima spoke on Saturday during a meeting with the Director-General of WTO, Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, on the sidelines of the ongoing BRICS Leaders’ Summit in New Delhi, India.

“I believe the world is greater than one nation. We will continue to support the WTO in championing the cause of multilateralism. We are essentially one human family and interconnected. You cannot divorce yourself from the global community,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

VP Shettima also made a case for migration as an important driver of development, innovation and economic growth, noting that immigrants have historically contributed to the building of nations and cities across the world.

“Nations are built by immigrants. Even cities are built by people who came from outside, not just by the locals. That goes to show that we have so much to gain from global migration,” he explained.

Citing the Nigerian diaspora as an example, the Nigerian vice president said Nigerians abroad have continued to distinguish themselves through education, enterprise and professional achievement.

“Recent Pew Research Center analysis of 2024 US Census Bureau data showed that 67 per cent of Nigerian-born Black immigrants aged 25 and above in the United States held at least a bachelor’s degree, the highest proportion among the major Black immigrant groups examined,” he stated.

The vice president also commended Mrs Okonjo-Iweala for her leadership of the WTO, urging her to continue deploying her experience in the service of global development.

“You are doing a very wonderful job at the WTO, but you still have a lot to contribute to humanity,” he told the WTO DG.

Mrs Okonjo-Iweala, the first woman and first African to head the WTO, began her second four-year term as Director-General in September 2025.

Meanwhile, Vice President Shettima will tomorrow, Sunday, present Nigeria’s partnership and foreign investment opportunities when he speaks to leaders of the BRICS alliance at the ongoing summit themed, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”

While seeking a more inclusive international order, the vice president will reiterate the objective of President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda to create sustainable opportunities for its people through reforms, the expansion of infrastructure, and the promotion of private-sector-led growth.

Stanley Nkwocha

World.title: Gateway Air ready to airlift Hajj pilgrims — Gov Abiodun
World.content:
Ogun State Governor, Prince Dapo Abiodun, has expressed the readiness of Gateway Air, the state-owned airline, to airlift not only Ogun pilgrims to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for Hajj, but also intending pilgrims from other South-West states.

The governor said Ogun would explore opportunities to participate in the emerging private-sector-driven Hajj airlift arrangement, particularly for pilgrims from Oyo, Osun, Ondo and Ekiti states.

Abiodun disclosed this on Friday when he received a delegation of the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria (NAHCON), led by its Commissioner of Operations, Anofiu Elegushi, at his office.

The governor said the state government had taken note of the new regulations governing private-sector participation in Hajj operations, while commending NAHCON for its support towards ensuring the successful and safe airlift of Ogun pilgrims from the Gateway International Airport to Saudi Arabia during the last Hajj exercise.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the state had always expressed its desire to charter an aircraft under the Gateway Air brand to airlift its pilgrims directly from the Gateway International Airport.

“We had always expressed interest that, based on what we saw last time, we would like to charter our own aircraft. We would like to brand it Gateway Air, and we would like to airlift our pilgrims ourselves because we believe that we can do it efficiently.

“The same level of efficiency that we demonstrated in building a world-class airport and also in establishing a world-class airline, Gateway Air, shows that we know how to do things and organise ourselves in Ogun State.

“The motivation and collaboration that we enjoyed with NAHCON was commendable and exemplary.

“For us, it was about facilitating our pilgrims to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia conveniently. We have invested in a world-class airport, and we thought there was no better way for our citizens to begin to enjoy that airport than for our pilgrims to board their flights from that airport.

“It was quite a challenge, but you held our hands and we both navigated through all the bumps and, at the end of the day, everything went very well,” he said.

While thanking NAHCON for sharing with the state government the new Hajj regulations released by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Abiodun said the early commencement of registration for the next Hajj exercise demonstrated the level of preparedness and organisation of the commission.

Speaking on religious harmony in Ogun, Governor Abiodun said the state had remained peaceful and had not witnessed any religious crisis under his administration.

He attributed this to the harmonious relationship among the people of the state, irrespective of their religious affiliations.

Abiodun also welcomed NAHCON’s suggestion that South-West states should come together to establish a single body, similar to the Oodua Investment structure, that could serve as a private representative for the participating states and coordinate Hajj operations on their behalf.

He said he would present the proposal to other members of the Oodua Investment Group for consideration.

Earlier, the NAHCON Commissioner of Operations, Mr Anofiu Elegushi, said the commission had commenced registration for the forthcoming Hajj exercise, adding that the registration deadline, which was initially expected to close on Friday, would be extended to accommodate more intending pilgrims.

Elegushi explained that the early commencement of registration was necessitated by the need to provide the Saudi Arabian authorities with accurate figures of intending pilgrims ahead of the exercise.

“The reason for this early registration is because Saudi Arabia wants to know the number of pilgrims in time so that they can prepare for the number and have enough preparation for the number the commission will be bringing for the Hajj operation.

“The portal has been shut now, but by the grace of God, before the end of today, the portal will be reopened for the registration process.

“We have also noticed that the slots are inadequate. We are also working on that to make sure we get more slots so that we have more pilgrims on board,” he said.

Elegushi congratulated the Ogun State Government on what he described as a landmark achievement in ensuring that the first batch of Ogun pilgrims travelled directly from the Gateway International Airport to Saudi Arabia.

He said the feat would remain significant in the history of Ogun State and the entire South-West.

According to him, Saudi Arabia had traditionally allocated about 95,000 Hajj slots to Nigeria, but the quota had gradually dropped to 50,000, with 10,000 allocated to tour operators and the remaining 40,000 shared among the states.

He said the development was linked to Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, under which the Kingdom was seeking greater private-sector participation and digitalisation of Hajj and Umrah operations.

Elegushi disclosed that NAHCON also undertakes pre-Hajj visits to Saudi Arabia, during which states are expected to identify accommodation facilities, contractors and service providers for their pilgrims.

He said the Kingdom had initially indicated that 98 percent of the Hajj quota would be allocated to private operators, leaving two percent for government operations.

This, he explained, prompted NAHCON to encourage the states to begin considering the privatisation of their Hajj operations and participate as private operators capable of competing with other operators in the country.

He, however, said one of the major challenges was the requirement by the Saudi authorities that any company seeking to operate independently must have a minimum of 2,000 pilgrims.

According to him, even Lagos State currently does not have the required number of pilgrims, making it difficult for individual states in the South-West to meet the requirement.

Elegushi said NAHCON had consequently considered the possibility of establishing a single South-West company, similar to the Oodua Investment structure, which would pool pilgrims from the participating states and meet the Saudi requirement.

The Commissioner urged Governor Abiodun to ensure that Ogun State also succeeds in using Gateway Air to airlift its pilgrims, just as the state successfully used the Gateway International Airport to airlift pilgrims during the last Hajj exercise.

He disclosed that payment for the forthcoming Hajj was still ongoing, with all payments expected to be completed by December 2, 2026.

He added that the uploading of pilgrims’ data would close ahead of the commencement of the airlift, which is expected to begin around the end of April or early May.

Elegushi further disclosed that the Saudi Arabian authorities had introduced about nine new health-related policies, including the screening of intending pilgrims for nine specified diseases before they are cleared for the pilgrimage.

He commended the Ogun State Government for its compliance with health protocols during the last Hajj exercise, urging the state to sustain its support and ensure that no default is recorded among its pilgrims during the forthcoming exercise.

World.title: Oluremi Tinubu’s N10m gift and the power of purposeful philanthropy, By Kayode Akinmade
World.content:
Sometimes, the future of a nation does not arrive with the noise of a grand ceremony. It announces itself quietly—in a classroom, on a football field, inside a workshop, behind a computer screen or on the pages of a child’s sketchbook.

And sometimes, all that future needs is for someone to notice.

The tragedy is not always that talent is absent. More often, it is that talent exists but remains unseen, unsupported and eventually extinguished by circumstances. This is why the story of 12-year-old Ogun State artist, Master Morenikeji Ebunoluwa Joshua, deserves more than passing applause. It deserves to be told, celebrated and, more importantly, understood as a lesson in what purposeful philanthropy can achieve.

On 18 August 2026, at the launch of the South-West Zonal National Food Bank Programme at the Cultural Centre, Kuto, Abeokuta, young Joshua displayed a portrait he had painstakingly painted of the First Lady of Nigeria, Senator Oluremi Tinubu.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The painting caught her attention.

But beyond the portrait was a child with an extraordinary gift—and the First Lady did something that can sometimes be as powerful as the gift itself: she stopped to see him.

She invited the young artist to the podium and pledged ₦10 million towards his education.

Less than a month later, that pledge has become a reality.

The First Lady has fulfilled her promise through the establishment of an Education Development Trust Fund to support Joshua through tertiary education, with an account specifically opened to preserve the fund for his educational needs.

That is the difference between a promise that generates applause and a promise that changes a life.

The significance of the gesture therefore lies not merely in the ₦10 million involved. It lies in the speed, structure and purpose with which the promise was fulfilled.

In a society where public pledges can sometimes fade with the applause that greeted them, Senator Tinubu has demonstrated that compassion acquires its fullest meaning when intention is followed by action.

A promise made to a child is not merely a ceremonial statement.

It is a moral obligation.

There is, however, another important dimension to Joshua’s story.

His journey of recognition did not begin on that August afternoon. Three years earlier, Ogun State Governor, Prince Dapo Abiodun, had encountered Joshua’s work at an exhibition. Upon learning that the talented artist was still in primary school, the Governor awarded him a scholarship covering his primary and secondary education.

That intervention created the first bridge between talent and opportunity.

The First Lady’s intervention has now extended that bridge to tertiary education. This is how a chain of public good is built.

One person identifies a gift. Another strengthens it. An institution provides structure. And a child who might otherwise have been constrained by circumstance is given the confidence and opportunity to imagine a much larger future.

Governor Abiodun deserves commendation for recognising Joshua early and investing in his education. Senator Tinubu deserves equal commendation for seeing the same promise, responding generously and, most importantly, keeping her word.

There is something profound about that sequence. It tells a child that his talent matters. It tells him that his circumstances do not have to define his destiny.

And perhaps most importantly, it tells him that society has not forgotten him. That is the deeper meaning of purposeful philanthropy.

We must therefore resist the temptation to treat Joshua’s story as merely a heart-warming episode to be admired today and forgotten tomorrow.

Nigeria is filled with Joshuas.

They are in classrooms in rural communities. They are in crowded neighbourhoods and underserved schools. They are on football pitches, in music studios, at roadside workshops and behind improvised computers. They are young inventors without tools, brilliant pupils without school fees, athletes without equipment, musicians without instruments, artists without materials and exceptional children whose potential is constantly threatened by circumstances beyond their control.

Their greatest disadvantage may not be a lack of ability. It may simply be that nobody has seen them. Or that someone saw them but did nothing.

Purposeful philanthropy changes that equation.

It is not the random distribution of money. It is the deliberate conversion of private means into public hope. It identifies genuine need, recognises measurable potential and creates a structure that allows the beneficiary to grow with dignity.

The Education Development Trust Fund created for Joshua is particularly instructive because it goes beyond an immediate cash gift. It creates a mechanism for preserving the intervention and directing it towards a sustainable outcome.

A cheque may open a door.

But education, mentoring, monitoring and sustained encouragement help a young person walk through that door and discover what lies beyond it.

Not everyone can give ₦10 million.

But everyone who has been blessed with some measure of influence, knowledge, access or resources can do something.

One person can pay a child’s WAEC or JAMB fees. A business can equip a school laboratory or sponsor vocational training. A lawyer, doctor, engineer, artist or retired public officer can mentor a promising young person. Alumni associations can establish scholarship funds. Religious organisations can support indigent families. Nigerians in the diaspora can adopt schools, clinics or community projects.

Sometimes, it does not even require money. A word of encouragement. A lesson. A referral. A useful introduction. An opportunity to exhibit a talent.

The opening of one door can change the trajectory of an entire life.

Corporate organisations, too, should move beyond occasional publicity-driven donations and make talent development a more serious component of their social responsibility. Traditional rulers, political leaders, professionals, philanthropists and community associations can establish credible platforms for identifying exceptional children and connecting them with sponsors.

Imagine the possibilities if every prosperous Nigerian deliberately supported one deserving child. Imagine the impact if every successful professional mentored one young person.

Imagine what could happen if every viable institution adopted one school, one community project or one talent-development initiative.

The cumulative effect would be enormous.

This is where philanthropy transcends charity and becomes nation-building. There is also a security dimension to this conversation.

A society that gives its young people education, recognition, dignity and a legitimate path to achievement strengthens their sense of belonging. It reduces the despair and hopelessness that can make vulnerable young minds susceptible to crime, substance abuse, extremism and other forms of exploitation.

Every properly supported child is therefore more than a life improved. It is resilience added to society. It is one less young mind abandoned to despair. It is one more citizen equipped to contribute meaningfully to the future.

Philanthropy, of course, cannot replace government. Government retains the primary responsibility for education, healthcare, welfare and equal opportunity.

But philanthropy can complement public policy by responding quickly, personally and creatively to individual circumstances that may require special intervention.

The most powerful results often occur when government, private citizens and institutions reinforce one another.

Joshua’s story offers a beautiful example.

Governor Abiodun recognised the talent and provided the educational foundation. Senator Tinubu encountered the young artist, recognised his promise and extended the intervention into the tertiary years. The result is not simply two acts of generosity.

It is a continuum of opportunity.

And that may ultimately be the greatest gift of all. The portrait painted by young Joshua captured a face.

The generosity it inspired may now help redraw his future.

There is poetry in that.

A child picked up a brush to paint a portrait, and in the process, painted a new chapter of his own life.

That is the enduring power of philanthropy.

It sees possibility where others may see only need. It recognises potential before the world has fully discovered it. And it converts privilege into opportunity for another human being.

Senator Oluremi Tinubu has lifted one gifted child. Her example can inspire the lifting of thousands more. Let those who have means look around their communities. Let them find a Joshua waiting to be seen.

A dream waiting to be protected. A talent waiting for encouragement. A life waiting for one decisive intervention.

Because when generosity is joined with discernment, structure and fidelity to promise, philanthropy becomes more than charity.

It becomes an investment in human potential.

And when human potential is deliberately nurtured, a nation does not merely help one child to succeed. It helps build the future.

Akinmade is the Special Adviser to the Ogun State Governor on Information and Strategy

World.title: Pay compensation for school takeover or lose it, court tells Akwa Ibom govt
World.content:
An Akwa Ibom State High Court in Uyo has given the state government three months to “assess and pay adequate compensation” for taking over a private school or return it to its original owners.

Justice A. Archibong gave the order in a judgement delivered on 14 July 2026.

The case was instituted on 8 August 2022 by five children, including Samuel Ebong, who sued as children and beneficiaries of the estate of late John Ebong, whose school, Christian Secondary School, Afia Etoi, was taken over by the then Cross River State Government in 1977.

Akwa Ibom State Government inherited the school following its creation from Cross River State in 1987.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Akwa Ibom State Secondary Education Board and Akwa Ibom State Government were the 1st and 2nd defendants in the suit, respectively.

The school, one of the most populated in Akwa Ibom State, is located off Oron Road in Uyo, close to Uyo High School, another major public secondary school in the city.

According to the court papers reviewed by PREMIUM TIMES, the state government has a little over a month left to comply or appeal the judgement, failing which the school could face an uncertain future if the plaintiffs enforce the repossession order.

Court affirms owners’ right to compensation

The plaintiffs — Samuel Ebong, Ekong Ebong, Moses Ebong, Blessing Ebong and Peace Ebong — told the court that their late father founded and operated Christian Secondary School in 1972 with his private funds.

They said the then Cross River State Government compulsorily acquired and took over the school in 1977.

The plaintiffs argued that the government failed to assess and pay compensation for the acquisition, despite their father’s repeated demands.

In its judgement, the court held that the relevant laws preserved and guaranteed the right of the school’s owner to compensation.

Justice Archibong also declared that the plaintiffs were entitled under the law to adequate compensation for the acquisition, takeover and operation of the school.

“That the plaintiffs are entitled under section 13(5) of Education Law, Cap. 44 Laws of Akwa Ibom State of Nigeria, 2000 to be paid adequate compensation for the acquisition, taking over and operation of Christian Secondary School, Afia Etoi, by the 1st and 2nd defendants,” the court ruled.

Plaintiffs demanded N430m compensation, N1.57bn interest

The plaintiffs had asked the court to order the state government to pay N430.49 million as compensation, based on a valuation report dated 29 September 2017 by Godwin Timothy & Co., an estate surveyors and valuers firm.

They also sought N1.569 billion in interest on what they described as arrears of unpaid compensation.

But the court did not grant the specific monetary claims.

Instead, Justice Archibong rejected the plaintiffs’ claims for the specific N430.49 million compensation and N1.569 billion interest.

The court, however, ordered that adequate compensation be assessed and paid.

Government acknowledged unpaid compensation

The plaintiffs said their father had demanded compensation from the Cross River State Government after the 1977 takeover.

According to the affidavit supporting the suit, the government acknowledged the claim in a letter dated 11 July 1978.

They said negotiations subsequently commenced but were not concluded before their father became ill and died on 9 June 2016.

Following his death, his children renewed the demand for compensation, writing to the Akwa Ibom State Government through the commissioner for education on 14 December 2016.

They said the commissioner responded in a letter dated 22 December 2016, admitting the non-payment and recommending compensation.

The plaintiffs further said the Akwa Ibom State Secondary Education Board acknowledged the outstanding claim in a letter dated 14 August 2017.

They later commissioned Godwin Timothy & Co to value the school’s assets, resulting in the N430.49 million valuation.

They told the court that compensation had remained unpaid despite the correspondence and valuation.

School could return to family

The court gave the government three months from the date of judgement to “assess and pay adequate compensation”.

Failure to do so, the court said, would entitle the plaintiffs to repossess the school.

“That the plaintiffs are entitled to re-possess the school, the subject matter of this suit; if the 2nd defendant fails to assess and pay adequate compensation for the acquisition, take-over and operation of the school within three months from the date of this judgment,” Justice Archibong ordered.

“That at the expiration of the said three months from the date of this judgement, if the 2nd defendant fails to assess and pay adequate compensation to the plaintiffs for the acquisition, take-over and operation of the school, the 2nd defendant shall, by an order of perpetual injunction, hereby be restrained by herself or her agents from further use and operation of the school, the subject matter of the suit,” the court stated.

The judgement therefore leaves the state government with a crucial decision: comply with the court’s order, pursue an appeal, or risk losing a school serving thousands of students.

The lead lawyer for the plaintiffs, Ndifreke Akpan, told PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday that the state government has not contacted them to state whether they are going to comply with or appeal the judgement.

“We had to contact the state government, asking it to comply with the judgement. At the moment, we’ve not been served with any notice of appeal,” Mr Akpan said.

The Akwa Ibom State Attorney General and Commissioner for Justice, Uko Udom, did not respond to calls seeking his reaction.

Mr Udom, a senior advocate of Nigeria, also did not respond to a question sent to his WhatsApp account asking whether the state government would comply with the judgement or appeal it.

World.title: Court remands man over alleged kidnapping, armed robbery in Edo
World.content:
A Benin High Court on Friday ordered the remand of one Haruna Ayuba, 30, in a correctional centre over alleged kidnapping and armed robbery in Akoko-Edo Local Government Area of Edo State.

The order followed an ex parte motion filed by the police prosecutor, Polycap Odion, of the Directorate of Legal Services at the police command in Edo.

Mr Odion prayed the court to remand the suspect in a correctional centre for an initial period of 14 days, pending legal advice from the State Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP).

He told the court that the suspect and another person, who is still at large, allegedly committed the offences on 6 July at Igue Farm Road, near Igarra, within the Auchi Division.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, the defendant allegedly conspired to kidnap Atorugh Simeon and Mary Godwin.

The prosecution further alleged that the suspect kidnapped the victims and robbed them of N15,000 in cash and foodstuffs valued at N40,000, while armed with guns and other dangerous weapons.

Mr Odion said the defendant was facing a five-count charge of kidnapping, armed robbery and conspiracy.

He said the alleged offences contravened Section 412(2) of the Criminal Law of Edo, 2022; Section 3 of the Edo Kidnapping Prohibition (Amendment) Law, 2025; and Section 1(2)(a) of the Robbery and Firearms (Special Provisions) Act, Cap. R11, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004.

The judge, Terry Momodu, granted the prosecution’s prayer and ordered that the suspect be remanded in a correctional centre for an initial period of 14 days, pending legal advice from the state DPP.

Justice Momodu subsequently adjourned the case till 25 September.

World.title: Xenophobia: Over 30 Nigerians killed by South African police since 2022 – Ambassador
World.content:
Over 30 Nigerians have been killed by the South African police in the last four years, the Nigerian Ambassador to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, says.

In a Facebook post on Friday night, Mr Fani-Kayode said there was a growing pattern of the South African Police Service and the South African Defence Force officials subjecting Nigerians residing in the country to abuse that sometimes results in deaths.

He also estimated that over 100 Nigerian nationals have been killed within the same timeframe, including eight in 2026.

“No less than 4 amongst the 8 were murdered by South African police officers.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Outside of that over 100 Nigerian nationals have been murdered in South Africa between 2022 and today and over 30 of them were killed by officers of the South African Police Service and South African Defence Force.

“Nigeria’s patience is running thin,” he declared.

The post followed the announcement of the death of two more Nigerians, which Mr Fani-Kayode said raised the number of Nigerians killed in 2026 alone to eight.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the latest victims, identified as James Nwankwo and Taiwo Fakunle, were murdered last weekend.

The Nigerian Consulate in Johannesburg provided an account of their murder earlier on Friday. Mr Nwankwo was reportedly killed by officials of the South African Police Service (SAPS) in Somerset West, Cape Town, on the 5th of September.

He is the latest Nigerian to be killed allegedly by the South African Police Service since April, when the latest wave of xenophobic violence began.

Mr Fani-Kayode said Mr James “died as a consequence of what has been described as gruesome interrogation techniques by the South African police.”

The other Nigerian, identified as Taiwo Fakunle, was shot on 4 September at his residence in Johannesburg.

“After issuing a series of threats, his killers went to his home and shot him dead,” Mr Fani-Koyode said, describing the victim as a bishop.

His killers are yet to be identified.

“What is most disturbing is the fact that despite our constant expressions of concern about this disturbing state of affairs, not one person has been arrested, detained, prosecuted or brought to justice for ANY of these heinous crimes. This is unacceptable,” the ambassador noted.

New deadline for foreigners

Mr Fani-Kayode also disclosed that a new deadline has been set for black foreigners in South Africa to leave the country.

An arbitrary deadline of 30 June was issued earlier. This paper reported that the deadline had intensified tension as South Africans marched in droves across cities to protest the presence of African migrants in the country.

The new deadline, like the last one, was issued by “brazenly racist, xenophobic and Afrophobic” groups, according to Mr Fani-Kayode.

He also stated that these groups have openly threatened to target and harm Nigerians and other African foreigners if their “illegal deadline is not complied with.”

“The Nigerian community in South Africa is deeply disturbed by these developments and lives in trepidation of what could happen next. So is the Nigerian Mission in South Africa,” he said further.

Mr Fani-Kayode demanded that the South African government step up to protect African foreigners from the excesses of the xenophobic groups and their misguided members.

He asked the government to “apply the full weight of the law against them for their lawless behaviour.”

He warned of potential consequences if the “vicious cycle of discrimination against and killing” is allowed to continue.

“South Africans are not targeted and killed in Nigeria by our people or our security forces.

“The least the South African Government can do is to reciprocate this gesture, protect our nationals and address our legitimate concerns,” he said.

The xenophobic attacks in South Africa have led to the exodus of thousands of Africans from the country. Countries that have repatriated many of their citizens include Nigeria, Ghana, Zimbabwe and Malawi.

World.title: The United Nations fail the Sahrawi, Africans must defend them, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
Given the duplicity in the UNSC, it is left for freedom-loving countries, peoples, groups and persons, to rise to the defence of the Sahrawi. In particular, Nigeria and South Africa have the duty to team up with Algeria and lead Africans to defend our brothers and sisters in Western Sahara.

The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) meets at the end of October on the future of Western Sahara. The emerging consensus in the 15-member body is not to renew the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), which expires on 31 October. Since the main objective of MINURSO is to organise a referendum on the Sahrawi demand for independence, this technically would mean handing over the founding member of the African Union (AU) to Morocco.

This itself would be in furtherance of the UNSC 31 October, 2025 Resolution 2797, which told the parties to engage in “unconditional talks, based on Morocco’s autonomy proposal.” The Moroccan proposal is to grant Western Sahara “semi-autonomy” under its 27-year monarchical ruler, King Mohammed VI. But for international pressure and how to explain to the African continent why one of its sovereign states is to be handed over to a dictatorship, the UNSC might have taken more retrogressive steps. The Sahrawi, before the UNSC, is like a chick pleading its case before a panel with two-thirds composed of hawks.

Eleven of the fifteen members of the UNSC are already committed to Morocco and its recolonisation agenda. Only Latvia, China, Pakistan and Russia are maintaining neutrality in the UNSC. The other eleven countries are in support of the dubious Moroccan plan.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But the Western Sahara issue is a straight forward one of a peoples’ right to decolonisation. It was colonised by Spain in 1884. Then the United Nations Resolution 1514 of 1960 declared the right of all colonised peoples to decide their future. On this basis, many countries gained independence.

However, in the case of Western Sahara, rather than decolonise, between 1975 and 1976 Spain handed it to two of its neighbours – Mauritania and Morocco. After armed struggle, the former withdrew and the latter seized more of the territories on the basis that Western Sahara was its pre-colonial territory. The UN referred the matter to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which found the Moroccan claims to be false. The UNSC, on 29 April, 1991, under Resolution 690, established MINURSO to organise a referendum in Western Sahara, which would enable the Sahrawi determine their future.

Morocco has since then rejected the UN resolution. But rather than insist on this, the European Union, the US, and their allies want to impose Moroccan autocratic rule on the Sahrawi.

UNSC member, the US, relying on its own national constitution, on 10 December, 2020 gifted Western Sahara, which it never owned, to Morocco. On that Day, an Executive Order was issued stating: “I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, do hereby proclaim that, the United States recognizes that the entire Western Sahara territory is part of the Kingdom of Morocco.” Morocco was ecstatic about the gift. But if in truth Western Sahara were owned by Morocco, why would it be excited that the US offered it as a gift?

A second UNSC member is Colombia. The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella declared that with effect from 7 August, 2026: “Colombia recognises Morocco’s sovereignty over all its territory, including Western Sahara.”

Bahrain, a third member, in February, sent its Foreign Minister, Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani to the occupied Western Sahara city of Laayoune and declared support for Morocco.

Denmark, which usually claims to be liberal, supports the recolonisation of Western Sahara. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen proclaimed the Moroccan plan as “credible” and a “serious and essential contribution to the ongoing UN process.” The country claims that the Moroccan takeover plan is a “good basis for a mutually agreed solution by all parties.”

Greece, a supposed neutral member of the UNSC, on 7 September flaunted its support for the recolonisation of the Sahrawi. Its Foreign Minister, George Gerapetritis, declared in Athens that this was the only solution to the Western Saharan Question. Greece, which claims to be the mother of democracy, argues that a plan that hands over Western Sahara to a monarchical dictatorship is the just solution. Greece, once ruled by fascists, added a ridiculous condition; that its support for the renewal of the MINURSO mandate will be conditioned on the acceptance of the Moroccan recolonisation plan.

Panama is a republic with a history of kowtowing to other countries. So, it was not surprising when in May its Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Arturo Hueyos Boyd flew to Rabat to pledge the support of his country to Morocco’s expansionism. He added the ridiculous declaration that his country’s embassy in Morocco would now extend its reach to Western Sahara.

What may be most tragic for Africa is that its three countries on the UNSC have also joined the West in the League of Re-colonisation Countries (LRC). Liberia and Ethiopia are the only two countries in the continent that were never colonised. It is therefore perplexing that Liberia would, in the UNSC, back the recolonisation of a fellow African country with which its seats in the hallowed chambers of the AU. In January, 2025, its Minister of Foreign Affairs, Sara Beysolow Nyanti, in violation of AU rules, illegally flew into Western Sahara to declare support for the Moroccan annexation.

One of the most duplicitous positions on this issue is that of the virtually failed state of Somalia. Its President, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, on 10 November, 2025, flew to Algeria and promised to stand by that country’s principled position on the fundamental human right of the Sahrawi to determine their future. Some days later, its Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali popped up in Rabat to back Morocco. In one of the most ridiculous diplomatic denials, the Somali Presidency claimed it learnt of its Foreign Minister’s Rabat outing in the Moroccan press. But it neither denounced him nor repudiated the agreement he signed with the Moroccans.

In April, 2025, a Memorandum of Understanding was signed between Western Sahara and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) on Sahrawi independence. SADC member, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is the third African member of the UNSC, denounced it. The DRC Foreign Ministry declared: “The MoU signed is not a binding document and therefore the Democratic Republic of Congo remains sovereign on this issue…the Congolese government defends the position of the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Morocco over Western Sahara.”

Given the duplicity in the UNSC, it is left for freedom-loving countries, peoples, groups and persons, to rise to the defence of the Sahrawi. In particular, Nigeria and South Africa have the duty to team up with Algeria and lead Africans to defend our brothers and sisters in Western Sahara.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: Haske joins APM, sets sight on a new Adamawa
World.content:
Determined to chart a new course for Adamawa State, businessman and politician, Hon Abdulrahman Haske, has on Saturday 12 September officially announced his membership resignation from the All Progressives Party (APC) and formally joined the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) as its governorship candidate, declaring his readiness to leverage APM’s progressive platform and growing grassroots momentum to deliver transformational governance and unlock the state’s vast economic and human potential.

The official declaration, attended by party leaders, stakeholders, traditional and community leaders, youth and women groups, loyalists, and supporters from all 21 Local Government Areas (LGAs) of Adamawa State. A statement on Saturday by Abdulgaffar Ahmed, Publicity Secretary for Abdulrahman Haske said the event marked the beginning of what Haske described as a renewed political movement anchored on principle, service, and the aspirations of the people.

Addressing party faithful and supporters, Haske said his decision to join the APM was informed by his conviction that the party offers the most credible platform to advance a people-centred development agenda and build a more prosperous, inclusive and secure Adamawa.

According to him, the decision represents “a convergence of principle and purpose” and underscores his commitment to accountable leadership, economic empowerment, youth inclusion, social development and sustainable growth.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Today is not merely about joining a political party; it is about strengthening a movement dedicated to the future of Adamawa State. Our objective remains clear: to build a state where governance works for the people, where young people have opportunities to succeed, where communities are connected to development, and where public resources are managed transparently for the common good,” Haske said.

The APM governorship candidate noted that the overwhelming support his movement continues to enjoy across the state has reinforced his belief that Adamawa is ready for a fresh approach to leadership. He pledged to mobilise citizens behind a development agenda focused on agriculture, infrastructure, education, healthcare, economic empowerment, security and accountable governance.

Haske also expressed profound appreciation to the leadership of the APM for the confidence reposed in him, particularly the National Chairman, the National Working Committee and the Adamawa State chapter of the party.

“I am deeply grateful to the leadership of the Allied Peoples Movement for their belief in our shared vision and for entrusting me with the responsibility of carrying the party’s flag in the 2027 governorship election. I accept this mandate with humility and an unwavering determination to justify this confidence through integrity, hard work and dedicated service to the people of Adamawa State,” he stated.

Speaking at the event, the National Chairman of APM, Yusuf Mamman Dantalle, described Haske as a leader whose political philosophy aligns closely with the party’s progressive ideals and commitment to people-centred governance.

According to Dantalle, the party’s decision to support Haske was informed by his demonstrated commitment to development, youth empowerment, inclusive leadership and social impact.

“After extensive consultations, we are convinced that Abdulrahman Haske embodies the values and principles for which the Allied Peoples Movement stands. His belief in empowering ordinary citizens, promoting inclusive development and building stronger communities aligns perfectly with our progressive vision. We are confident that he possesses the leadership capacity, credibility and energy required to offer Adamawa a compelling alternative in 2027,”Dantalle said.

Also speaking, the Adamawa State Chairman of APM, Hon Badejo Bello, said the party was proud to welcome and present Haske as its governorship candidate, describing him as a bridgebuilder with a clear understanding of the developmental challenges and opportunities facing the state.

“Hon Abdulrahman Haske represents the kind of leadership that resonates with the aspirations of our people. His vision, record of service and commitment to inclusive development are fully aligned with the progressive direction of our party. We are confident that under his leadership, APM will provide a platform for genuine transformation, renewed hope and sustainable progress for the people of Adamawa State,” Bello said.

The declaration ceremony concluded with a call for unity among party members and supporters as stakeholders pledged to work collectively towards building a stronger political movement ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

With enthusiastic participation from supporters across all 21 local government areas, the event underscored the growing momentum behind Haske’s candidature and reinforced APM’s determination to provide a credible and formidable platform for transformational leadership in Adamawa State.
