The world's leading Palestinian writer, Raja Shehadeh, has been on a mission to save his most personal work: his diaries.

The award-winning author of more than 20 books has been documenting decades of Palestinian life, starting in 1967 at the very beginning of Israel's occupation of the West Bank when he was a teenager.

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh

His diaries capture a unique voice and front row view of history: his meetings with world leaders, his work as a human rights lawyer, and his role as legal advisor to the Palestinians during peace talks with Israel.

Shehadeh, now 75, feared his diaries and archives — kept in his garage in the West Bank city of Ramallah — were at risk of destruction from Israeli military operations. (The Israeli foreign ministry did not respond to requests for comment about Shehadeh's fears.)

toggle caption Hannah Harper



So he took part in a two-year, discreet effort to spirit them to Scotland, where he has spent many summers. The archives are now at the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Exeter in England has published thousands of pages online .

Sponsor Message

Shehadeh spoke with NPR's Daniel Estrin about his decades of diary writing, and the secret effort to preserve his archives.

The interview text below has been edited for length and clarity.

How keeping a diary consistently for so long impacted who he is as a writer

It's been a daily effort...in order to understand better what is happening around me, in order to record and document what is happening. I started when I was...fifteen years old, just before the occupation. It has been a very good discipline because it helped me understand myself and what's happening around me...I was feeling that we are entering into a historic period that needs to be documented. So I went about writing everything down that was happening and preserving whatever I could preserve.

Excerpts from Shehadeh's diary during Israel's invasion of Ramallah at the height of the Palestinian Intifada in 2002

April 2, 2002

Last night was very noisy. I was awakened many times from the sound of the bombing and shooting ...

My mood was not good today. I just got too many telephones. The problem then became that the news spread that my spirits (so it was interpreted are down) so I got more calls from those who thought it is their duty to call me to help raise my morale ...

I am beginning to feel like a prisoner in the house, in solitary confinement ... I am thinking of exercising by pacing around the house ...

Then Samer called to say: now they have lifted the curfew ... I was glad to lift the garage door and to turn my car on ... There was absolutely no one on the street. There was dirt and stones and wind and fog but no cars ...

I continued driving up to the center and then saw two big tanks- how big they look, like elephants in a zoo where they don't belong, parked by our office blocking the street entirely ...

The satellite stations show the suffering of the Palestinians like a soap opera ... [Palestinian leader Yaser] Arafat is a rebel rouser. He is now very popular and he dramatizes everything. The Palestinians rather than be a force of change are a source of drama and emotionalism throughout the arab world ...

On Shehadeh's anger at Palestinian leaders for signing a peace accord in the 1990s that didn't stop Israeli settlement expansion

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh

My diaries after that point showed a great anger which I was glad I didn't publish. I mean, it was good that I put all my frustration and anger in the diaries because otherwise I would not have been able to live in Palestine because I was so angry and so frustrated by the leadership and so critical of it. And so the diary played an important role in helping me vent that frustration without getting myself into trouble.

Sponsor Message

The leadership...didn't realize that the settlements were the disastrous thing and that they had to be stopped, and no agreement should happen without all settlement activities stopped, and they didn't do that.

On his diary entries documenting Israel's expanding control of the West Bank

I started recording the changes in the geography and in the roads and in the landscape and in the effect of the settlements. I used to walk a lot in the West Bank hills, and after the walks, I would record what I saw and how I felt and how the land looked.

I was so confused by what was happening and so wanting to understand it, and so writing it helped me understand it. I had my own way and my own nonconformity. And so describing my world in words helped me grasp it better.

Shehadeh's fear for the safety of his archives due to Israeli military operations

toggle caption Mariana Cook

I n the Nakba (the Arabic word for "catastrophe," commonly used to refer to the displacement and dispossession of Palestinians when Israel was established) in 1948, they destroyed so many of the journals and private papers of Palestinians, and they were never found again. And then in 1982 in Lebanon, in Beirut, they went to the Palestine Research Center and took all the papers and all the journals and everything there and destroyed it. And in 2002, in the re-invasion of Ramallah, they went into so many homes and destroyed the private papers and everything. And so I was worried that they would do the same for me.

In 2023, with the Gaza war and the destruction of so much of the archives in Gaza, I became really worried and thought that I must do something to preserve these diaries. I kept the diaries in the garage. If the soldiers, as they did once, (would) enter my house, go to the garage and see them, they would just throw them all over the place and maybe set fire to them.

Sponsor Message

The two-year effort to move the archives from the West Bank to Scotland

I was very worried that the Israelis would stop it. So the first step was to digitize...page by page by page by page according to the highest standard with the cooperation of the University of Edinburgh University and Exeter University. And so three people worked day and night to digitize the diary … and all the documents that I had collected as well.

And the second step was to slowly start sending the documents out by ordinary mail without raising any attention to it.

Shehadeh's 40-year quest to investigate the 1985 killing of his father , a prominent lawyer — and the Israeli police investigation files of the killing, which Shehadeh obtained in 2025

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh



In the archive is the process by which I went about trying to get the police to investigate and the feelings that I had about it, which extended from '85 to 2025.

It was clear that they had not investigated the main culprit, the man who had sent the letter to my father from prison threatening to kill him if he did not withdraw from a case of land that the family thought belonged to them or they were squatting on it. My suspicion, strong suspicion, is because this man was a collaborator, and he wanted to be protected, and Israel wanted to protect him as a collaborator.

This is where it ended. We could not go beyond that.

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh



The Israeli police revealed all the investigation, but all the investigation was extraneous. It was distracting because the main suspect was not investigated, and that we have found out.

I had always suspected that it was this man who did it, and when I realized through this case that they have actually not investigated him, I felt that my suspicions were correct, and it gave me closure.

Sponsor Message

About Shehadeh's diary entries documenting Israel's transformation of the West Bank over the years

I understood from early on that it was a matter of...staying put and persevering. Because I realized that what the Israelis wanted was to make life so difficult for the Palestinians in the occupied territories, to make them leave.

The only antidote to that is sumud [Arabic for "steadfastness"]. Staying put and entrenching our existence by building institutions, by making work for people, by making it clear that we are here to stay. And I never changed my mind about this. I always realized that sumud was the most important resistance to what Israel was trying to do.

What Shehadeh hopes his legacy will be

toggle caption Raja Shehadeh

I'm not so worried about legacy, but I'm concerned that, through the diaries, people will understand how things happened and the developments that things went through. That's very important for me, and this would be perhaps a greater way that I would have served human rights and truth than any other way, whether through my writing of books or articles or speeches. The diaries might bring about the results that I haven't been able to achieve in any other way. I think that is the important thing.

World.title: Neighbor turned on neighbor after Charlie Kirk's killing. Is the divide here to stay?
World.content:
Neighbor turned on neighbor after Charlie Kirk's killing. Is the divide here to stay?

toggle caption Jim Urquhart/Reuters

A week into fall semester at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah, the campus's grassy, terraced courtyard bakes under the heat of full late August sunlight. The sound of trickling water from a fountain that meanders through the space beckons students to stop, chat and unwind. But Collin Grannis, who graduated over the summer, said the space hasn't had much activity since Charlie Kirk was assassinated there last year.

"It used to be very lively. People doing homework, people taking their food to eat outside, people to hang out. I remember people taking naps on the grass, like right in that area," Grannis recalled. "And it's been fully cleared out because people have that association with it."

Sponsor Message

The quiet of the courtyard belies the violence that took place in it a year ago, and the deepened social rupture that followed. The hard-right activist was killed in front of an audience of thousands while he was debating a student with progressive political views. The co-founder and then-leader of Turning Point USA, Kirk was arguably the most influential conservative youth movement leader in a generation – and his death set off an unprecedented frenzy of intimidation, harassment and threats that seemingly reached into every corner of the country.

toggle caption Jim Urquhart for NPR

As the country has seen an accelerated erosion of political norms over the last decade, violence and personal attacks have become a persistent dynamic. A wide array of civic actors - from elected officials and judges, to teachers and librarians – have found themselves at the receiving end of abuse and intimidation over political differences and culture war rifts. Despite this, everyday Americans could largely avoid the mob's ire as long as they weren't singled out by high-profile social media accounts like LibsOfTikTok. But Kirk's death changed this, according to several security experts who help prevent and mitigate online abuse.

"After Charlie [Kirk was assassinated]. … you didn't need to be [targeted by] one of the big [social media] accounts, obviously, for anyone to find you," said Shauna Dillavou, CEO of Brightlines, a doxing prevention service. "Your neighbor found you or your friends found you. A comment in a closed group chat that would get screenshotted and passed up the chain. And that was the big shift: the neighbor-on-neighbor, trusted circle, inner sanctum violence."

Sponsor Message

Doxing, the public release of someone's personal identifying information without their consent, is a tool that has been used by the political right and left. Dillavou said that in the U.S., its use has evolved and shifted – first largely seen within gaming subculture, then among violent extremist groups and actors, and later deployed by high-reach social media accounts. Kirk's death, Dillavou and other experts said, removed the final guardrails – democratizing the practice of doxing at a speed and scale they never had imagined.

"That creates terrible impacts for people," Dillavou said. "It's job losses. It's career losses. People have to move. They get death threats, and lawsuits. And … those impacts are lasting."

"Hell, call their employer"

Just hours after Kirk was gunned down, a website devoted to exposing "anyone celebrating Charlie's death" invited the public to submit leads. Titled "Expose Charlie's Murderers," the website billed itself as "the largest firing operation in history," and suggested that individuals posting speech unsympathetic to Kirk or his death were "supporting political violence online."

According to Kat Green, founder of the doxing mitigation nonprofit Endora, it was one of several websites attempting to "out" Kirk detractors. Together, Green says these sites listed names, pictures, employers, social media handles and other information about scores of people who likely never imagined that their social media posts would be dangled in front of an angry mob. She said she and others in her line of work had never before been so busy.

"It's a limited pool of people who help with that right now, and everybody was slammed," said Green. "So we all started working together to see what we could learn about the sites and who was behind them."

toggle caption Doug Mills-Pool/Getty Images

The phenomenon of using technology to corral negative attention to crowdsourced targets was not new. In fact, for many years Kirk's own organization, TPUSA, featured a "Professor Watchlist" that encouraged college students to report professors teaching "leftist propaganda." But Green and others said this felt different because the call to participate came from the highest levels of leadership. On the Monday after Kirk was killed, Vice President Vance sat in the host chair of Kirk's podcast and implored listeners to "get involved."

Sponsor Message

"So when you see someone celebrating Charlie's murder, call them out – and, hell, call their employer," Vance said. "We don't believe in political violence, but we do believe in civility. And there is no civility in the celebration of political assassination."

"There is just a very different speed and power dynamic around the post-Charlie Kirk assassination, where you have the vice president essentially endorsing some of this," said Shannon Hiller, executive director of the Bridging Divides Initiative at Princeton University.

To Dillavou, the tech-enabled outing of Kirk critics felt less like a call to civility, and more like incitement to violence.

"Doxing is stochastic terrorism," she said, referring to a phenomenon in which an influential voice's call to violence increases the likelihood that a random "lone wolf" will act on it. "The idea with doxing is not that the information about you – your personal information, your home address, your phone number – exists online. It does. It's that … that someone takes up the mantle to come after that person. "

While the "Expose Charlie's Murderers" website eventually came down, mirrors of the site remain online. Just as concerning, said Hiller, is the possibility that the cultural shift that Kirk's death unleashed – the use of doxing to silence opposing political views – will stick around as a feature of the country's disintegrating political discourse.

"We're trying to grapple with which of these things are persistent dynamics in our environment and which are new … in the current context with the current administration in an online environment," she said.

Kirk memes

Inevitably, discussions around doxing will land on subjective questions about when, or whether, the practice is acceptable or necessary. For Dillavou and Green, doxing is different from unmasking someone to hold them accountable for harmful behavior. The latter, they say, also promotes safety by alerting members of the broader community to a potentially dangerous person.

Sponsor Message

"It's the same as like a sex offender registry, in my mind," Dillavou said, noting that she does not struggle much with the question of whether it's ethical for antifascists, for example, to dox members of white nationalist groups. "What their membership in that [white nationalist] group suggests is that they believe that some people should be harmed on the basis of their skin color or on the basis of their political beliefs."

But Dillavou said that societally, any tolerance of doxing puts everyone at risk.

"Any doxing anywhere is harmful to all of us everywhere," she said. "We are all vulnerable to it."

This larger discussion – about whether it is appropriate to post personal information about people with whom we disagree – is one that Hiller said has not meaningfully taken place, even after Kirk's death. Technology has, she said, made it all too easy to circumvent the uncomfortable work of speaking across the political divide.

toggle caption Jim Urquhart for NPR

"We've been living in that world of accelerating reduction of barriers to doing that sort of thing online versus face-to-face to your neighbor," Hiller said.

" I … actually know all my neighbors and disagree politically significantly with some of them. If one of them ever posted something that I felt really worried me or my family, I would talk to them about it. I would say, 'Hey, you may not have realized the impact this has on me,' " she said. "But I think that people don't do that. It's unexpected to do that in person."

Ironically, it was also technology that ultimately helped bring the frenzy of doxing to an end In the aftermath of Kirk's assassination.

"That continued for months and really only subsided once people started pushing back legally and once younger audiences on the internet made a joke out of it and just flooded the zone with the meme-ification of Charlie Kirk," said Green. "I think opening the floodgates to every piece of surrealist garbage about Charlie Kirk just made it impossible to track down. It was too much to wade through."

Sponsor Message

Kevin Haslem, a sophomore at Utah Valley State University, said that even in the period leading up to the anniversary of Kirk's killing, it felt like adults on the campus couldn't directly talk about what happened.

toggle caption Jim Urquhart for NPR

"Professors, especially around this time of year as being it's the first anniversary, are kind of a little bit uneasy or a little bit guarded on how to talk about it," Haslem said, "Because just mentioning Charlie Kirk, of course, brings up a lot of a lot of heated emotions."

This story was made possible in part by the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting.

World.title: Miami crash raises concerns about the jet's operator, and why it's flying for Amazon
World.content:
Miami crash raises concerns about the jet's operator, and why it's flying for Amazon

toggle caption Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty Images

In the moments before an Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday, automatic warning signals were blaring in the cockpit. One pilot warned the other that the plane was coming in too fast, according to details of the cockpit voice recordings released this week by the National Transportation Safety Board.

But the flight crew pushed ahead with the landing anyway.

"In my 60 years of flying, I've never seen such a terrible performance from a crew," said Ross Aimer, the CEO of Aero Consulting Experts, and a retired airline captain who worked in the industry for more than 40 years.

Sponsor Message

The plane was traveling roughly 180 miles per hour when it touched down awkwardly on the runway, flight data recordings showed. The pilots tried briefly to take off again before the plane hurtled roughly 1300 feet past the end of the runway and smashed into two vehicles on the ground.

Five people were killed, all of them workers for a company that cleans planes. Five more were injured.

"It was a very, very unstable approach from the beginning, from the get go," Aimer told NPR. In that situation, he says, pilots are trained to go around and attempt the landing again. "These fellows should have gone around long before even getting close to that airport."

The cargo plane crash in Miami is raising concerns about the safety culture at 21 Air, the little-known carrier that operated the flight for Amazon. Former pilots were sounding alarms about the company's safety practices long before Sunday's accident, though the company disputes their claims.

It's also prompting questions about the retail giant's practice of contracting with multiple smaller carriers instead of operating its own fleet of planes.

"The main question would be," Aimer said, "why is it that a major company, a very rich company like Amazon Prime, is contracting their flying to several of what I would call fly by night operations like 21 Air?"

toggle caption Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty Images

Amazon vigorously disputed that characterization. An Amazon spokesperson says its carrier model is standard practice across the aviation industry, and that it contracts with carriers that are certified by air safety regulators at the Federal Aviation Administration.

Sponsor Message

"Nothing is more important to us than safety — this includes the safety of the people who operate flights in our network, the safety of the communities around the airports we use, and the safety of the people who handle our cargo," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement to NPR.

The Miami crash is the third major accident involving a 767 flying for Amazon. In 2019, a flight operated by Atlas Air crashed into Trinity Bay during its approach to Houston, killing the two crew members and one passenger on board. The NTSB found the probable cause was pilot error. (Atlas Air is still a major cargo airline, but no longer operates flights for Amazon.)

In 2024, another Boeing 767 flying for Amazon overran the runway at Vancouver International Airport in Canada. In that case, the Cargojet crew reported mechanical problems with the wing flaps on the plane. No one was injured during the high-speed landing. The plane was damaged, but later repaired and returned to service, Amazon said.

Amazon is not the only shipper to suffer a deadly crash. In November, a UPS cargo jet exploded shortly after takeoff in Louisville, Kentucky, killing all three crew members on board and 12 people on the ground. The NTSB investigation has focused on a faulty part in an engine bracket on the McDonnell Douglas MD-11.

Pilot experience

Amazon currently contracts with nine different air carriers, with more than 100 planes total in service, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company. They include major names like Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air and Cargojet, as well as lesser-known carriers like 21 Air that specialize in cargo.

21 Air operates a total of eight planes for Amazon, according to Cirium, including the Boeing 767 involved in the Miami crash. The company, which is headquartered in North Carolina, also flies for DHL.

For pilots, smaller cargo airlines such as 21 Air often serve as "a stepping stone into a bigger and better job," said Aimer, who spent much of his career flying for United Airlines.

Sponsor Message

"They attract guys that are not that experienced," Aimer said. "And even if they are, they're only looking to get on to a better job, like with UPS, with FedEx."

The crew of the 21 Air flight that crashed in Miami had relatively little experience with the type of plane they were flying. The captain had been certified on the Boeing 767 for less than five months, while the first officer had been certified on the 767 for less than 18 months, according to the NTSB.

21 Air did not reply to NPR's requests for comment. But in a statement to The Wall Street Journal the company said, "Our entire organization has focused on deploying the right training, protocols and procedures in all aspects of operational safety."

The company said it would evaluate the NTSB's findings.

Past safety concerns

Former 21 Air employees raised concerns about the safety culture at the airline long before the Miami crash. Karl Seuring, a veteran pilot and the former president of 21 Air's pilot union, said he was not surprised by that accident.

"We anticipated and we feared it. And we knew the day would come, and there wasn't anything we could do," he said.

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Seuring says he was fired in 2022 for raising concerns about the 21 Air's safety standards after being told repeatedly that "it's not going to change," according to the federal whistleblower lawsuit he filed. His lawyer, Mike Anello, shared documents from the case with NPR.

"Everywhere I looked there are issues," wrote Don Helmig, the departing safety director, in an email to the company's owner in 2021, in which he accused the company's leaders of paying "lip service" to safety. "In my opinion, what they wished me to do is say nothing, but that is not how Safety is supposed to operate."

The company's CEO at the time pushed back on those allegations in his testimony for the lawsuit. He denied that 21 Air discouraged employees from reporting their safety concerns, and said the company follows "all the rules."

Sponsor Message

The company also had trouble attracting experienced pilots, Seuring said, because it paid them less than other carriers. Seuring says he presented management with a plan to change that.

"If we want to get experienced pilots here, we have to be willing to compensate them," he said. "And then, unfortunately, when that was lower than standard, guys would simply go elsewhere with opportunities that looked more promising."

Amazon says it's aware of reports of the former 21 Air employees' safety concerns.

"We believe the allegations pre-date our relationship with the company and the current leadership team at 21 Air. Nonetheless, we take any allegation related to safety with the utmost seriousness," Nantel said in a statement.

Investigation ongoing

Both 21 Air and Amazon say they are cooperating with the NTSB investigation into the Miami crash.

NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy says investigators are seeking to understand how the two companies work together.

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

"We're going to want to see what that relationship is. Who does what? What safety provisions might be in any sort of contracts or any sort of policies? And then we'll see from there we might even have additional information that we seek," Homendy said during a press briefing on Monday.

At a briefing on Tuesday, Homendy said she was not familiar with complaints about the safety culture at 21 Air. But she did encourage the public to share anything that might be "relevant to this investigation."

Amazon is a financial supporter of NPR and pays to distribute some of our content.

World.title: AI industry needs to slow down for safety measures to catch up, Anthropic CEO says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The CEO of Anthropic said on Saturday that the artificial intelligence industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.

Without it, Dario Amodei warned, AI could be capable within six to 12 months of leading a swarm that could take over the entire internet, among other risks.

Amodei also offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, one part of which he said Anthropic is undertaking by itself already. The others would require co-ordination among the broad industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.

"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei said.

Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said in posts on X that they agree with Amodei.

"This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks," Altman said.

The stakes are high, even as some critics dismissed earlier warnings as hype to gin up excitement. Anthropic, an AI research and safety company, said two days earlier that it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons.

In July, rival OpenAI shook the industry after saying its AI system hacked into another AI company on its own in an "unprecedented cyber incident."

Amodei's post comes only a few days after one of Anthropic's researchers announced he's resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development.

WATCH | Anthropic insider warns AI could kill all humans within a decade: Chance AI kills all humans within a decade, Anthropic insider warns | Duration 2:08 Two AI experts are warning that AI is getting too smart, too quickly. One former employee accuses Anthropic and OpenAI of 'gambling with our lives.' A current Anthropic safety executive said he thinks there's a ten per cent chance AI kills all humans within a decade.

Another former Anthropic employee, Joe Benton, wrote in a Substack post published on Friday that he left his job as part of a safety team "to hold AI companies accountable" and that humanity "may not survive this transition."

"Many of the people I know who work on safety research at AI companies want to do what is right for the world," Benton said in his posting. "But they feel their companies are trapped in a race to build superintelligence: either they stop and other, less conscientious people take their place; or, they continue, and risk participating in enormous harm themselves."

To help rein in such risks, Amodei suggested that all companies at the frontier of AI commit to giving "ongoing, employee-like access" to a team of outside evaluators, who can monitor safety practices. He said Anthropic already plans to do so itself, including offering desks in its offices, access badges and company laptops.

The other parts of Amodei's suggested plan may be more difficult to implement. One asks the U.S. government to potentially issue waivers that would allow American AI companies to co-ordinate and set safety standards without running afoul of antitrust laws.

Another asks the U.S. and other democratic governments to try to co-ordinate with authoritarian governments, so that companies from China and other countries don't accelerate their efforts when U.S. rivals are intentionally pacing theirs.

"The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy," Amodei said. "But I believe we owe it to humanity to try."

Altman said in his post that third-party evaluators with employee level access is a "great idea," and pledge to introduce such a measure in the near future.

World.title: Alberta separatists expect a win, regardless of numbers that say otherwise, poll suggests
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta separatists think they’re going to win a referendum that surveys suggest they are poised to lose by a wide margin, according to exclusive new polling.

And that mismatch of expectations has consequences for what comes next — including the likelihood that Albertans shouldn’t expect this issue to be put to rest with this one vote, say the pollster and a political scientist.

Abacus Data CEO David Coletto presented the results of the new poll, done during the first week of September, to CBC’s West of Centre on Friday.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on a question with two choices: Option 1 is to stay in Canada, while Option 2 supports commencing the legal process to hold a binding referendum on Alberta separation.

That ballot question will be in addition to nine others that focus on constitutional and immigration issues.

Coletto’s poll found 64 per cent of respondents would vote to remain a province in Canada and 24 per cent would vote to start the separation process. Nine per cent were undecided and three per cent said they would skip the question.

But the poll also found that Option 2 supporters have surprisingly high expectations, believing that the separatist option will garner a winning 57 per cent of votes.

Coletto chalks it up to the political bubbles people live in and the natural hopefulness that comes with their strong support of the separatist camp.

Lisa Young, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, says that inflated expectation is worth noting — especially in the context of post-referendum ramifications.

"What he found, I think, should be setting off alarm bells in all of our heads," Young told West of Centre.

"If you do walk into this with the expectation that Option [2] is going to get 57 per cent and the actual outcome is 28 per cent ... the first question is going to be, 'Was this a proper result? Can we trust the outcome?'"

Premier Danielle Smith has said the upcoming referendum will be a gut-check of where Albertans stand, and that the province can hold a vote and move on .

But Young and Coletto don't see it that way.

In the event that the winning side supports remaining in Canada, the poll found many Option 2 voters expect the separatist movement to keep growing. Only six per cent of them said they expect the issue will be settled.

"There seems to be this assumption in the UCP premier's office ... that if you let this group let off steam, it will make the issue go away," Young said.

"This does not simply go away afterward. We're going to live with it one way or another for the next months, if not years."

A ballot for the Oct. 19 Alberta referendum shows the question about separating from Canada and the two options voters will choose between. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Who is the typical Option 2 voter?

According to the polling, the typical Option 2 voter is a conservative partisan, somewhat more likely to be a man and tends to be slightly older than the provincial average.

They are more likely to live in small cities or in bedroom communities around Calgary and Edmonton. While rural Alberta contributes more than its share, the communities ringing Alberta's main metropolitan centres provide the most voters.

But the group is more distinguishable by its grievances than its demographics, the poll suggests.

It says Option 2 supporters are far more likely to put being an Albertan ahead of being a Canadian, and have a more favourable view of the United States and Donald Trump. That said, the group is split on whether Alberta should become a U.S. state.

The group also shares near-unanimous agreement that Alberta contributes more to Canada than it gets back, the province’s interests are ignored in Ottawa, and the rest of the country does not respect Alberta, the poll suggests.

Young said she wonders if the separatist camp is adequately reflected among people who were polled.

"I did start thinking back to 2016 in the United States," Young said. "People wouldn't tell a pollster that they were going to vote for Trump because it was seen as sort of socially unacceptable."

Coletto said he's confident his poll factored in as many Option 2 voters as possible, but he also acknowledged this is not a typical election.

"Partisan politics can get divisive. But this is being felt much more deeply and much more emotionally on both sides."

"Whatever side you're on, you've still got to live together no matter what happens going forward."

Do they actually want to leave?

What Option 2 voters hope to get out of a favourable result varies significantly. When asked to identify their main motivation for choosing to commence the process for a binding referendum, only 26 per cent said independence.

The rest are voting for leverage, to send a message or on principle, Coletto said.

"For many Albertans who are inclined to look at Option 2, it's not just a black or white, in and out."

That result aligns with recent messaging from the separatist camp.

“Independence isn't actually on the ballot,” Keith Wilson, with independence group Let Alberta Decide, told West of Centre last month.

“Voting Option 2 sends a message that no, we can do better. We want a more respectful and balanced and fair relationship with Ottawa.”

“Others are prepared to vote for Option 2 when they don't even support independence. And that's why I have some optimism we're going to win on Oct. 19.”

University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young, left, and David Coletto, CEO of Abacus Data, speak to CBC's West of Centre on Friday. (Diane Yanko/CBC)

Methodology

Abacus Data surveyed 1,000 Alberta adults online from Sept. 4 to 7, 2026, six weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum. Results are weighted by region, age and gender to census data. A probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

World.title: Trade 'war' or not, are Canada and the United States now dug in?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer might not like to think of it as a trade "war," but whatever you call it — a difference of opinion? an incongruity? the unpleasantness? — it's now been going on for more than 19 months.

In February 2025, Donald Trump, in defiance of a free trade deal he himself signed in 2018, first announced tariffs on a number of Canadian products.

And it seems now it could be several more months before hostilities are reduced, let alone ceased.

"I think it is more likely than not that the current situation remains unchanged until the end of the year," said Wolfgang Alschner, a professor of business and trade law at the University of Ottawa.

"From the latest rounds of talks, we know that there is a potential landing zone but also that positions are currently too far removed to easily reach an agreement. The status quo is painful, but not so painful as to drive either side into forcing a change in position."

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Mark Carney described the latest round of American tariffs announced earlier this week as " relatively modest ," at least "in the context of other things that the U.S. administration has done."

That might suggest Carney doesn't see a need to respond with further measures against American imports. The recent cycle of escalation may have reached a kind of equilibrium.

Carney also said Canada is "always ready to strike a fair deal." But if one is willing to entertain war analogies, it might be said that both sides now seem dug in.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer leave a meeting in Washington, D.C., in mid-August. (Kelly Geraldine Malone/The Canadian Press)

The fact that the principal negotiators — Greer on the American side, Dominic LeBlanc and Janice Charette for the Canadian government — have largely avoided the political fray and acted professionally may serve to keep a door open to negotiations, suggests Meredith Lilly, a professor of international economic policy at Carleton University and a former foreign policy and trade adviser to Stephen Harper.

Lilly also sees a few potential "trigger moments" in the months ahead that could restart talks. If the United States and Mexico were to come to an agreement on their issues, for instance, that could put pressure on Canada. The results of the midterm elections in the United States could also change the political calculus on the American side. And lingering in the distance is an American threat to impose new auto and truck tariffs on Jan. 1, 2027.

Trump could also conceivably try to force the issue with a new threat of tariffs, like he did this summer.

Perhaps less optimistically, there is Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew's account that provinces have been told to plan for "two-plus years" of turmoil.

Is anyone winning this fight?

American officials may believe that U.S. economic power ultimately gives them the advantage — U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has likened Canada to a "yippy" dachshund trying to pick a fight with a German shepherd.

But both Paul Krugman , the American economist, and Roland Paris , the Canadian foreign policy scholar, argued this week that Canada may have the motivational or political advantage, with Canadians largely united against a clear and potentially existential threat.

"Trade wars test not only economic strength but also political resolve," Paris wrote.

Recent polls have shown high support among Canadians for taking a tough approach with the United States. And the Angus Reid Institute found a significant bump in support for Carney's Liberals in the wake of trade talks collapsing.

That may strengthen Carney's hand at the negotiating table, but could the Canadian public's reaction conceivably make it harder to get to some kind of deal with the United States?

WATCH | Carney 'looking closely' at Trump's import bans, tariffs: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

Before negotiations were formally suspended, Charette reportedly warned her American counterparts that a breakdown in talks and the imposition of new American tariffs could push discussions over a cliff — the public and political reaction, she said, would only shrink the Canadian side's room to negotiate.

David Coletto of Abacus Data has now made a similar argument, suggesting that public sentiment could be a serious impediment to a new deal.

"My sincere hope is that the temperature is turned down in both countries," Lilly said. "In particular, the president really needs to reduce this very aggressive social media campaign that he's pursuing. It makes it politically very difficult, if not impossible, for the Canadian side to engage."

Lilly said she wonders if it would be harder now to even get back to whatever deal the two sides were broadly in agreement about when Trump first announced in August that one was likely .

A fight that will take the measure of Carney and Canada

Some Canadians may trust Carney enough to defer to his judgment on what constitutes a good deal — or the best possible deal under the circumstances. And public opinion polling would suggest he has ample political capital to draw on right now.

But no level of support ever amounts to a blank check. The Carney government may have been acknowledging as much with its decision this week to not move forward with at least some of its most controversial proposals to amend environmental assessment laws.

For the sake of maintaining a strong hand, there might be more Carney could do in the days and weeks ahead.

The Liberal government obviously didn't heed the Conservative opposition's calls to reconvene Parliament, while releasing the text of any draft agreement, as the Conservatives also demanded, may have been impractical or unwise.

But there is also something to be said for the emphasis Conservatives have put on transparency, not only as a matter of accountability, but for the sake of building trust. That might be particularly important for Carney if this fight is to only get longer and harder — and after he was criticized for his handling of the agreement to open the Gordie Howe Bridge.

On a larger scale, the collapse of trade talks and everything that has ensued over the last two weeks may only add credence to Carney's contention that there has been a "rupture" and that Canada's "old relationship" with the United States is over.

Much of the onus for responding to that falls on the prime minister, and it's still too early to know exactly what path Canada will set out on.

WATCH | Poilievre calls on PM to release cost analysis of counter-tariffs: Poilievre calls on PM to release cost analysis of counter-tariffs | Duration 1:15 When asked at a news conference if he supports the federal government's planned counter-tariffs on the U.S., Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Canadians need to see how much the counter-tariffs will cost families and businesses, and what measures Prime Minister Mark Carney is taking to offset those costs.

But it is perhaps not too early to wonder if this moment is already leaving a mark on the Canadian psyche.

According to polling by the Environics Institute , Canadians held a decidedly favourable view of the United States for some 20 years, from the early 1980s to the early 2000s — from the presidency of Ronald Reagan through to the election of George W. Bush.

Canadian attitudes then plummeted around the time of the American invasion of Iraq, but more or less fully recovered with the election of Barack Obama as president.

There was another marked drop when Trump became president. But unlike the rebound when Obama came to office, the Canadian view of the United States did not fully recover when Joe Biden succeeded Trump, suggesting perhaps that some lasting damage was done.

If anything, the second four years of Trump have been more contentious among Canadians than the first four. And so even if a deal is reached in the next few months, it might be a long while before this trade war — for that is how people on this side of the border will surely remember it — is either forgiven or forgotten.

World.title: Celine Dion's return to the stage draws thousands of ecstatic fans to Plenitude Arena in Paris
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scores of devoted Céline Dion fans are in Paris ahead of the Canadian singer's sold-out comeback tour, six years after her career was derailed by the rare autoimmune neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome.

As the sun began to set in the Paris suburb of Nanterre on Saturday, concertgoers made their way through thousands of feet of barricades, past security and into Europe's largest indoor concert venue. They wore anything from jeans and graphic T-shirts to sparkly mini skirts and floor-length gowns.

For C é line Dion, one woman wore her wedding dress.

"I cancelled the party with all my family and friends to come see Céline," said Fanny Sucheyre, who celebrated her one-year wedding anniversary at the concert.

"I said to myself, if one day I had the chance to see her, I would wear my best dress. So it's my most beautiful dress."

Fanny Sucheyre wears her wedding dress on the way into Dion's show. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

Thousands of devoted fans travelled to Nanterre's Plenitude Arena to watch Dion return to the stage for her first full concert in six years. The show opens a sellout Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder sidelined Dion's career.

Outside the venue, fans belted out lyrics in both French and English. Several said they had loved the Canadian singer since childhood.

Inside, special edition Céline champagne glasses sold out within minutes and the lines for champagne itself stretched more than 30 metres. Even the men's washroom had snaking line ups.

"It's a dream. I haven't slept for three days. I'm 50 years old and right now I feel like I'm 15," said Guylene Richardson, heading into the arena with her daughter, both in Dion concert tees. "With [Dion's] disease, I didn't think she would come back, so it's great. I'm really happy for her. I'm happy for us."

Guylene Richardson, right, outside the arena with her daughter. (CBC News)

One of the best-selling artists of all time, she announced a diagnosis of stiff person’s syndrome — which causes stiffness and muscle spasms — and disappeared from the spotlight in 2022. She broke her hiatus to perform Edith Piaf's Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.

Dion is scheduled to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months. The City of Light has buzzed with anticipation for the singer's comeback, with signs dotting the length of the Champs-Élysées or along the famed river Seine.

World.title: Iraq scrambles to address fallout from alleged militia attack on Saudi oil pipeline
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Global oil supply fears are mounting after a drone attack launched from inside Iraq led to Saudi Arabia closing the East-West pipeline facility in the country’s Hejaz region.

Iraq's government was racing Saturday to contain the fallout after local Iran-backed militias were accused of attacking and shuttering a key Saudi pipeline.

Though an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied their involvement, Iraq's government confirmed the attacks had originated from its territory. The government pledged to investigate and dismissed a military commander.

The country is under mounting pressure to prevent local militias from aiding other Iran proxy groups across the region. The Iraqi government has set a Sept. 30 deadline for non-state groups to disarm, but several of the most powerful militias have said they will not comply.

Pressure to disarm the militias is especially acute as the Iran-backed Houthi rebels make an advance across Yemen’s west coast in a major setback to the Saudi-backed coalition that risks escalating the war in the region. The Houthis on Friday seized an island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key shipping lane through which about 12 per cent of global trade passes.

Their virtual control of the strait could send global oil prices — already inflated by the six-month Iran-U.S. war — spiralling. The strait has become a vital commercial lane for Saudi oil ever since the Iran war disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Asked about the region on Saturday while speaking to reporters in Dublin, U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack but tried to calm concerns.

He said his administration has "had discussions" with the Houthis, though he did not specify to which talks he was referring.

"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."

Iraq to investigate attack on Saudi pipeline

A group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied in a statement on Saturday that they were responsible for the attacks on the East-West crude oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, while praising the Houthis for their "ongoing battlefield victories against Saudi forces."

The group said it would co-operate with the Iraqi government's investigation.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said earlier Saturday that he'd ordered an investigation into the operations command of Maysan province, along the border with Iran, and dismissed the province's commander.

Saudi Arabia shut down the major, cross-country oil pipeline on Friday, calling it a "precautionary measure" after the pipeline came under drone attack. It blamed the attacks on several drones that came from Iraq but said the kingdom would not retaliate, to give the Iraqi government "an opportunity to take the necessary measures."

Several Arab countries, including Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Egypt, condemned the attack on Saturday, according to the Saudi state news agency.

Built in the 1980s, the East-West pipeline has played an important role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. By early June, Saudi Arabia had more than doubled oil exports from the Red Sea port at the pipeline's end to more than five million barrels per day, according to the International Energy Agency.

Tehran-backed Iraqi militias have carried out strikes on U.S.-linked targets both inside and outside of Iraq since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, and have co-ordinated with Yemen's Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.

Iraq closes border crossings with Iran

In a move possibly linked to the investigation, Iraq closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq's state-run news agency reported Saturday.

The report said that Iraqi officials were at the border, investigating previous "violations and infractions" at the crossings.

Valiollah Hayati, the deputy governor of Iran's southwestern Khuzestan province, named the closed crossings as Shalamcheh and Chazabeh. They are among the main official border crossings between Iran and Iraq.

Iranian state media said the measure would halt all passenger and commercial traffic through the two crossings until further notice.

Saudi Arabia and the United States bombed Iranian-backed militias in Iraq in July after blaming them for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities that had been claimed by the Houthis. Regional officials told The Associated Press that the Houthis helped the Iraqi militias plan and execute the attacks.

Fighting threatens to reignite Yemen’s civil war

The escalating fighting threatens to end a fragile truce that had largely halted Yemen's civil war since 2022. At stake are 40 million people in the Arab world's poorest country. The conflict killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.

The surge in fighting in the past week has sent more than 46,000 people fleeing, the United Nations migration agency said Friday.

The Houthis have been at war with Yemen's government since 2014, when the rebels seized much of northern and central Yemen and the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia entered the war the following year on the side of the government.

World.title: Zelenskyy describes Canada-U.S. tensions as 'strange,' draws comparison to Ukraine and Russia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy calls U.S. threats to annex Canada 'very dangerous' and urges the two neighbours to work their differences.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday described the unfolding tension between Canada and the United States as a "strange" sight to behold, drawing a comparison to his own country's fight with neighbouring Russia.

In a wide-ranging, exclusive interview with CBC News, Zelenskyy described American threats to annex Canada as "dangerous" and said both countries have a duty to resolve their differences.

"Strange," the president told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, speaking to the tension in North America.

"It's very dangerous [when] there are some problems between neighbours and we [Ukraine and Russia] are the example."

Russia and Ukraine are, like Canada and the U.S., neighbours with a lengthy border and history, though their current tensions are vastly different: Moscow's four-and-a-half year invasion of Ukraine is a deadly war, while the issues in Ottawa and Washington are largely economic.

"I think that the United States and Canada, will have to have … very constructive dialogue. They have to have it. It's dangerous. [There's] no choice," he said.

Zelenskyy's remarks come at the end of a visit to Canada, which was focused on Ukrainian air defences and winter preparation as the war with Russia enters its fourth year.

He spoke about Ukraine's new strategic partnership with Canada, efforts to revive peace talks with Moscow and his view on any potential face-to-face meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

WATCH | No 'win-win' in war: Zelenskyy says war holds no 'win-win' scenario for Russia and Ukraine | Duration 1:24 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejects comments from U.S. officials about finding a 'win-win' solution to the war with Russia, saying too many lives have already been lost.

100-year partnership with Canada

Canada and Ukraine signed a long-term strategic and political partnership on Thursday that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones to defend both countries. The declaration established a 100-year partnership that stretches across defence and security, trade and investment, as well as energy and critical minerals.

On Friday, Zelenskyy said the length of the deal with Canada, one of Ukraine's most vocal supporters in the war, was chosen as a symbolic gesture.

"It's about roots," he said. "It says that we will be together for a long period of time. Our children and our grandchildren, we will work together. We will share the experience of security [and] a lot of different things."

WATCH | No desire to meet Putin: Why Zelenskyy has no desire to sit down with Vladimir Putin | Duration 2:02 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has no desire to sit across the negotiating table from Russian President Vladimir Putin since only Russia's defeat will stop his aggression.

Zelenskyy's visit to Canada came not only as the relationship between Canada and the U.S. hit another low, but as the Trump administration renews its push to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

After U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump 's son-in-law Jared Kushner discussed potential proposals to end the war during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, Trump said the Russian leader wanted to make a deal.

But on Friday, Zelenskyy expressed doubts the Kremlin is interested in ending the war. He said he believes Russia maintains its goal of occupying Ukraine, but said he would sit face-to-face with Putin if trilateral negotiations came to fruition — though he said he doesn't expect any movement until after Russian parliamentary elections on Sept. 20.

"It's not my wish … Better to sit with my family," he said of a possible meeting with the Russian president. He described Putin as an "enemy," but said sitting down with an enemy "can bring us closer" to peace.

Diplomatic efforts to end the war have been stalled for months, while both countries have escalated attacks on the other. Moscow has continued its bombardment of Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv has intensified its strikes inside Russia in an effort to reduce its economic ability to continue with the war.

"To be honest, there is no win-win in this war. It can't be so because [there's been] so many human losses. It stopped being win-win at the first day of this war between us," Zelenskyy said.

"The most important victory for everybody, it's not for Ukraine and Russia ... For the world, it's peace. To stop this war. And this is a victory for a human lives."

World.title: Time to tighten your cybersecurity, researchers warn. AI-driven worms could be trying to access your devices
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Artificial intelligence researchers are warning the public to use strong passwords and promptly install software updates on their devices to combat "AI-driven computer worms," a new breed of cyber-threat they say can launch custom attacks on devices, sapping processing power and information as they hunt for new victims.

In June, a University of Toronto team led by Canadian Institute for Advanced Research AI chair Nicolas Papernot announced that publicly available AI models can power a worm capable of adapting its attack on the fly as it spreads between devices connected to the internet, including laptops, printers and cameras.

The research, conducted in collaboration with the AI development hub the Vector Institute, was shared with "national science, security and defence bodies" prior to its publication, the university said.

Now Papernot, a U of T associate professor of computer engineering and computer science, is warning the public not to ignore or delay prompts to update software, and to change passwords regularly.

"We can no longer be sloppy with our cybersecurity hygiene," he said on Thursday at a panel discussion hosted by U of T.

"We can no longer afford to reuse passwords. We have to use multi-factor authentication. We have to keep our devices up to date, and organizations have to change their processes to make sure that these software patches are deployed as quickly as possible."

WATCH | Nicolas Papernot shares his research on AI worms:

Worms that learn

Unlike other computer viruses, worms spread from machine to machine without human intervention. The U of T researchers said the worm they created in a lab gathers information as it moves between devices. Every new breach reveals passwords and weak points that can unlock another machine.

In an uncontrolled setting, the researchers say, such a worm could gain internet access and learn from warning notices about newly discovered vulnerabilities, outpacing the software patches meant to stop them.

"Some of these [issues] can be fixed with software updates. But others are human errors such as weak passwords and sloppy IT setups that can’t be solved by pushing out a patch," U of T wrote in a blog post about the discovery.

"That means a hacker doesn’t need the most advanced AI models to cause unprecedented damage."

In 2017, a worm called " WannaCry" wreaked havoc across 150 countries , freezing computers and encrypting files, while demanding a ransom payment in bitcoin.

Back then, U of T said, this type of attack typically followed a "fixed script" programmed by a human that would often fail when confronted by defensive software it wasn't designed to crack.

"The difference here is that the AI-driven computer worms are able to design attack strategies that are specific to each victim device that they interact with. So, rather than use a single vulnerability, they will work and interact with the victim device, and find an attack strategy that's customized and tailored," Papernot said.

"We can no longer stop their propagation by fixing a single vulnerability, or a small number of vulnerabilities."

WATCH | Research say AI race is 'gambling with out lives': Anthropic insider warns AI could lead to human extinction | Duration 1:49 Two artificial intelligence experts are warning that AI is getting too smart, too quickly. One former employee accuses Anthropic and OpenAI of 'gambling with our lives' in the race to develop AI.

Papernot’s warning comes as fears about AI hit a fever pitch.

In July, hundreds of artificial intelligence agents from OpenAI went rogue, hacking into the online platform Hugging Face. The situation prompted warnings from tech experts about AI systems escaping human control.

Earlier this month, researchers at a California-based security firm announced they had used AI to build a "zero-click" worm in a matter of days that can spread through WeChat calls on iOS and Android operating systems.

And on Tuesday, a researcher at Anthropic made headlines after musing on social media that there’s a more than 10 per cent chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.

The federal government released its national artificial intelligence strategy in early June. The five-year framework is focused on accelerating business AI adoption, expanding sovereign computing capacity and building public trust.

According to a Bank of Canada survey released in June, AI adoption among Canadian firms remains at an early stage. Canada’s big five banks are among the companies enthusiastically adopting the technology.

'Big change' to cybersecurity risk

Papernot warns AI-driven worms aren’t just more effective than their predecessors, they’re also much cheaper to build and deploy.

Samir Chhabra, director general of marketplace framework policy at Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, says the lower costs of driving these worms will enable hackers to attack more targets.

"This worm [runs] on compute that it’s stealing from its victims, which essentially makes the cost of the next attack a marginal cost, essentially zero," he told audience members at U of T’s event Thursday. "That’s a big change in how we think about what defence looks like."

A survey conducted in January by the Communications Security Establishment (CSE), the government’s cryptologic intelligence and cybersecurity agency, found 87 per cent of respondents regularly update the software on their devices— with 46 per cent claiming to always do so when prompted.

In addition, 77 per cent said they use complex passwords with a mix of letters, numbers and symbols. However, only 31 per cent reported using a unique password all the time.

The CSE said its online survey was conducted Jan. 9-29 among 2,330 adult Canadians. The sample was drawn from a representative probability-based panel and weighted by region, age and gender, yielding an overall margin of error of ±2.1 per cent.

Papernot says his findings show more needs to be done to bolster cybersecurity in Canada.

"If you think about critical infrastructure like power grids, water supply, hospitals, schools, grocery stores … the fact that all these systems are exposed to the internet is something that we should all be concerned about," he said.

World.title: Bears, caribou and other animals are messing with this researcher's equipment, and he's got photos to prove it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | How lynx, moose and bears keep destroying this wildfire researcher's work: Quirks and Quarks 9:38 How lynx, moose and bears keep destroying this wildfire researcher’s work

Lucas Brehaut was hoping there’d be a lot of interest in his research, though it might be a case of “be careful what you wish for.”

Seemingly every animal in Newfoundland's wilderness wants to know what he's up to — and they're not always gentle with his equipment.

Brehaut, a wildfire research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service, is studying how forests in Atlantic Canada regrow after forest fires. Though the region is cooler and wetter than much of the rest of the country, forest fires are getting more common.

After a forest fire hit south of Grand Falls-Windsor, N.L., in 2022, he set out to understand how forests might regrow on a planet when temperatures are rising due to climate change.

To do that, he and his team needed to lug 19 open-top chambers (OTCs) through the forest and set them up around seedlings they’d planted. OTCs are like mini greenhouses, and look like clear hexagons with an opening at the top. They can increase the temperature anywhere from one to three degrees, mimicking the effects of a warming planet. Brehaut's study is currently in year three of five.

Brehaut says he expected some difficulties — the treks of up to a kilometre in difficult terrain, and the infamously dour Newfoundland weather, for example.

But in September 2023, on one of his regular check-ins, he ran into a problem he didn’t expect.

“That’s when we started to notice that some of these greenhouses had some visitors, and might not have been as strong as I had hoped,” Brehaut said.

Those “visitors” included caribou, moose, black bears, wolves, rabbits and owls. Brehaut found out who the culprits were because of cameras set up around the sites that were originally meant to look at snow depth over the winter.

A black bear dismantles a plexiglass greenhouse in Newfoundland. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

Out of 19 sites, 11 have sustained damage at some time or another. And the animals wouldn’t just trample the greenhouses — some made off with the temperature sensors.

“The greenhouses had been completely obliterated. And by obliterated, I’m talking broken, smashed to smithereens,” Brehaut said.

“There were certain times where we would spend more time at a site finding the temperature sensors than we would actually measuring the seedlings themselves.”

In Brehaut’s case, four — not 13 — is the unlucky number.

“I have a site that I specifically call the problem child. Because every time I went to that site, it was damaged in one way or another,” he said.

“It’s site number four, but I call it 'The Problem Child.' Every time I walk to it, I know that it’s going to be challenging.”

But the animals aren't always smashing — they’re grazing. Brehaut has seen moose and rabbits go into the greenhouses for a bite to eat. They even occasionally manage to get through the top of the greenhouses without damaging anything.

A baby moose walks over a mangled mini greenhouse in Newfoundland. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

Brehaut isn’t mad, just disappointed. He hopes that the animals are enjoying themselves, even if it’s at the expense of his research.

“You see the amount of joy that, potentially, a black bear is experiencing by actually sitting in a greenhouse and playing with that plastic, and taking that temperature sensor and moving it,” he said.

“Yes, the research gets damaged to some capacity, but we’re in nature. This is their habitat. We are only visitors to this spot.”

A caribou rests near a mini greenhouse in Newfoundland. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

What are you doing in my backyard?

That's exactly why some animals are so keen to mess with equipment, says Kaitlyn Gaynor, an assistant professor at the University of British Columbia.

"If someone puts something weird in your backyard, wouldn’t you want to go investigate it?" she said.

Gaynor, who studies the impacts of human disturbance on animal behaviour, said intelligent animals are especially curious about anything novel in their environment. After all, it could be a new source of food, or it could pose a threat. This boldness and willingness to explore could have been an advantage as species evolved.

Bears are a great example, Gaynor says.

"It’s in their nature to be curious about whether new objects are resources to be exploited," she said.

"They’re these generalist omnivores that will eat a whole bunch of different things, and so when they see something new, the first question is like, is this food?"

A black bear walks by a plexiglass mini greenhouse in Newfoundland. Kaitlyn Gaynor, a professor at the University of British Columbia, said bears are especially curious about new objects in their ecosystem. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

Also, there's the smell factor — we stink.

"Often these objects we leave behind have our scent on them, and so our scent might attract animals to these places and to these objects," Gaynor said.

She added that researchers can lessen the effect of research on animals by getting in and out of the field as quickly as possible, by leaving as little scent as possible, and by obscuring or camouflaging research equipment.

Down in Africa

Animals interfering with research is a worldwide phenomenon.

Gaynor has seen a lot of it during field work in Mozambique.

"Baboons are always coming up to the cameras. We get a lot of great baboon selfies," she said.

"Hyenas just want to chew on everything, so they’ll chew on our research equipment."

A baboon takes a selfie in Mozambique on one of Kaitlyn Gaynor's research cameras. (Submitted by Kaitlyn Gaynor)

But the worst offenders are the elephants. They like to knock down trees and feast on leaves, which is bad news for research equipment.

"Elephants are also just highly intelligent, and curious, and very large and destructive," she said.

Gaynor said animals are her biggest cause of equipment loss or failure.

"It’s not that the electronics go out, and it’s not that things get stolen by people, it’s that animals tend to be a little bit destructive."

Hartebeests stare at one of Kaitlyn Gaynor's research cameras in Mozambique. Gaynor says animal interference is the biggest factor for equipment loss. (Submitted by Kaitlyn Gaynor)

But, to be fair, Brehaut has also had issues with that most destructive animal — the homo sapien.

"We've had some visitors accidentally run over these sites in the winter," he said.

"We have an extremely snowy winter in Newfoundland, and snowmobiles basically went over one of my plots."
