World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Exports and gas production hit record highs as patriotic spirit swells
World.content:
Listen to this article

Bilateral communications were front and center in Mexico the week of Sept. 7, with developments running the gamut from encouraging to combative. U.S. President Donald Trump’s remark that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs beyond “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” caught fire over the weekend, unleashing a fresh round of provocations from Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the days that followed.

Mexico, however, continued to highlight trade and security collaboration with its northern neighbor, though the PISA test results and next year’s midterm elections sparked more conversations at home. Meanwhile, the annual inflation rate ticked up to 3.26% — as expected according to Banxico, which forecasts inflation of 3.5% by the end of 2026. President Claudia Sheinbaum remained optimistic through it all, especially as her administration makes its plans for 2027. Overhead, punishing heat baked Mexico’s northern border states even as monsoon rains drenched the Pacific coast and center of the country.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

2027 budget takes shape

On Monday, Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora submitted a 10.6-trillion-peso (US $627.8 billion) budget proposal for 2027 to Congress, an increase of about 1% in real terms over this year. Amador framed the package around “five pillars” — economic growth, protecting government priorities, strengthening revenue, more efficient spending and fiscal discipline. The government is banking on those pillars to shrink the budget deficit to 3.9% of GDP next year from an estimated 4.1% in 2026, even as public debt climbs to 55% of GDP. No new taxes or fuel-price hikes are planned.

Health care gets a 10.9% real-terms boost to 1.1 trillion pesos, largely for IMSS-Bienestar infrastructure and medicine supply, while education rises about 7% to 1.3 trillion pesos to fund new schools. Pension and welfare programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, and debt servicing alone eats up 1.6 trillion pesos — roughly one of every seven pesos the government spends. Security agencies see an 11.6% bump to 331.4 billion pesos, while Pemex funding falls 69.2% as the state oil company pushes toward self-sufficiency.

The National Electoral Institute (INE) is the biggest percentage winner of all, with an 87.5% real-terms increase ahead of 2027 midterm elections, while the Energy Ministry, the National Human Rights Commission and the Federal Electricity Commission absorb the steepest cuts. Sheinbaum said the following day that she is “very satisfied” with the package and that growth could exceed the official forecast of 1.5-2.5%, citing anticipated stability in trade relations with the U.S. and Canada.

Homicides continue to fall

Security officials reported this week that daily homicides fell 53% in August compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration, making it the least violent August since 2015.

More than 67,000 people have been arrested for high-impact crimes since Sheinbaum took office, though Security Minister Omar García Harfuch cautioned that “the job is not done.” Days later, from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the president highlighted a 63% drop in Chiapas’s homicide rate since Gov. Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office, alongside nearly 10,000 arrests in the southern state. The same briefing revealed the discovery of a clandestine hospital the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) used to treat injured members.

Olmeca Refinery notches record month

Pemex’s Olmeca Refinery in Tabasco posted its best month yet for fuel production in July, averaging 252,498 barrels per day, a 78.8% jump over June. Gasoline output rose even more sharply, up nearly 128% month-over-month, after equipment fires forced repairs earlier in the year. Despite the milestone, the plant — which began operating approximately two years ago — is still running at roughly two-thirds of its 340,000-bpd capacity.

Fox and PRI’s Alito Moreno join forces

In a striking political reunion, former President Vicente Fox met with PRI leader Alejandro “Alito” Moreno to discuss “the need to build a strong opposition” ahead of 2027 midterms — 26 years after Fox became the first opposition candidate to sweep the once-dominant PRI out of the presidency, and years after he called the party “black vipers, vermin and tadpoles.”

Morena, for its part, dismissed the pairing as “the reorganization of the power elite,” saying in a statement that “they change the names, they invent new organizations, but behind the facade, it’s the same old faces.” The PRI, which ruled Mexico for 71 years, now holds just two of the country’s 32 governorships — the same number as the much smaller Citizens Movement (MC) party.

At her Monday press conference, Sheinbaum branded the reunion “PRIAN” politics dating to the “neoliberal” era of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and called Fox a “traitor of democracy” — a jab tied to his role in Mexico’s disputed 2006 election.

Bilateral high points

Trade and security cooperation produced some of the week’s more encouraging bilateral news. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. hit a monthly record in July: US $60.55 billion worth of goods were sent north, pushing Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market above 18%.

Along the border, Mexican and U.S. forces carried out “High Eagle,” a binational operation to detect and disable drones cartels use to surveil authorities near Tijuana and San Diego. And though bad weather grounded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s flight to Mexico City on Wednesday, he and Sheinbaum still held a video call on USMCA negotiations that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard described as “cordial” and “very useful,” with talks on steel, aluminum and automotive tariffs continuing ahead of a fourth bilateral review round.

Bilateral low points

Other exchanges were considerably more combative. Over the weekend, Trump proposed to rename New Mexico “New America,” despite having no legal authority to rename a U.S. state, drawing pushback from the state’s Democratic leaders. Later in the week, from Ecuador, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio doubled down on claims that cartels control “vast territories” of Mexico, hinting the threat may eventually have to be “confronted one way or the other.” Sheinbaum shot back on Thursday morning, telling Rubio to keep Mexico out of U.S. midterm politics and calling his remarks electorally motivated. Rounding out the week, U.S. Vice President JD Vance labeled the Mexican flag “a symbol of the far left” after a protester interrupted his convention speech in Dallas, telling the man to “get your ass over there” if he loved Mexico so much.

Poor PISA scores spark a debate over screens

New results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), given to 7,843 students across 297 Mexican schools, showed that four in 10 15-year-olds — 41.8% — scored below the basic level in science, math and reading, more than double the 19.7% OECD average and Mexico’s worst showing since 2009.

Mexican students averaged 388 points in math, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, and the country has shed seven points in both math and reading since the 2022 test. The decline wasn’t unique to Mexico — the OECD’s education director called it part of a “dramatic” global drop, particularly in reading — and Mexican students still reported unusually high curiosity (80%, versus a 24% global average who called school “a waste of time”). Education International, the global teachers’ federation, pinned the broader slide on shrinking attention spans, heavy AI use and a worldwide teacher shortage. China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada topped the rankings.

Education Minister Mario Delgado blamed excessive screen use for the drop in reading comprehension — arguing that “screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images” — while defending the New Mexican School curriculum model and promoting traditional games like yo-yos, marbles and spinning tops as a substitute for phone time. He conceded the PISA sample was “statistically representative” even as he questioned whether the test amounts to a comprehensive evaluation of Mexican education. Sheinbaum later told reporters Mexico will roll out new math and reading textbooks next year, including poems and short stories, and push a “return to pencil and paper,” tying the effort to new national guidelines already restricting cellphone use in schools.

Education Ministry, UNESCO team up on AI in schools

Also this week, Mexico’s Education Ministry signed a letter of intent with UNESCO to guide the “responsible” rollout of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with the U.N. body offering technical assistance, teacher training and research support. Officials said the goal is to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes for, teaching and critical thinking, and the deal also opens the door to new rules on cellphone use in schools.

Mexico prepares for El Grito and Independence Day

With the country’s 216th independence anniversary approaching, more than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are readying for the Sept. 16 military parade through Mexico City, featuring drones, horses, dogs and a float marking the country’s World Cup hosting duties this past June and July. The holiday kicks off the night before, with Sheinbaum leading the Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony and Tejano band Intocable headlining a concert in the Zócalo.

Festivities and gritos will ring out from cities across the country, including in Sinaloa, whose capital city of Culicán will hold a public celebration of Independence Day for the first time in two years.

Points of 🇲🇽 pride

A 20-year-old engineering student from a Chihuahua farming family, Luis Ángel Robles Morales, won a national innovation award for an irrigation filter that is already helping 500 drought-stricken farmers use water more efficiently.

Forward Julián Quiñones and Club América’s Scarlett Camberos earned historic Ballon d’Or nominations, marking the first time two Mexican players — and a Mexican club — have featured on the shortlist for world soccer’s top individual honor.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Witnessing the explosive sledgehammer ritual in San Juan de la Vega, Guanajuato
World.content:
A door in the street cracked open just enough for a hand to slip through. A kid, maybe 15, curled his fingers toward himself: come here, come here, then pulled back into the dark. I looked around the street. Nobody. I stepped inside.

The house looked like a drug kitchen. Two folding tables stretched across the room, their surfaces dusted white and yellow. On one side, a bucket of potassium chlorate. On the other, sulfur. Three kids stood around the tables, working the powders together with their bare hands. One kid looked up at me and grinned, then went back to scooping powder into small plastic bags.

Josué was the one who had waved me in from the doorway. One of the boys had no hands. Both arms ended at the wrists. I didn’t want to ask. I asked anyway. He told me it happened during the explosions, a few years back. He said it the way someone tells you about a stolen bicycle, part of life.

Don Juan David, Josué’s father, walked into the room. He greeted me with a handshake and a smile, glanced at the tables of explosive powder where their children worked, and walked back out.

A dangerous tradition

Every year, on Shrove Tuesday, the townspeople of San Juan de la Vega pack homemade explosives onto sledgehammers, carry them to the streets and open fields, and slam them against the ground. People lose limbs. This time, something was different. For the first time in the town’s history, authorities had banned the use of explosives during the carnival.

Families wanted to talk. Each family insisted theirs was the true story. The carnival, they all agreed, celebrates San Juan de la Vega, a saint who saved the town from gold robbers centuries ago. The explosives reenact the gunshots from his battles.

Every family also wanted to make sure we knew that the big explosions, the ones the town is famous for, are not the real tradition. The real tradition is small. Modest. A respectful crack of gunpowder in honor of the saint. Kids started making bigger and bigger explosives, destroying city piping. Everything breaks, they said, shaking their own heads. This is not what we are.

A man named Aquino de la Vega was moving silver shipments by mule along the Camino Real when bandits started robbing him. He prayed to San Juan Bautista. The robbers stopped. Aquino vowed he would honor the saint every year, forever, and so would his sons.

Six families still carry that vow. Each one is tied to a barrio. The families fund the music, the food, the processions. They keep the image of the saint in their home for a year.

Adrenaline and danger

The word I heard more than any other was adrenalina. The afternoon before the carnival, I found Josué sitting on a curb outside a corner store, rolling a cigarette. He was quiet.

“I’m always scared before I do it,” he told me. “But once I blow up one, I can’t stop. The adrenaline is too strong. I want to keep going.”

I asked about the dangers, and stories came easily: a man who burned, another who was paralyzed, people who lost fingers, hands, arms, legs. Accidents happen because the explosives are powerful enough to send 25-kilogram sledgehammers flying through the air. A hammer goes up, a hammer comes down, and sometimes there is a head in the way.

“Police always try to take them away,” one man said, sitting in a plastic chair outside his house, two kids playing in the dirt beside him. “But they will never stop the tradition. Nothing will change.”

On the afternoon before the main event, the streets were empty. Doors closed. No music. No voices.

Boom. The first hammer hit the ground as soon as night fell.

The sound moved through me. The ground shook under my feet. My ears whistled, even from 100 meters away. My chest vibrated. Windows cracked. The pipes beneath the street groaned and split.

Then came another. And another.

Parades took the streets. Villagers singing, dancing, playing instruments, carrying the image of San Juanito through the town. Following them in the back, kids dressed as soldiers, some in boots and gas masks, others with no gloves, no protection of any kind. Everyone carried sledgehammers and backpacks stuffed with explosives.

Defying the ban

I found Josué in the crowd. Face covered in soot, eyes wide. He swung a hammer down and the detonation threw him sideways. He got up laughing and loaded another charge.

Around midnight, the first police cars appeared.

The crowd froze. About 10 men climbed out with SWAT gear, assault rifles and bulletproof vests. They walked toward the kids with the backpacks. The boys scattered.

I saw a grandmother crack her front door open. She let the kids shove their backpacks full of explosives through the gap; she closed the door, and she stood in front of it. When the police asked to enter, she stood immobile like a statue until they were gone.

The police confiscated what they could, caught a few guys, and left. Within minutes, the parades reformed. The hammers came back out. The explosions picked up where they had stopped.

At around 3 a.m., we walked back toward town to catch some sleep. I did not sleep. The bed shook after every boom. Even with earplugs, my ears hurt. It went on until 7 a.m.

We walked outside. Over 10 police cars patrolled the town. They had shut everything down. But beyond the edge of town, we could hear it. Boom. Boom.

We followed the sound.

Moving to the tracks

The townspeople had moved to the train tracks. Flat, open land, sand, rocks and gravel, not a piece of shade anywhere. They placed explosives on the rails and waited for trains to roll over them. Between trains, they took turns blowing up hammers on steel bars laid flat against the ground.

There, away from the police, the hammers got bigger.

It was noon. The sun was directly overhead. People packed more and more powder onto the sledgehammers and took turns. Huge hammers flew tens of meters into the air.

I watched a kid swing a hammer down. The explosion threw him back onto the ground. The hammer launched upward, spinning, and came down on his head. The ring of steel on skull. He tried to stand. Blood ran from his scalp, down his face, into his eyes. His friend pulled off his own shirt, wrapped it tight around the kid’s head, and hauled him onto the back of a motorcycle. They disappeared down the road.

Nobody stopped. The next person stepped up.

The next morning, the market opened in the square as always. People walked slowly, said good morning to each other. A dog slept in a doorway. The church bell rang at 8.

Here was Josué, down the road. He waved.

I went to say goodbye to Don Juan David. He pulled me into a hug that lasted a long time. He held on. We had barely talked. When he finally let go, his eyes were wet. He thanked me. He begged me to come back next year.

“Sí, San Juanito permite,” he said. If San Juanito allows it.

Mattia Astori and Daniele Colucci make Sacratos, a documentary project on extreme rituals with photos, interviews, articles and videos. They’ve worked in Mexico, India, Bolivia, Thailand and Italy.

World.title: Turtle power: Volunteer to protect Mexico’s sea turtles
World.content:
Turtle camps can be found all over Mexico’s coastline, including the Gulf Coast, allowing volunteers to liberate baby turtles.

With the fifth-longest coastline in all of Mexico — a country that is internationally known and beloved for its beach offerings — Veracruz is certainly a sea-loving state, boasting some 450 miles of Gulf Coast access. For the record, Baja California Sur, a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, has the longest total coastline at more than 1,350 miles of beach.

Historically, Veracruz is celebrated for its seafood and coastal tropics, as well as being the site of Mexico’s largest and oldest port with access to the Atlantic Ocean.

But what has been lost in the greater narrative is that, as part of its cultural significance along the Gulf Coast, Veracruz has also become one of Mexico’s leading states for turtle conservation.

The legacy of turtle conservationism in Mexico

The earliest federal efforts to focus on sea turtle nesting in Mexico began in 1962, led by the National Institute of Biological and Fisheries Research on both of Mexico’s ample coasts. In 1963, the Center for Turtle Culture opened on Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo.

Shortly after, in 1966, Rancho Nuevo — located in Tamaulipas, just north of Veracruz — was among the first turtle conservation camps to formally open in Mexico. The National Commission of Protected Natural Areas outlined the importance of these efforts from the mid-1960s; the investments significantly helped to maintain the growth of Mexico’s turtle populations by increasing local awareness and participation. During that time, the National Sea Turtles Conservation Program was founded as a result.

Rancho Nuevo, along with the other turtle conservation camps that would spring up all over Mexico’s beaches — from the Gulf to the Pacific — has become a crucial element of turtle protection efforts since then, utilizing a mix of dedicated turtle conservationists and public volunteers. Responsibilities include the protection of nesting sites via monitoring and safeguarding turtle nests, and assisting (or “liberating”) fresh turtle hatchlings to ensure they make it to the sea.

Milestones in national protection rights

Since the 1960s, Mexico has become a global leader in turtle conservancy; in 2025, Mexico was recognized as an exemplar for its turtle protection efforts. Currently, Mexico federally operates 26 turtle conservation centers, in addition to various independent organizations and nonprofits extending across 13 coastal states. Officials announced a record of more than 34 million newborn olive ridley turtles that reached the ocean in a single season, in Oaxaca’s Morro Ayuta region alone.

In 1990, federally backed turtle protection rights gained further ground when then-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari decreed an end to the commercial harvesting of all sea turtles and related products. The landmark move shifted former turtle hunting communities — such as areas in Mazunte, which had among the highest rates of turtle slaughter — into epicenters of turtle conservation. Mazunte opened the Mexican Turtle Center in 1991, aiding the area’s turtle population and ecotourism alike.

Mexico’s role as a sanctuary for sea turtles

According to a 2008 report from the Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), “Mexico is the country with the largest number of sea-turtle species worldwide. Seven of the eight species known … nest in Mexican beaches, both in the Pacific and in the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean littorals: loggerhead turtle, white or green turtle, black turtle, hawksbill turtle, Kemp’s ridley, olive ridley and leatherback turtle. Two of them, Kemp’s ridley and black sea turtle, nest exclusively in Mexican beaches.”

A more recent investigation from 2023, published in Revista Mexicana de Biodiversidad, revealed that southeastern Mexico, including Veracruz, is the most diverse region for turtle conservation in the country: “According to our results, southeastern Mexico supports three-fourths of the families — and more than half of the genera — found nationwide in Mexico. These findings highlight southeastern Mexico as a region of high importance for the composition of land and freshwater turtles at the national level … Oaxaca, Chiapas and Veracruz stand out as the states with the highest species richness and endemism, respectively. These three states are located within the region considered the richest in total herpetofauna, a result of complex orography, diverse habitats and environments, and the biogeographic history of Mexico.”

An afternoon with turtle conservationists in Veracruz

Jeanne A. Mortimer, a world-renowned marine biologist known as “Madame Torti” who specializes in sea turtle conservationism, once wrote that “The importance of the central coast of Veracruz (for turtle nesting) may be attributed to the fact that the beaches are easily accessible from the ocean without great obstacles like rocks, pronounced slopes or coastal developments that prevent the movement of the adult females along the length and breadth of the beaches.”

It partially explains why Veracruz has been able to cultivate a long-lasting ethos and engagement around turtle protection, with civic initiatives like Fundación Yépez and the Veracruzano Center for Research and Conservation of the Sea Turtle having launched decades ago. Additionally, Veracruz boasts Veracruz Reef System National Park, which played a role in a major environmental ruling by Mexico’s Supreme Court to conserve sea turtle habitats by restricting the construction of industrial ports in endangered areas (although reports that the ruling hasn’t been properly enforced have been published).

Vida Millenaria is among Veracruz’s most prominent turtle conservation groups. The project began in Tecolutla in 1974 as a personal mission for Fernando Manzano, whom locals began to call “Papá Tortuga,” or Turtle Father. Over half a century later, his efforts have expanded to include other members.

To date, the nonprofit has protected and released thousands of baby turtles each year. Visitors arrive year-round to receive public education and help to release newborn turtles into the water along the beaches on the city’s northern outskirts, about a 20-minute drive from the town’s center, along a mostly deserted dirt path.

Camping under the stars in Tecolutla

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kate Levasseur (@katelevass)

I personally drove out to experience it for myself. Depending on your budget, you can rent a group-sized or personal tent near the beach at a campsite that includes outdoor showers, bathrooms and a common area for campers and volunteers who arrive at different hours of the day to participate in the turtle release. The camp area is shaded by palm trees and is relatively cool due to the strong coastal breeze.

The camping experience adds a layer of memory-making, as you sleep beneath the moonlight on a private, mostly isolated beach while the waves wash ashore in the near distance. A rotation of Vida Millenaria workers takes turns patrolling the area on ATVs around the clock, mostly to keep an eye on the turtles and their nests. (Note: If you decide to camp overnight, be sure to bring plenty of supplies, water and food, as a one-way trip back into town requires more than 20 minutes of off-roading to reach the edge of Tecolutla). There, you can enjoy a paradisiacal beach to yourself, undisturbed, until the next day.

A volunteer brigade assembles

Early in the morning, around 7:30 a.m., volunteers of all ages begin to arrive and assemble at the center of camp. A local expert introduces the nonprofit’s history, and a musician plays music dedicated to sea turtles. Maps and visuals are used to show and explain a brief history of turtle conservation in the state, and an adult-sized turtle replica stands in as a faux mascot for guests to take pictures with.

Afterwards, participants are escorted to the nearby souvenir shop, where everything is turtle-related (of course) and handmade. Each purchase grants a set of baby turtles for group liberation — so the more things you buy, the more turtles you’re able to liberate (prices start around 150 pesos and include turtle plushies, stuffed animals, mugs, shirts, etc.). For breakfast, a local volovanero (a savory pastry vendor common in Veracruz) brings a freshly baked batch for about 50 pesos each.

Releasing hatchlings into the wild

Then, the finale: Everyone strolls down to the beach together, lines up, and is given baby turtles to release into the ocean together. It’s a spectacular sight to see upwards of 50 small creatures — more or less, depending on the volunteer group’s size that day — crawling their way into the waves for the first time. They are swept away, their tiny heads occasionally poking out from the shimmering waters before completely disappearing into the distance by the dozens.

Of course, if you’re nowhere near Veracruz, you can search for your nearest beach. You’ll likely discover a turtle conservation group awaiting your participation. It makes a memorable weekend trip — and most importantly, it helps to keep an essential part of Mexico’s ecosystem intact.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: MND goes all in on Mexico City: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Mexico City is having a long-overdue and well-deserved moment in the spotlight. People from all over the world of all ages are discovering the city and everything it has to offer. Entire neighborhoods are being influenced and transformed by the influx of new foreign residents and tourists. Some locals lament the changes, others celebrate them. We had one of our local CDMX writers reflect on it here.

As of late, I now hear from several people a week who have just visited the city for the first time and were blown away by how awesome it is. I can’t help but smile. When I first visited the city over 30 years ago, it was love at first sight — the history, the energy, the people, the contrasts. I would always tell people that it was one of my very favorite cities in the world and have gushed about it in articles and podcasts:

The team at Mexico News Daily is excited to announce that, starting this week, we will be further increasing our coverage of Mexico City. In addition to our regular daily content that very frequently covers news happening in the city, we are now going to begin a weekly MND Local CDMX feature that will give readers even more detailed news and information.

The idea behind this new weekly feature article is to provide the next level of news and information about the city. Perhaps most importantly, we are being very thoughtful in who we are writing for and what should be included. The goal is to write it for a wide audience: those currently living in the city, those considering moving to the city, or others just interested in learning more and being better informed for planning future trips. We hope to inspire first-timers to come check the city out, and those who have been there to come back again soon!

It is NOT written to help you understand what to do in the next 24 hours. It is NOT meant to replace local event calendars and local social media pages. It IS written to help you learn more about the city and better plan your time there. We will give you insight into new openings to be aware of, important events to plan for and new trends shaping the city. We hope to introduce you to new people, new places and new things to check out — all in an effort to inspire you to spend more time discovering this wonderful city.

World.title: ‘Confidently Wrong About Tipping in Mexico’: A new podcast from MND
World.content:
Many people say religion, abortion and politics are topics one should avoid discussing in public. I think I would add tipping to that list! Tipping, both in Mexico and the U.S., was a pretty straightforward affair for years — that is, until the pandemic. What used to be a generally accepted 15% in the U.S. became … 18%? 21%? 24% or more? No purchase, no matter how minor, seemed free of a tip request.

Here in Mexico, tipping has also gotten more complicated for a number of reasons. Since the COVID pandemic, there has been increased awareness about the wages of service workers, and many people have raised their standard tip from 10% to 15%.

More foreigners spending more time in Mexico has also put upward pressure on tipping practices. This trend has not always been well-received by some locals who feel that they are being pressured to tip more or receiving lower quality service due to what their tip is perceived to be. Obviously, that creates an uncomfortable situation.

There is also the debate as to the rationale behind higher tips. Some people say, “If I have the money and I want to give it, who cares?” Others, meanwhile, seek to be cognizant of local norms, seeing that as a form of respect for the culture.

So who’s right? What is standard? And who else besides restaurant servers in Mexico are supposed to be tipped?

Check out our recent article here: Mexico and My Money: The tricky business of tipping in Mexico

And the latest episode of our Confidently Wrong podcast here:

World.title: Mexico’s 2027 election cycle has begun: What to know
World.content:
Listen to this article

The 2026-2027 election cycle began on Thursday, and though the stakes are high for the control of Congress, the majority of governorships and all 16 Mexico City borough leaders, the process has already been marred by accusations about the autonomy and transparency of the agency in charge.

A record 102 million Mexicans are eligible to participate in the June 6, 2027, vote. The National Electoral Institute (INE) said it will set up 176,141 polling places, some 6,000 more than during the 2024 federal elections.

Controversy flared up during the agency’s opening electoral session, however, when INE Councilor Arturo Castillo challenged the institution’s credibility.

“The INE seems to have abdicated its role of overseeing and arbitrating elections,” he said, describing a scenario of premature campaigning and irregularities that he said could compromise confidence in the outcome.

Castillo also criticized INE President Guadalupe Taddei for appointing 12 new executive directors over the past year without the consensus of the General Council, some of whom did not meet legal requirements for their appointment.

Two other INE councilors raised questions about new procedures and past oversights, while representatives of opposition political parties complained about what they see as the failure to enforce electoral regulations.

These denunciations contrasted with Taddei’s assertion that the INE was ready to organize the election, while insisting the playing field is level.

What’s at stake in next June’s election

Beyond the selection of more than 20,000 public officials, the vote will serve as a national referendum on the governing project of Morena and the performance of President Claudia Sheinbaum. It will also determine the relative strength of opposition forces ahead of the 2030 presidential election.

While Morena seeks to consolidate its territorial dominance and protect its legislative majority in the Chamber of Deputies (all 500 seats are on the line), some parties will be battling for political survival. The election will also see 17 states choose new governors.

The once-dominant PRI is fighting to remain one of the top five parties in Congress, while the conservative PAN is desperate to preserve its hold on three governor’s mansions.

These two parties also hope to remain relevant in Mexico City, where PRI-PAN alliances control five of the capital’s 16 borough halls, while the PAN aims to maintain its status as the No. 2 party in the Mexico City Congress.

Two new political parties will make their debut in the upcoming elections: PAZ (a party linked to the evangelical church) and Somos México (a center-left party that emerged from opposition to reforms of the INE championed by Morena).

Although the election cycle has officially begun, the formal candidate selection process is not due to begin until Jan. 4, with parties permitted to hold primaries through Feb. 12. After that, the formal campaign season will take place from April 4 through June 2.

Complaints about alleged irregularities

Criticism of the INE is primarily related to alleged violations of the campaign schedule regulations.

Ahead of the 2018 elections, Morena designated so-called state coordinators who were tasked with guiding the party in the run-up to gubernatorial elections. Since they were then inevitably nominated as candidates, critics say their actions as state coordinators should be regarded as campaign violations.

At the same time, office-holders seeking re-election or aiming for a new post have been known to stage public events and rallies before the official campaign season, proceedings that could be seen as violating election law.

With reports from El País, Animal Político, El Universal, Texas Public Policy Foundation and Lider Empresarial

World.title: Mexico’s Supreme Court allows home cannabis edibles, but with a limited practical effect
World.content:
Mexico’s Supreme Court has ruled that people with personal recreational cannabis authorizations can now make marijuana-infused edibles for their own personal use — but people still cannot legally buy or sell them.

The ruling — which applies to gummies, brownies and other homemade edibles laced with cannabis — expands what the Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risks (Cofepris) must allow under an authorization for adult recreational self-consumption.

The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation (SCJN) said incorporating marijuana or THC into prepared or semi-prepared food for personal consumption is ordinary cooking, not the manufacture of a product subject to specialized health controls.

The ruling, approved by a 7-2 vote and issued on Thursday, ordered Cofepris to issue new authorizations allowing such food preparation for the permit holder’s exclusive personal consumption.

The practical effect is narrow: A person with a Cofepris authorization for recreational self-consumption may prepare a THC-infused brownie, cookie or gummy for personal use. But the authorization does not allow sales, public retail, distribution or supply to third parties, including giving the food to friends.

The decision arose after Cofepris granted an applicant a recreational self-consumption authorization but expressly barred the preparation of cannabis in prepared or semi-prepared foods.

The Supreme Court found that restriction to be improper if the food was intended exclusively for the applicant’s personal use, and ordered Cofepris to issue an updated, corrected authorization.

The decision does not cover cannabis used in medicines, herbal remedies, cosmetics, vaping products, dietary supplements or other goods subject to specialized health controls.

The ruling is the latest development in Mexico’s piecemeal approach to adult marijuana use.

In 2021, the Supreme Court invalidated portions of the General Health Law that imposed an absolute administrative prohibition on recreational self-consumption of cannabis and THC. The Court held that the ban disproportionately restricted the right to the free development of personality.

The declaration allowed for the legal planting, cultivating, harvesting, preparing, possessing and transporting of cannabis and THC for personal recreational use.

But it did not establish broad legalization or a regulated commercial market.

It also required protections for third parties: Cannabis cannot be used in front of minors or in public places where nonconsenting people are present, and users may not drive or operate dangerous machinery while under the influence.

Cofepris reiterated in July that the court’s decisions do not recognize a right to commercialize, supply, sell, distribute or import cannabis. The permits apply only to authorized recreational self-consumption.

In an opinion column in the newspaper El Universal, Jorge Larrea Espinosa called Mexico “an intermediate legal zone” — a place where adults have limited, permit-based self-consumption rights, while a fully regulated recreational market remains stalled in Congress.

With reports from Infobae, Expansión, Zeta Tijuana and EFE

World.title: Costa Rica Ordered to Fix Roundabouts Built Too Small for Its Own Trucks
World.content:
COSTA RICA · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts — The order The Contraloría General de la República has ordered CONAVI to correct safety defects on Route 32.

— The defect Seven roundabouts were designed for a 16.8-metre articulated vehicle. The corridor carries 22.4-metre cargo units.

— The gap 5.6 metres, which is why heavy vehicles cross into opposing lanes and pedestrian space.

— The evidence Drone footage confirmed the violations.

— The deadlines Corrective measures adopted by 30 October 2026, full implementation by 30 March 2027.

— The cost US$1.4 million more on four roundabouts, on top of about US$6.8 million already spent against an original US$5.4 million budget.

Costa Rica built seven roundabouts on its main Caribbean freight corridor for trucks 5.6 metres shorter than the ones that use it.

Costa Rica Ordered to Fix Roundabouts Built Too Small for Its Own Trucks

Costa Rica’s comptroller general has ordered the national roads council to correct design defects on Route 32, after finding that roundabouts on the country’s principal Caribbean freight corridor cannot accommodate the vehicles that use it.

What Is Wrong

Seven roundabouts on Route 32 were designed around a WB-15 articulated vehicle, 16.8 metres long. The corridor serves the Caribbean ports and carries WB-20 cargo units of 22.4 metres.

The difference is 5.6 metres, and the consequence is that heavy vehicles negotiating the roundabouts cross into opposing lanes, into pedestrian and cycle space, and onto green areas.

The Contraloría confirmed the violations with drone footage rather than relying on reported incidents, which is why the finding is difficult to contest.

Route 32 serves the Caribbean ports at Limon and Moin.

What It Costs

Correcting four of the problematic roundabouts will require an additional US$1.4 million.

That comes on top of roughly US$6.8 million already spent against an original budget of US$5.4 million. The Contraloría describes the result as direct patrimonial damage to the public treasury.

CONAVI’s board must adopt corrective measures by 30 October 2026, with full implementation required by 30 March 2027.

The comptroller describes direct patrimonial damage to the public treasury.

Why Route 32 Matters

Route 32 connects San José and the central valley to Limón and Moín on the Caribbean coast, which is where the great majority of Costa Rican container traffic moves.

It is a single corridor carrying a national export function, and it has a long history of landslides, closures and delayed expansion work. Every disruption on it reaches the ports within hours.

A design error that forces the country’s largest trucks to leave their lane at seven points on that corridor is therefore a freight problem as much as a safety one.

The comptroller’s finding does not allege corruption. It describes a specification that did not match the traffic, approved and built anyway, and a bill the public is paying twice.

How a Specification Error Survives to Construction

Roundabout geometry is set by a design vehicle, a standard template that determines turning radii and lane widths. Choosing the wrong template produces a structure that works on paper and fails in traffic.

The WB-15 and WB-20 designations are standard classifications, and the difference between them is exactly the kind of decision that is made once early in a design and then propagated through every drawing that follows.

What the comptroller is describing is therefore a single early error that nobody caught in review, on a corridor whose traffic composition was known to everyone involved.

The corrective bill of US$1.4 million on four roundabouts, against US$6.8 million already spent, is the price of that omission.

The Corridor’s Longer Record

Route 32 has been under expansion for the better part of a decade, on a project financed with Chinese credit and repeatedly delayed by landslides, design disputes and contractor problems.

The road crosses the Braulio Carrillo national park, where the terrain is steep, saturated and prone to slides, and closures there cut the central valley off from the Caribbean ports for hours or days at a time.

Costa Rica has no practical alternative route for container traffic to Limón and Moín. That is what turns every engineering problem on this corridor into a national logistics problem, and it is why a comptroller’s order about roundabout geometry is worth reporting at all.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Contraloría order?

That CONAVI correct safety defects on Route 32, with measures adopted by 30 October 2026 and implemented by 30 March 2027.

What is the defect?

Seven roundabouts designed for 16.8-metre articulated vehicles on a corridor carrying 22.4-metre cargo units.

What does it cost to fix?

An additional US$1.4 million on four roundabouts, against roughly US$6.8 million already spent on an original US$5.4 million budget.

How was it established?

Drone footage confirmed heavy vehicles crossing into opposing lanes and pedestrian space.

Why does Route 32 matter?

It is the main corridor between San José and the Caribbean ports at Limón and Moín, carrying most Costa Rican container traffic.

Sources: Contraloria General de la Republica, Delfino, La Nacion Costa Rica.

World.title: France Sends Its Trade Minister to Panama With the Canal First
World.content:
PANAMA · TRADE

Key Facts — The visit French trade minister Nicolas Forissier arrives in Panama on Monday 14 September.

— The priority The Panama Canal.

— Who he meets Canal Authority officials including administrator José Ramón Icaza Clément, plus the foreign affairs, economy and security ministers.

— The interest Water management, urban transit and metro expansion, railway and security projects.

— The aim Opportunities for French companies in Panamanian infrastructure.

— The context Panama’s infrastructure pipeline has been the subject of sustained international attention through 2026.

France is sending its trade minister to Panama with the Canal at the top of the list, and a shopping list of everything attached to it.

France Sends Its Trade Minister to Panama With the Canal First

Nicolas Forissier, France’s minister for foreign trade, visits Panama on Monday with the Canal as the stated priority of the trip.

The Programme

Forissier is scheduled to meet Panama Canal Authority officials, including administrator José Ramón Icaza Clément, together with the ministers of foreign affairs, economy and security.

The stated purpose is to explore how the Canal and Panama’s wider infrastructure programme can generate opportunities for French companies.

The specific areas named are water management, urban transit including metro expansion, railway projects and security infrastructure.

Every transit consumes fresh water from the Gatun and Alhajuela reservoirs.

Why Water Management Is First Among Them

The Canal’s binding constraint is not capacity in the locks. It is fresh water.

Every transit consumes a large volume of water from the Gatun and Alhajuela reservoirs, and the drought of 2023 and 2024 forced the Authority to cut daily transits and auction slots at extraordinary prices. The revenue effect was measured in hundreds of millions of dollars.

The long-term answer under discussion is a new reservoir on the Río Indio, a project with substantial engineering requirements and a displaced population to resettle.

That is precisely the kind of project a European engineering sector wants to be near, and it is why water management sits at the top of a trade minister’s list rather than at the bottom.

Panamanian infrastructure tenders draw Spanish, Chinese, Korean and Brazilian contractors.

The Competitive Setting

Panama has been the object of unusual international attention through 2026, with United States pressure over Chinese-linked port concessions at either end of the Canal running through the year.

A French approach framed around infrastructure contracts rather than strategic alignment is a different proposition, and a more comfortable one for Panama City to receive.

Whether it produces anything depends on procurement rather than diplomacy. Panamanian infrastructure tenders are competitive and Spanish, Chinese, Korean and Brazilian contractors are all established there.

A ministerial visit is the beginning of that process rather than the end of it.

What France Already Has in the Region

French infrastructure and utilities groups have a long presence in Latin America, in water treatment, urban transport and energy transmission.

Panama is a smaller market than Brazil or Mexico and a more concentrated one. Its infrastructure pipeline is dominated by a handful of very large projects, and the Canal Authority is an unusually well-capitalised counterparty by regional standards.

That combination is attractive to a European contractor. The projects are large enough to matter, the payer is creditworthy, and the currency is the dollar.

What the Metro Adds

Panama City’s metro is the first in Central America and is being extended, with the third line built on Japanese financing and monorail technology.

Urban transit expansion is the second item on the French list after water, and it is the one with the clearest procurement pipeline attached.

A trade minister arriving with water, transit, rail and security on the agenda is describing essentially the whole of Panama’s capital programme. What emerges from that will be visible in tender awards over the next two years rather than in anything announced on Monday.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is visiting Panama?

Nicolas Forissier, France’s minister for foreign trade, on Monday 14 September 2026.

What is the priority?

The Panama Canal, along with water management, urban transit, railway and security projects.

Who will he meet?

Panama Canal Authority officials including administrator José Ramón Icaza Clément, and the ministers of foreign affairs, economy and security.

Why does water management matter?

Canal transits consume fresh water from the Gatun and Alhajuela reservoirs, and drought in 2023 and 2024 forced transit cuts.

What is the competitive picture?

Spanish, Chinese, Korean and Brazilian contractors are all established in Panamanian infrastructure.

World.title: Argentina Braces for an El Nino That Peaks Over Its Harvest
World.content:
ARGENTINA · CLIMATE

Key Facts — The event The World Meteorological Organization describes an extremely strong El Niño peaking from late 2026 into February 2027.

— The probability Argentina’s infrastructure ministry puts very strong conditions at 90 percent.

— The regions Misiones and Corrientes carry above 55 percent probability of above-normal rainfall, with Formosa, Chaco, Santa Fe and the Paraná basin also flagged.

— The port risk Swelling on the Paraná threatens access to the Buenos Aires port complex.

— The harvest INTA warns the 2026-27 campaign will need revised management for heavy rain and high temperatures.

— On the name Súper Niño is media shorthand. It is not a formal meteorological classification.

Argentina is being told to expect the strongest El Niño in decades over its next harvest, and the river that carries that harvest to market is the thing at risk.

Argentina Braces for an El Nino That Peaks Over Its Harvest

Argentine agencies and the World Meteorological Organization are warning of an exceptionally strong El Niño peaking between late 2026 and February 2027, with the Paraná basin and the northeast carrying the highest flood risk.

What Is Forecast

The World Meteorological Organization describes the event as extremely strong, peaking from late 2026 through February 2027. Argentina’s infrastructure ministry puts the probability of very strong conditions at 90 percent.

Misiones and Corrientes carry probabilities above 55 percent of above-normal rainfall. Formosa, Chaco, Santa Fe and the wider Paraná basin and delta are also flagged.

The national agricultural technology institute, INTA, warns that elevated rainfall combined with high temperatures will require revised management for the 2026 and 2027 campaign.

Súper Niño, the term circulating in Argentine media, is not a formal classification. The technical description remains an intense or strong El Niño episode, and the shorthand should be read as journalism rather than meteorology.

INTA warns the 2026-27 campaign will need revised management.

Why the River Is the Problem

The Paraná carries the great majority of Argentine grain exports to the Atlantic through the Rosario port cluster and onward to the estuary.

Both extremes hurt it. The low-water event of 2021 forced vessels to load below capacity and cost the sector hundreds of millions of dollars. Swelling brings the opposite problem, with flooding on the delta, disrupted access to terminals and damage to the low-lying infrastructure along the route.

Reporting flags risk to access to the Buenos Aires port complex specifically, which is the alternative route when Rosario is constrained.

The Parana carries the great majority of Argentine grain exports.

The Regional Picture

This is the same underlying Pacific event that Peru is tracking, and the two countries are watching different manifestations of it.

Peru’s multi-agency ENFEN committee monitors the coastal Niño, a regional ocean-warming pattern off the Peruvian coast, and has put the probability of an extraordinary event at 62 percent. Peru has declared a state of emergency across 893 districts in more than 20 regions.

Argentina is exposed through rainfall and river levels rather than through coastal ocean temperature. Colombia, at the other end, generally gets drought in an El Niño year rather than flood.

One event, three different problems, and no single regional response to any of them.

What Happened Last Time

Argentina has run this cycle in both directions within five years. The 2020 to 2021 La Niña drought produced the lowest Paraná levels in more than seventy years, forcing grain vessels at Rosario to load below capacity and imposing costs measured in hundreds of millions of dollars on the export chain.

The 2022 and 2023 drought then cut the soy and maize harvests severely enough to remove several percentage points from Argentine GDP and to gut the central bank’s dollar earnings.

An intense El Niño is the opposite phase and generally the more favourable one for Argentine yields, because it brings rain to the Pampas during the growing season.

The risk is not drought this time. It is too much water at the wrong moment, in the wrong places, on a river that has to carry the result to a ship.

Frequently Asked Questions

How strong is the forecast event?

The World Meteorological Organization describes it as extremely strong, peaking from late 2026 into February 2027. Argentina’s infrastructure ministry puts very strong conditions at 90 percent probability.

Which regions are at risk?

Misiones and Corrientes above 55 percent probability of above-normal rainfall, with Formosa, Chaco, Santa Fe and the Paraná basin also flagged.

What is the economic risk?

Flooding on the Paraná and delta, disrupted port access including to the Buenos Aires complex, and a 2026-27 harvest requiring revised management.

Is Súper Niño an official term?

No. It is media shorthand. The technical description is an intense or strong El Niño episode.

Is this the same event as Peru’s?

It stems from the same Pacific pattern, but Peru tracks a coastal Niño through its ENFEN committee, which has put an extraordinary event at 62 percent probability.

Sources: World Meteorological Organization, INTA, La Nacion, Infobae.

World.title: One Rate Trade, Two Opposite Results on the Ibovespa
World.content:
BRAZIL · MARKETS

Key Facts — The winner Assaí rose 8.15 percent over the week of 7 to 11 September.

— The driver Relief in the interest rate curve after the August deflation print.

— The loser Direcional fell 8.64 percent, the worst performer of the week.

— The downgrade JP Morgan cut its Direcional target from R$19.00 (about US$3.73) to R$17.50 (about US$3.44), keeping a buy rating.

— The horizon That target runs to December 2027.

— The oddity Both are rate-sensitive names, and they moved in opposite directions.

The best and worst Ibovespa performers of the week were both supposed to be trading off the same interest rate curve.

One Rate Trade, Two Opposite Results on the Ibovespa

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Assaí gained 8.15 percent over the week to 11 September and Direcional fell 8.64 percent, the best and worst performers in a week defined by an improving interest rate outlook.

The Week

August inflation came in at minus 0.32 percent, a deflation reading, and the curve moved in response. The central bank meets on 15 and 16 September with a fifth consecutive cut priced.

Assaí, the cash-and-carry food retailer, rose 8.15 percent. It carries significant debt and is one of the most directly rate-sensitive names in Brazilian retail, so an improving curve reduces its financing cost and its valuation discount at the same time.

Direcional, a homebuilder focused on the lower-income segment served by the Minha Casa Minha Vida programme, fell 8.64 percent.

Assai is one of the most directly rate-sensitive names in Brazilian retail.

Why They Diverged

Both are rate-sensitive, which makes the divergence the interesting part.

For a leveraged retailer, a falling curve is straightforwardly good. It cuts the interest bill and it lifts the multiple.

For a lower-income homebuilder the mechanism is different. Its buyers are financed through a subsidised programme rather than at market rates, so the policy rate matters less to demand than the programme’s funding does. What moves the shares is margin, land bank, and the terms on which units are sold.

JP Morgan cut its Direcional price target from R$19.00 (about US$3.73) to R$17.50 (about US$3.44) on a December 2027 horizon while keeping a buy rating, which is the standard shape of a house trimming expectations without changing its thesis.

Direcional builds for the subsidised lower-income housing segment.

What It Says About the Rally

Market commentary this week linked the broader Ibovespa move to election positioning, the so-called trade eleitoral, on expectations of gains for Flávio Bolsonaro and Augusto Cury.

The single-stock performance complicates that reading. A week where the leader is a leveraged grocer and the laggard is a subsidised-housing builder looks a great deal more like a rate story than a political one.

Both explanations can be partly right. Disentangling them from a single week of price action is not possible, and any account that presents one as settled is overstating what the data supports.

What Assai and Direcional Actually Do

Assaí operates atacarejó stores, the Brazilian cash-and-carry format that sells in bulk to small retailers, restaurants and price-sensitive households at the same time.

It expanded aggressively by converting hypermarkets acquired from the Casino group, and that expansion was debt-funded. Leverage is the reason its shares move so sharply on the rate curve.

Direcional builds for the lower-income segment served by Minha Casa Minha Vida, Brazil’s subsidised housing programme. Its units are financed through the FGTS severance fund at rates set by policy rather than by the market.

The two are therefore exposed to interest rates through completely different channels, which is the mechanical explanation for a week in which one led the index and the other trailed it.

What the Week Did Not Settle

Two stocks are two stocks. A week in which the extremes of the index are explicable by rate exposure does not establish that the whole move was a rate move.

The Ibovespa contains a large commodity block whose prices are set abroad and a banking block that gains from a steeper curve and loses from credit deterioration. Neither responds cleanly to the same signal as a leveraged grocer.

What the week does establish is that at least part of what has been described as election positioning has a simpler explanation available. That is worth saying because the alternative explanation is the one that gets repeated.

What did JP Morgan do?

Why did two rate-sensitive names diverge?

Assaí benefits directly through its financing cost. Direcional’s buyers are financed through a subsidised programme, so the policy rate matters less to its demand.

World.title: What the Will Bank Collapse Cost the Card Networks
World.content:
BRAZIL · PAYMENTS

Key Facts — The liquidation Brazil’s central bank placed Will Bank in extrajudicial liquidation on 21 January 2026.

— The parent It followed the Banco Master liquidation decreed in November 2025.

— The hole Mastercard absorbed roughly R$2.5 billion (about US$491 million) of unprocessed transactions, against an estimated R$5 billion (about US$982 million) of liability in the first 30 days.

— The guarantee fund The FGC released R$6.06 billion (about US$1.19 billion) to around 312,000 creditors.

— A parallel case Amex and Fictor are disputing around R$893 million (about US$175 million) separately.

— Where it stands Abecs said repasses had begun normalising by 15 April. No court filing has been confirmed.

A card network absorbed half a billion dollars of payments that consumers had already made and merchants had not been paid for. Then it mostly went away.

What the Will Bank Collapse Cost the Card Networks

The failure of Will Bank left card networks holding payments that consumers had made and merchants had not received, and the argument about who carries the loss has never reached a court.

What Happened

Brazil’s central bank decreed the extrajudicial liquidation of Will Bank on 21 January 2026, extending the Banco Master liquidation of November 2025. Will Bank had been under temporary special administration in between.

A card issuer that stops operating mid-cycle leaves transactions in flight. Consumers have paid, acquirers have processed, and the issuer that owes the money no longer exists as a going concern.

Mastercard absorbed roughly R$2.5 billion (about US$491 million) in unprocessed transactions, with total estimated liability of about R$5 billion (about US$982 million) in the first thirty days after the liquidation.

The deposit guarantee fund, the FGC, released R$6.06 billion (about US$1.19 billion) to around 312,000 creditors, which covers depositors rather than the payment chain.

Who Was Arguing With Whom

The dispute is between the card networks and the acquirers, the companies that sign up merchants and process card payments. Both sides were left short by the same failure and neither accepts the loss.

A parallel case involves American Express and Fictor over roughly R$893 million (about US$175 million).

Abecs, the Brazilian card industry association, pressed publicly for a solution in February 2026, calling the situation critical for the sector’s credibility. Its framing was that these were resources already paid by consumers and not yet passed through.

The central bank decreed the liquidation on 21 January 2026.

What Was Never Established

Reporting at the time said the dispute could go to court absent an agreement. The Rio Times has found no confirmation that any lawsuit was actually filed, and does not report one.

Descriptions of Mastercard having told a Brazilian court that Will Bank’s liquidator halted pass-throughs have circulated. That specific claim is not supported by the available reporting.

What the record does show is a resolution of sorts. Abecs president Giancarlo Greco said on 15 April 2026 that repasses had begun normalising.

The Rio Times has found no September 2026 development reviving the dispute. Anyone encountering it as current news is most likely reading a recirculation of the January to April episode.

Nothing comparable to deposit insurance covers payments in flight when an issuer fails.

Why It Still Matters

The Banco Master group failure produced a criminal investigation, a Supreme Court crisis and an election . The payments hole is the least discussed of its consequences and the one that touched the most people directly.

It also exposed a structural gap. Brazil’s deposit guarantee covers depositors. Nothing comparable covers payments in flight when an issuer fails, and the loss allocation between networks and acquirers is a matter of commercial contract rather than regulation.

That gap has not been closed. It was absorbed, which is a different thing.

How a Card Transaction Actually Settles

A card payment involves four parties. The cardholder’s bank issues the card, the merchant’s acquirer processes the sale, the network routes and clears it, and the merchant receives the money days later.

The money flows backwards through that chain. The issuer pays the network, the network pays the acquirer, the acquirer pays the merchant.

When an issuer fails mid-cycle the chain breaks at the first link while every later link has already performed. Merchants have delivered goods, acquirers have promised payment, and the money that should fund all of it sits inside a liquidation.

That is why the loss lands on the network and the acquirers rather than on the cardholders, and why the argument between them has no obvious legal answer.

Frequently Asked Questions

When was Will Bank liquidated?

21 January 2026, by Brazil’s central bank, extending the Banco Master liquidation of November 2025.

How much did Mastercard absorb?

Roughly R$2.5 billion (about US$491 million) of unprocessed transactions, against an estimated R$5 billion (about US$982 million) of liability in the first thirty days.

Did it go to court?

No court filing has been confirmed. Reporting said it could go to court absent an agreement.

Is it resolved?

Abecs said on 15 April 2026 that pass-throughs had begun normalising. No September 2026 development has been found.

What did the FGC cover?

R$6.06 billion (about US$1.19 billion) to around 312,000 creditors, covering depositors rather than payments in flight.

Sources: InfoMoney, Jornal de Brasilia, Let’s Money, Abecs.

World.title: Peru Pays the Highest Diesel Price in Latin America
World.content:
PERU · ENERGY

Key Facts — The price Peruvian diesel stood at US$7.40 a gallon on data to 7 September.

— The region Comparable prices across fourteen Latin American countries run between roughly US$3.00 and US$6.00 a gallon.

— The position Peru is at the top of the list, and not marginally.

— Who pays it Road freight, fishing, agriculture and mining haulage, all of which are Peruvian export sectors.

— The backdrop Brent has been above US$100 a barrel since 9 September.

— The comparison Several neighbours subsidise fuel directly. Peru does not.

Peruvian diesel costs more than twice what it costs in the cheapest country in the region, and every Peruvian export sector moves on it.

Peru Pays the Highest Diesel Price in Latin America

Diesel in Peru stood at US$7.40 a gallon on data to 7 September, against a regional range that runs from about US$3.00 to US$6.00.

The Comparison

The Gestión survey covering fourteen Latin American countries places Peru at the top at US$7.40 a gallon. Mexico, Guatemala, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama, Chile, Costa Rica, Brazil, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Colombia, Ecuador and Bolivia all fall below it, in a band running roughly from US$3.00 to US$6.00.

That is not a small premium. At the bottom of the range Peruvian hauliers are paying more than double what their counterparts pay.

Diesel moves freight, fishing fleets, farm machinery and ore in Peru.

Why It Is So High

Three things separate Peru from the cheaper end of the table. Several of those countries subsidise fuel directly, Bolivia and Ecuador among them, at considerable fiscal cost.

Peru also imports a large share of its refined diesel rather than producing it domestically, which adds freight and margin to every gallon.

And its tax treatment of fuel is heavier than several neighbours, with the selective consumption tax applying on top of the import cost.

None of those is new. What has changed is the oil price. Brent passed US$100 a barrel on 9 September and has stayed there, which raises the whole table and raises the top of it most.

Peru has not announced a fuel subsidy comparable to its neighbours.

Who It Lands On

Diesel is not a consumer fuel in Peru in the way petrol is. It moves freight, it runs fishing fleets, it powers agricultural machinery and it hauls ore.

All four are export sectors. Peru shipped US$63.5 billion in the first seven months of 2026 and the cost of moving every tonne of it is set by this price.

The fishing exposure is the sharpest. An anchoveta fleet facing an extraordinary coastal El Niño, which ENFEN now puts at 62 percent probability, will be operating at reduced catch against the region’s highest fuel cost.

Neighbouring governments have responded to the oil move with subsidies. Brazil is spending around R$7 billion (about US$1.37 billion) a month holding its pump price. Peru has not announced anything comparable.

How Peruvian Fuel Pricing Works

Peru operates a fuel price stabilisation fund, the FEPC, which is designed to smooth the pass-through of international price moves to the pump rather than to subsidise the price outright.

The mechanism sets a reference band. When international prices sit above it the fund compensates importers, and when they sit below it importers pay in. It has spent much of the past four years in deficit.

That is the structural difference from Bolivia or Ecuador, where the state simply sells fuel below cost and absorbs the gap permanently. Peru smooths, and smoothing does not reduce the level.

What Happens If the Price Stays Up

Brent above US$100 a barrel puts sustained pressure on the stabilisation fund, and a fund in deficit eventually stops smoothing.

Peruvian governments have faced this before. Transport strikes over fuel costs have been a recurring feature of Peruvian politics, and the haulage sector is well organised and quick to act.

A six-week-old government facing the region’s highest diesel price, an El Niño emergency across 893 districts and a fund with limited room has a narrow set of options, none of them cheap.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is diesel in Peru?

US$7.40 a gallon on data to 7 September 2026.

How does that compare?

Against a regional range of roughly US$3.00 to US$6.00 a gallon across fourteen Latin American countries. Peru is the most expensive.

Why is it so high?

Peru does not subsidise fuel, imports much of its refined diesel, and applies a heavier tax load than several neighbours.

Who pays it?

Road freight, fishing, agriculture and mining haulage, all export sectors.

What about the oil price?

Brent has been above US$100 a barrel since 9 September, which raises the whole regional table.

Sources: Gestion.

World.title: Peruvian Hiring Intentions Reach 40 Percent for the Fourth Quarter
World.content:
PERU · LABOUR

Key Facts — The figure ManpowerGroup puts Peru’s net employment outlook at 40 percent for the fourth quarter of 2026.

— The move Up 13 points from the third quarter and 16 points from the fourth quarter of 2025.

— The rank Second in Latin America, behind Brazil at 53 percent.

— The share 49 percent of employers expect to add headcount between October and December.

— Where it is strongest Cusco at 71 percent, Arequipa and La Libertad at 47, Lima at 42.

— On the wording The survey describes it as among the highest in recent years rather than as an absolute record.

Peruvian employers say they intend to hire at a rate they have rarely reported. What happens to the intention when El Niño arrives is a different question.

Peruvian Hiring Intentions Reach 40 Percent for the Fourth Quarter

ManpowerGroup’s employment outlook survey puts Peru’s net hiring expectation at 40 percent for the final quarter of 2026, a jump of 13 points in three months.

What the Number Is

The net employment outlook is the share of employers expecting to increase headcount minus the share expecting to reduce it, seasonally adjusted. At 40 percent it is up 13 points from the third quarter and 16 points from the same quarter of 2025.

Forty-nine percent of employers surveyed expect to expand headcount between October and December.

Peru ranks second in Latin America on the measure, behind Brazil at 53 percent.

The survey describes the reading as among the highest recorded in recent years. It does not declare an all-time record, and The Rio Times does not report one.

Cusco and Arequipa lead on tourism and mining.

Where the Hiring Is

Cusco leads at 71 percent, a figure driven almost entirely by tourism and the services attached to it.

Arequipa and La Libertad are tied at 47 percent, Lima is at 42, Piura at 33 and Ucayali at 30.

The regional spread tells its own story. Cusco and Arequipa are tourism and mining. Lima is services. Piura and Ucayali, both agricultural and both more exposed to weather, sit at the bottom.

A state of emergency covers 893 districts in more than 20 regions.

The Variable Nobody Can Price

Peru’s national multi-agency committee ENFEN has put the probability of an extraordinary coastal El Niño at 62 percent, and the government has declared a state of emergency across 893 districts in more than 20 regions.

A coastal El Niño damages the anchoveta fishery within a single season, disrupts northern coastal agriculture and washes out infrastructure. Those are precisely the sectors in the regions reporting the weakest hiring intentions.

Hiring intentions are collected before the event and revised after it. A 40 percent reading taken in a quarter when the emergency has been declared but the damage has not arrived should be read as what employers expect, not as what they will do.

Against that, the export side is strong. Peru shipped US$63.5 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 33 percent, on copper and gold.

What the Survey Measures and What It Does Not

The ManpowerGroup outlook is a survey of employer intention, not a record of hiring. It asks firms what they expect to do in the coming quarter and nets the expansions against the reductions.

That makes it a leading indicator with a well-known weakness. Intentions track sentiment closely and outcomes loosely, and they revise hardest when something unexpected arrives between the survey and the quarter.

Its value is in the direction and the spread. A 13-point jump in one quarter is a genuine change in how Peruvian employers are reading the year ahead, whatever the eventual payroll numbers show.

The Informality Problem Underneath

Roughly seven in ten Peruvian workers are in informal employment, which is among the highest rates in Latin America and has barely moved through a decade of growth.

A survey of formal employers therefore describes a minority of the labour market, and the minority that is least exposed to the shocks that hit everyone else.

That is worth holding alongside a strong reading. Formal hiring intentions at 40 percent and an informality rate near 70 percent describe the same economy, and the second number is the one that determines how a bad El Niño season is actually experienced.

What is Peru’s hiring outlook?

A net employment outlook of 40 percent for the fourth quarter of 2026, per ManpowerGroup.

How much has it moved?

Up 13 points from the third quarter and 16 points from the fourth quarter of 2025.

How does it compare regionally?

Second in Latin America behind Brazil at 53 percent.

Which regions lead?

Cusco at 71 percent, Arequipa and La Libertad at 47, Lima at 42, Piura at 33 and Ucayali at 30.

Is it a record?

The survey calls it among the highest in recent years rather than an outright record.

World.title: Another Tremor in Choco as Colombia Debates a Tourism Tax Cut
World.content:
COLOMBIA · RECONSTRUCTION

Key Facts — The tremor A magnitude 4.6 earthquake struck Istmina, Chocó, at 06:16 local time on Saturday 12 September.

— The depth 43 kilometres, with the epicentre about 13 kilometres from Sipí.

— Where it was felt Cali, Pereira, Armenia, Yumbo, Buga, Circasia and Dosquebradas.

— The response Some buildings in Cali were evacuated as a precaution. No major damage reported.

— The context One month and two days after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake of 10 August.

— The proposal AmCham Colombia has backed a temporary VAT cut on airline tickets to help tourism in the affected areas.

The ground under Chocó has not stopped moving, and the reconstruction is now arguing about the price of a plane ticket.

Another Tremor in Choco as Colombia Debates a Tourism Tax Cut

A magnitude 4.6 aftershock struck Chocó on Saturday morning, felt across the coffee region and into Cali, as the government weighed a temporary tax cut aimed at restoring tourism to the earthquake zone.

The Tremor

The Servicio Geológico Colombiano recorded a magnitude 4.6 event at Istmina, Chocó, at 06:16 local time on Saturday 12 September, at a depth of 43 kilometres with the epicentre around 13 kilometres from Sipí.

It was felt in Cali, Pereira, Armenia, Yumbo, Buga, Circasia and Dosquebradas. Some buildings in Cali were evacuated as a precaution and no major damage was reported.

This falls one month and two days after the magnitude 7.4 earthquake of 10 August, which killed 321 people. More than 1,300 aftershocks have been recorded since, and one report puts the wider swarm above 1,200 events.

A 4.6 is small in energy terms and not small in effect on a population that has been feeling tremors for a month, or on buildings already weakened by the main shock.

The epicentre sat about 13 kilometres from Sipi, at 43 kilometres depth.

The Tax Proposal

Separately, AmCham Colombia’s president María Claudia Lacouture publicly backed a temporary reduction in value added tax on airline tickets, aimed at restoring tourism to the Quindío and coffee-region areas hit by the earthquake.

She described the government’s evaluation of the measure as well judged for driving tourism and accelerating recovery.

The measure is at the evaluation stage. No rate and no timeframe has been announced, and no decree has been issued. Reporting it as a decided policy would be premature.

Sixteen departments and 498 municipalities recorded effects from the August earthquake.

Whether It Would Work

Air fares into the coffee region are a real constraint on domestic tourism, and Colombian domestic aviation carries a heavy tax load relative to the base fare.

The argument against is the one made against every sectoral tax break. It costs revenue immediately, the benefit accrues partly to airlines rather than passengers, and removing it later is politically harder than granting it.

The argument for is that the coffee region’s economy is unusually tourism-dependent and the alternative forms of support are slower to reach it.

What is not in dispute is the need. Sixteen departments and 498 municipalities recorded effects from the August earthquake, and the reconstruction programme now runs to eleven decrees.

Why Aftershocks Keep Coming

Aftershock sequences follow a well-described statistical pattern. Frequency declines roughly in inverse proportion to the time since the main shock, and magnitude is capped at somewhat below the main event.

A magnitude 7.4 releases an enormous amount of energy along a fault, and the surrounding rock adjusts for months. More than 1,300 recorded events in a month is high but not anomalous.

The practical danger is cumulative rather than individual. A structure cracked by the main shock can fail in a tremor a fraction of its size, which is why engineering assessment before reoccupation matters more than the magnitude of any single aftershock.

What the Coffee Region Lost

Quindío and the wider Eje Cafetero are among Colombia’s most tourism-dependent departments, built around coffee estates, small hotels and a national park economy.

That model has almost no shock absorption. A small hotel with no bookings has no revenue, and the sector employs a large share of the local workforce directly and indirectly.

It also has a precedent. The 1999 Armenia earthquake killed around a thousand people in the same region, and the reconstruction took years. The tourism economy that rebuilt afterwards is the one now exposed again.

That history is why a tax measure aimed at restoring visitor numbers is being discussed at all, ahead of the more conventional instruments.
