World.title: ‘Happy, relieved, respected’
World.content:
Councillor Garfield James (JLP, Sheffield Division) vows to support Councillor Julian Chang (JLP, Savanna-la-Mar Division), saying he will not allow anyone from inside the Westmoreland Municipal Corporation to bully her. Rosalee Wood Condell

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — Councillor Julian Chang (Jamaica Labour Party, Savanna-la-Mar Division) officially crossed the floor during Thursday’s sitting of the Westmoreland Municipal Corporation (WMC) after a tumultuous time with the People’s National Party (PNP).

She is the third defection from the PNP benches, with Ian Myles of the Little London Division and Garfield James of the Sheffield Division making the switch in 2024.

The formal announcement confirming Chang’s change of allegiance came with WMC Chief Executive Officer Marlette Wellington reading a letter submitted to Mayor Danree Delancy. The initial letter had been emailed, stalling the process as protocol dictates that it has to be submitted in hard copy.

“At this point, in consultation with my constituents, we have come to the decision that I can no longer sit with arrogance, disrespect, and of fundamental importance, poor representation. Hence, my crossing the floor to join the JLP, that practises progressive peopleism. I, therefore, choose Jamaica” said a section of the letter.

Its reading prompted an outburst of applause from PNP councillors within the chamber, raising questions from Myles and James as to whether the reaction was intended as commendation or political sarcasm.

Following the notice, a motion was immediately tendered to strip Chang of her assignments on three municipal committees: Poor relief, human resources, and the finance sub-committee.

Reading from municipal correspondence, CEO Wellington detailed the swift replacements: Councillor Arthur Colly (PNP, Negril Division) now goes to poor relief; Councillor Lidden Lewis (PNP, Frome Division) is now on the human resources committee; and Councillor Jerome Bacchas (PNP, Darliston Division) is now named to the finance sub-committee.

Addressing her abrupt removal from the committees, Chang remained unfazed.

“I don’t feel no way,” she told the Jamaica Observer following the meeting. “I feel happy and relieved. I am now respected.”

Her transition was warmly received by her new JLP colleagues, with James stepping forward to pledge full backing for the Savanna-la-Mar representative.

“I will give you the support that you need,” James asserted. “And we will not allow anyone inside this corporation to bully you.”

Chang emphasised that her decision to align with the governing JLP stems from a desire to deliver tangible infrastructural development to her constituents in Savanna-la-Mar, support she claims was consistently denied to her while under the PNP banner.

“I know and believe that more can be done for the people of Savanna-la-Mar, for the parish of Westmoreland, and for the city that we now live in,” Chang explained.

She pointed to the severe degradation of local infrastructure.

“A classic example is we have a road which is called Segre Street, which is supposed to be maintained by the Municipal Corporation, and right now, there is neither road, pass, nor anywhere for people to walk,” Chang charged.

“Segre Street has deteriorated under the over 40 years of PNP having this council, and it is still not fixed and there are many other roads that are going bad,” she added.

Chang stated that through her new alignment with the governing party, the road has now been slated for rehabilitation under the Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to Our Road Network (SPARK) programme.

“It will be fixed by the Jamaica Labour Party, by this Government, for the people of Jamaica, for the people here,” she declared. “And it’s time. It’s time. We need Savanna-la-Mar to be fixed. We need structural infrastructure to come into the areas.”

She added that she looks forward to collaborating with agencies such as the National Infrastructure Renewal and Rehabilitation Agency (NaRRA) to address historical deficiencies across the parish.

When asked whether she intends to seek re-election on a JLP ticket in the next local government elections, Chang sidestepped the question, saying, “I will continue to represent the people of Savanna-la-Mar.”

Her formal crossing of the floor marks the culmination of months of escalating internal friction within the PNP.

Elected councillor for the Savanna-la-Mar Division in the local government elections of February 2024, Chang served under the party for two years and four months before tendering her resignation from the PNP on June 29, 2026.

The roots of the rift trace back to February 2025, when she reported experiencing unwanted advances and receiving explicit messages from Member of Parliament for Westmoreland Central Dwayne Vaz. The fallout deepened following the September 2025 General Election, during which allegations surfaced accusing Chang of working against PNP interests within the constituency.

The conflict spilled into the public domain on January 26, 2026, when Chang aired her grievances against Vaz during an interview on

Nationwide News Network. On January 30, the PNP announced the creation of a special investigative committee, separate from its Internal Affairs Commission, to probe the harassment allegations and political fallout.

By late June 2026, citing a two-year backlog of unresolved grievances and institutional disrespect, Chang cut ties with the PNP, paving the way for her formal integration into the JLP this week.

Outside the Westmoreland Municipal Corporation building on Thursday, two loyal constituents waited to greet Chang as she exited, offering enthusiastic approval of her political switch.

Icilda Johnson, a local resident and former PNP supporter who encouraged Chang to make the jump, recalled advising her early on to realign. Another constituent, Carol Waisome, expressed similar joy, recalling how she embraced Chang despite their past political differences.

“My girl this. She a hard-working lady. A di right party she deh pon now. Right side. She deh pon the good ship and the right side,” said Waisome.

World.title: Beyond saving lives, restoring them
World.content:
Level 2 physiotherapist and Lamaze childbirth educator at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) Monique Richmond (centre) shows a model of a human pelvis to (from left) UHWI’s Senior Director Clinical Services Dr Carl Bruce; the hospital’s Acting Chief Executive Officer Sydney Powell; dean of the Faculty of Medical Sciences Professor Joseph Plummer; head of the hospital’s Physiotherapy Department Dionne Bennett; and Opposition spokesperson on health Dr Alfred Dawes, at the department’s open day on Thursday.Naphtali Junior

FOR patients of the University Hospital of the West Indies’ (UHWI) Physiotherapy Department, rehabilitation has meant more than recovering from injury or surgery; it marks the return of independence to their daily lives.

When Dr William Aiken took the stage during the department’s open day on Thursday in a leg cast supported by crutches, he showed up in the capacity of a patient, though he also bore the titles of consultant urologist and head of surgery at UHWI.

“On the 26th of July, I had a little tussle with a croaking lizard, and had severed my left Achilles tendon and had surgery on the 3rd of August to repair it. And as you would know, physiotherapy is a critical part of the rehabilitation process after undergoing an injury like that,” said Aiken, as he chuckled at his misfortune.

He was among other patients who shared their rehabilitation testimonies during the open day which formed part of activities to mark the 2026 World Physiotherapy Week.

For a specialist whose days are dedicated to treating diseases of the urinary tract and male reproductive system, the sudden accident altered Aiken’s routine. However, given the nature of his job, the head surgeon could not stay away from his duties for long. He began occupational rehabilitation, a process designed to return a patient to a functional state within their professional role.

“I reached out to Dr Bennett [director of the physiotherapy department], and she accepted me as a patient with alacrity, and she and her staff have been very kind to me. I have benefited from her expertise. When I come here, I’m treated royally, and I can speak to the facilities that are here; they are second to none…So I can truly say that I’m very proud of this physiotherapy department and what it offers,” said Aiken.

Now back in the operating room, the head surgeon has adapted to his recovery by sitting to rest his leg during procedures, a minor adjustment that allows him to press on with his life’s work.

“I have never met an unpleasant physiotherapist, never. In all the years I’ve been working here, and I’ve been here 30 plus years, physiotherapists are really an important backbone of the services offered in the hospital,” said Aiken.

Opposition spokesperson on health Dr Alfred Dawes also gave high praises to the physiotherapy department, as the greeting he was slated to deliver turned into a testimony.

“For most of my career, I was never really was enthusiastic about physiotherapy. It was [just] another speciality…But then something magically happened that changed my entire outlook on physiotherapy; I turned 40. And every joint in my body had a press conference to announce that they were there,” Dawes said while laughing.

His once active lifestyle derailed by ageing pains, led Dawes to seek rehabilitation at UHWI’s Physiotherapy Department, which, he said, allowed him to pivot, heal, and remain spry.

“It was physiotherapists, some of you in this room, who helped me to get back to normal from the injuries I sustained while trying to be physically active, from my toe all the way up to my neck, literally. So physiotherapy is more than just a discipline adjacent to surgery. After I became a patient and a client, I became the best friend of many physiotherapists… And what I’ve learned could never be taught in any textbook at all,” said Dawes.

He added that a physiotherapist does more than repair torn muscles or broken bones as they give people hope that inspires them to continue living despite injury.

“We have built a health system that is very good at saving lives, but not very good at restoring lives. We [doctors] stabilise the heart, but yet we abandon the patient. The stroke patient survives the night on the ward and then everything that matters afterwards is in your hands. You, the therapist, not in the theatre, not in the pharmacy, [but] on the mat, the parallel bars, six weeks on, six months on, 16 months on…. Medicine adds years to the life, but physiotherapy adds life to the years,” Dawes said.

Minister of National Security Horace Chang sent a pre-recorded message that shared his experience with physiotherapy after undergoing major cardiac surgery.

“I have had the experience of going through triple bypass surgery in the end of October to November 2025. It was successful and I chose to do the cardiac rehab at the University Hospital’s physiotherapy department. I could not have made a better decision. They are professional, courteous, and committed to their jobs. They look after their patients proficiently, irrespective of who they are. Recovery went smoothly, and today I am doing better than I was before surgery,” said Chang.

He congratulated the department on the work they have done over the years, and encouraged the physiotherapists to continue positively impacting ailing Jamaicans who yearn to regain normalcy and autonomy over their lives.

“Dr Bennett and her team have made one of the finest professional units in the country, they deserve every support, and I send my commendations and best wishes to the university’s physiotherapy department,” said Chang.

World.title: Will Lagarde bite the apple? ECB President leaves everyone guessing in Normandy
World.content:
On stage, she even encouraged reporters who made the trip to Normandy to cover her potential political comeback to pack up early, promising that they would be disappointed.

But there are signs suggesting that the ECB chief, who entered into politics during the presidency of France's apple-loving Jacques Chirac, is increasingly willing to weigh in on the campaign.

While she promised to stay at least until the end of the year, Lagarde previously refused to rule out leaving before the end of her term, which ends in October 2027.

Earlier this week, she announced that she would publish her first autobiography, Lady First, in January. She also waded into the French presidential debate by rejecting French far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s proposal to wipe out government debt.

Her presence at the apple festival in the 15th-century Manoir de la Fortière — an unconventional locale for a central banker's speech — might be yet another signal. Opening the event, Morin said that he tried to invite her for years but never managed to make it work. Until this year.

Christine Lagarde at the Fête de la Pomme, France, on September 12, 202. | Giorgio Leali/POLITICO

“Everyone is happy to have you here and I realized to what extent you have an exceptional reputation,” said Morin, who worked with Lagarde when they both served as ministers under conservative president Nicolas Sarkozy, including during the 2008 financial crisis.

World.title: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see a united Ireland
World.content:
Donald Trump and Taoiseach Micheál Martin listen to a question from the media at Farmleigh House in Phoenix Park in the Irish capital Dublin on September 12, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

“It’s going to happen eventually”, the U.S. president said in Dublin during a golf-focused trip to the long-divided island.

DUBLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump waded into another age-old conflict Saturday, declaring on a golf-focused visit to Ireland that he’d like to see the island unified — the nightmare scenario for Northern Ireland’s British unionists.

Sitting beside Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin after an overnight flight from Washington, Trump said he couldn’t understand why Northern Ireland — the part of the island that remained in the U.K. when the rest of Ireland won independence over a century ago — hadn’t already joined the Republic of Ireland.

“I’d love to see it unified. I think it’d be great. A great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually,” Trump said, gesturing to Martin, who has spent years trying behind the scenes to build better relations with unionists, to little avail. “You’ve got the right man over here to get it moving. But I think it would be a fantastic thing. Now the U.K. will have something to say about it obviously. But I think it’d be a great thing. How can it be bad?”

World.title: Farage’s Reform UK gets two £36m donations from crypto billionaires
World.content:
Delo argued in an opinion piece for The Telegraph that Reform needed the injection to make the election “a fair fight.” Delo, who was already one of Reform’s largest donors, said he wanted to give Reform “a level playing field” at the next general election.

The paper on Saturday also published an opinion piece from Harborne, where he called his donation “a philantropic gift to our country.”

Farage thanked the two men for their contributions. “Both men know that we are the only party that can turn the country around,” he said in a statement.

Reform UK was leading the polls since April 2025 , according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. But the party has now slumped slightly behind Labour, with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the helm and after a bizarre by-election where Farage defeated satirical candidate Count Binface.

The right-wing force is currently rushing to get battle-ready amid speculation Burnham could trigger an early general election, though one is not due until 2029. Reform UK is on the hunt for potential candidates to run as MP, and has only about 100 star candidates considered ready to run at the moment.

World.title: Portugal wants EU cash to pay for firefighting goats
World.content:
José Manuel Fernandes Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries of Portugal at the European Council in Brussels in Belgium on 9 December 2024. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

As budget negotiations intensify, capitals are reaching for a new argument to keep money in the farming pot: climate change.

Portugal’s minister for agriculture has a burning desire for the next EU long-term budget: more goats.

José Manuel Fernandes wants Brussels to help pay shepherds to let goats, cows and sheep graze on shrubs in areas at high risk of wildfires — a low-tech approach that experts say the EU has been ignoring for too long. Portugal and some regions in Spain are already running their own programs.

“We are using our national money, but it is work that we are doing for all the European Union,” Fernandes told POLITICO at an informal meeting of ministers in Dublin, arguing that preventing fires helps lower carbon emissions.

World.title: EU delays key tobacco tax vote until after Swedish election
World.content:
The European Commission proposed increasing levies on cigarettes and setting minimum rates on newer products like vapes, heat-not-burn tobacco and nicotine pouches in July last year.

The plan has become a flashpoint for Sweden, which has a long tradition of using snus — a pouch of tobacco that sits between the gums. As such, Stockholm has strongly opposed raising taxes on similar nicotine pouches.

Delaying the vote gives extra time for Sweden to appoint a new finance minister and for the capitals to negotiate a way out of the current stalemate.

The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, confirmed the vote has been pushed from October to November's ministerial meeting.

Four diplomats granted anonymity to speak candidly about the sensitive negotiations said the postponement is meant to give Sweden's next government extra time to change its mind.

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said they will "continue[s] to engage bilaterally with the aim of securing unanimous political agreement at the November ECOFIN" meeting of finance ministers.

World.title: Escaping the AI safety nightmare: What can governments do?
World.content:
A case in point is that OpenAI agents hacked a German website back in May to use it as a messaging board, Reuters reported last week. OpenAI had not publicly announced the incident and responded to the Reuters reporting on X saying: “We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment.”

“[Reporting] timelines are going to need to be dramatically shortened [for incidents], and so we need much better continuous monitoring capabilities,” said Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at London-based think tank the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, adding that the data will be needed in real time “and that will be true for governments and for labs.”

Speaking at a London event for U.K. lawmakers arranged by campaign group ControlAI on Monday, computer scientist Stuart Russell said that the most concerning aspect of the Hugging Face incident for him was that “by running a thousand agents communicating with each other, they were able to generate behaviors that no one agent could do by itself,” referring to investigations showing the incident was far more severe than OpenAI first acknowledged.

“But [in] the evaluations, standard testing is done with a single AI system, not with a thousand,” he told lawmakers, so now the industry must anticipate the possibility of many agents all collaborating at once.

Out of alignment

Beyond avoiding any obvious mistakes in testing, there are issues in the culture of AI testing that are more deeply embedded.

The concept of the alignment of AI models or agents — i.e. making sure AI systems do what they're told by human users and don’t go off-piste — has been one of the cornerstones for AI safety in the industry’s eyes.

World.title: ‘Abuse of power’: Von der Leyen rapped after backing space mega deal
World.content:
“Endorsing a merger at a conference covered by the media, without any substantive review, is an abuse of power and misconduct,” the French MEP wrote on X.

Von der Leyen was referring to Project Bromo, a joint venture between satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to compete, at least in part, with the Starlink satellite-internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which recently went public in the U.S. and is valued around $2 trillion.

“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” von der Leyen said.

Her words would have been music to the ears of the summit host, French President Emmanuel Macron, who has publicly backed the project together with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

But they raised red flags with the antitrust community in Brussels, where the project has yet to be formally notified or assessed by the EU executive’s competition department led by Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera.

“What is the point of Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera and the Directorate General for Competition if it is the president of the Commission who unilaterally decides a case?” Yon-Courtin asked.

World.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls on AI companies to slow down development amid superintelligence risks
World.content:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence (AI) companies to slow down the development of the powerful technology, as concerns mount over the risks of "superintelligent" computer systems.

 

Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI's capabilities exceed human intelligence.

His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies and industry giants of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," wrote Amodei in a post on his personal website.

"AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious."

FILE - Pages from the Anthropic website and the company's logos are displayed on a computer screen in New York, Feb. 26, 2026 Patrick Sison/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way," said Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic, which developed AI model Claude, with his sister Daniela in 2021.

"But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence," added the Anthropic chief executive.

Amodei's statement echoes another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development. Then in late July, Sam Altman, head of Anthropic rival OpenAI – developers of ChatGPT – said developers might need to voluntarily pump the brakes on their rapid advances to give society a chance to catch up.

Around the same time as the June statement, more than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies, including Amodei himself, signed a petition calling on the US government to help "deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development."

OpenAI had revealed that during testing, the AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code.

Earlier this week, 27-year-old Jacob Coxon, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pre-training AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.

Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data of all different kinds, from pictures to videos to voice recordings, which help it understand things to then be able to generate images or answer user prompts on chat platforms.

"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," said Coxon in a chain of posts on X on Tuesday.

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he added.

World.title: Capgemini sells US unit criticised over ICE contract
World.content:
French IT giant Capgemini announced on Saturday that it has reached a definitive agreement to sell its US subsidiary, following controversy over its links with ICE, Donald Trump's immigration police force.

 

The buyer is ITC Federal, "a US provider of digital services and solutions for federal agencies responsible for homeland security and defence", Capgemini said in a press release (source in French).

"This transaction is subject to the usual conditions for a deal of this kind and is expected to be completed in the coming weeks," the group said.

In February, Capgemini announced its intention to sell Capgemini Government Solutions, its US subsidiary specialising in services for federal agencies. The decision came after the disclosure of a contract with ICE covering the provision of a tool designed to identify foreign nationals present on US soil and track their movements.

At the time, Capgemini argued that "the usual legal constraints in the United States on contracting with federal entities engaged in classified activities did not allow the Group to exercise proper control over certain aspects of this subsidiary's operations".

Members of parliament, along with Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure, then called on the company to shed light on its activities in the United States.

Tasked with implementing the hardening of Donald Trump's immigration policy, the heavily armed ICE officers have faced fierce criticism across the United States for intervention methods considered violent. The agency was notably blamed after the shooting deaths of two US citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.

Operating in around fifty countries, Capgemini is among the leading French companies listed on the stock exchange. The group generated turnover of 22.5 billion euros in 2025.

The subsidiary in question represented only 0.4% of the group's global turnover that year, and less than 2% of its revenues in the United States, according to Capgemini.

World.title: AfD's Ulrich Siegmund's comments on arms and 'remigration' spark fiece criticism
World.content:
The AfD's lead candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state, Ulrich Siegmund, has sparked fierce criticism with remarks about the possible use of military equipment in a future "remigration and deportation offensive".

 

The background is the planned establishment of a production site of the Israeli defence company Elbit Systems in Sangerhausen. At a press conference, Siegmund drew a link between the production of armaments, domestic security and the migration policy his party is pursuing.

Siegmund initially stated that the AfD did not fundamentally oppose the production of armaments. Arms production could, among other things, be important for domestic security, the stability of the country and national defence. He then referred to his party's migration policy objectives.

"The production of military equipment was not being demonised across the board," he said, because suitable means would be needed later for "remigration and deportation offensives."

Following the criticism that ensued, Siegmund clarified his remarks.

Arms production was a broad field and covered not only weapons but also vehicles, protective technology and other equipment on which the Bundeswehr, the police and security agencies depended.

In his view, these areas needed to be strengthened, not least in order to enforce the law, carry out deportations consistently and make a "genuine remigration offensive" possible.

If a new site served national defence, domestic security and the enforcement of law and order, this was, from the AfD's point of view, a duty of the state.

'No arms for foreign wars'

At the same time, the AfD politician stressed that his party rejected supplying military equipment for "foreign wars".

There was, he noted, a major difference between Germany producing such equipment itself and supplying it to conflicts abroad and thereby possibly taking part in them.

The AfD therefore wanted to examine closely what would be produced in Sangerhausen and under what conditions.

The possible arrival of Elbit Systems in Sangerhausen has already been causing controversy for some time. There have been protests against the project from the local population, which are also supported by the The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

The company is an Israeli defence group based in Haifa that develops and manufactures, among other things, drones, howitzers, rocket launchers as well as communication and self-protection systems for military use.

Its best-known products include the Hermes and Skylark drone models.

In Germany, the company's headquarters are in Ulm. According to its own information, Elbit is already working for the Bundeswehr and supplies, among other things, self-protection systems for aircraft.

No stance yet on Israeli arms manufacturer

An industrial site of around 130 hectares has been earmarked for the potential factory in Sangerhausen. The town's mayor, Torsten Schweiger, recently stated that neither final assembly of drones nor of shells or ammunition was planned there.

A final decision on the plant has not yet been taken. Siegmund also said that his party had not yet adopted a definitive position. In addition to security and foreign policy issues, the economic impact on the region also has to be taken into account.

The AfD politician's remarks, meanwhile, have prompted fierce reactions.

The Social Democratic Party's (SPD) parliamentary group leader in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament, Katja Pähle, described Siegmund's comments as a political threat. In her view, they were not a case of an unfortunate choice of words.

"Anyone who brings military equipment into play in connection with a planned mass expulsion of people is talking about violence as a means of politics," Pähle said. At the same time, she called on the BSW to state its position on the AfD politician's statements.

The BSW in turn also reacted critically. Fabio De Masi, the party's co-chair at federal level, accused the AfD of backing rearmament and of justifying the possible arrival of the Israeli defence company by linking it to the use of military technology for "remigration".

This showed, in his view, that the AfD had no real intention of governing and was instead seeking a way out through provocation.

The statements are politically explosive also because the BSW is the only party in the new Saxony-Anhalt state parliament that is fundamentally willing to hold talks with the AfD. No decision on cooperation has however been taken yet.

Following the state election, the BSW signalled that it was prepared to discuss cooperation on specific projects and issues. The Christian Democratic Party (CDU), SPD, Greens and Left Party continue to rule out working with them.

In the Saxony-Anhalt state election, the AfD emerged by a clear margin as the strongest party. It won 43.8 percent of the vote but still fell short of an absolute majority.

Siegmund subsequently reaffirmed his party's claim to form a government. He did not rule out a government with an extremely narrow majority. The aim, the AfD politician said, was to form a government that was as stable as possible.

World.title: Jimek: Polish hip-hop is one of the best in Europe, and I won't even apologize for saying that
World.content:
Radzimir Dębski's creative life is crawling with the number twelve. On June 12, 2026, his album "Études for Piano, Sampler, Orchestra and Friends" came out, on which he invited twelve rappers, and on September 12 of that same year he'll be sharing the stage with them at a concert in Warsaw's Bemowo district.

 

And that's not all. It was back in 2012 that he won the remix contest for Beyoncé's single "End of Time," beating out more than three thousand creators from 25 countries. He happened to be in Berlin when Beyoncé herself called to tell him, "I wanna congratulate you because you are the winner." It was Queen B. herself who opened the door to a string of foreign gigs that have kept multiplying ever since. He's collaborated with, among others, Snoop Dogg at the BET Awards 2025 in Los Angeles and, in December of that same year, at "Snoop's Holiday Halftime Party" in Minneapolis.

The album "2015," which he made with Miłosz "MIUOSH" Borycki (a recording of a concert held at the headquarters of the National Symphony Orchestra of Polish Radio in Katowice), caught the attention of the legendary Deutsche Grammophon. Video clips from the concert were shared with admiration by stars including Ashton Kutcher, Mobb Deep, and Nicki Minaj. His artistic activity isn't confined to Poland and the United States, though. He's performed in Japan, Germany, and Kenya, among other places.

Jimek Chooses Poland Again

Despite these global opportunities — bolstered by the universalism of classical, symphonic music — Jimek is once again choosing Poland, and it's in Poland that he's preparing his next big musical project, one that completes his hip-hop-classical trilogy. In an interview with Euronews, he explains why:

"First of all, being at home, meaning going back to where you're from, is something that's become a need for me, and at the same time a way of searching for my own balance. If my own identity gets warped, that's something dangerous for me. But at the same time it's also an enormous pleasure and relief. Being yourself in Warsaw in the summer... There aren't many places in the world I like more. And I don't just mean Warsaw, but Poland in general," he says, adding that these are "down-to-earth" reasons.

There are also artistic reasons behind it. The album "Études (...)" (org. "Etiudy na pianino, orkiestrę, sampler i kolegów") is the result of a journey that, after many twists and turns, is coming full circle.

"First there was the story of American hip-hop, and because of how it spread, I understood right away that I'd have to do the story of Polish hip-hop too. At the same time, I dreamed from the start that all the artists I might want to include would be together on stage. Logistically, that was almost impossible."

Three Acts of One Story

The first concert at Bemowo (2022) was a test of whether it was even possible to get that many rappers in one place. The second — with the National Symphony Orchestra of Polish Radio at Silesian Stadium in 2023 — was a bigger risk, but it worked out. The third chapter is a concert with people he met while working on those earlier projects, with whom Jimek created songs from scratch.

"This concert will be different in that, having had all these opportunities, we also recorded a new album — new tracks came out of it, which might give this whole story its best possible punchline," Jimek explains to Euronews.

Just as in the previous two editions, both classic tracks and new material are featured.

An Album with Friends After 20 Years in the Basement

Classical music is clearly the glue holding the entire album "Études for Piano, Sampler, Orchestra and Friends" together, with the titular piano as the lead instrument — though it's clear that Jimek, as the host, approaches each of the twelve artists individually, trying to uncover what they need. In the case of Bedoes 2115's Étude No. 3, for instance, a guitar makes an appearance.

"When you've spent 20 years sitting alone in a basement with a computer, at some point you also want to meet another human being and see what different creative decisions get made in someone else's company," Jimek tells Euronews. "So I went looking for exactly that — a situation with another person that changes our decision-making process right from the start, just to see where it would take these tracks."

Polish Hip-Hop and the Power of Language

Jimek makes no secret of having two musical loves — classical and hip-hop. Especially the Polish kind, which, in his view, is among the best in Europe.

"This is completely biased, and I won't even apologize for it. Polish hip-hop is one of the best in Europe. It's very strong musically. That also comes from the samples — from the fact that it grew out of old Polish records, Polish jazz, Polish film scores, Polish popular and entertainment music, sometimes even electronic music," he lists.

"Maybe it's a coincidence, maybe it's the fact that our parents listened to good music. Under communism, jazz was the language of freedom. This Polish hip-hop never tried to be American, never tried to be different. It was Polish from the start, in that same genuine, honest way that a truly genuine and honest person doesn't even realize they're genuine and honest. And that's something you come to appreciate in hindsight — that introversion, the problems that came up in it, those lyrics," he adds, speaking with Euronews.

"I often translate Polish lyrics — from Polish tracks — for friends from abroad. And they're deeply surprised by how good it sounds, how much content is in there, philosophically too, all sorts of heavier things show up in it, and that it's something different. That's also the power of a language that has seven cases."

Radzimir Dębski and Aleksandra Gałka-Reczko at the Hotel Polonia Palace. Paweł Głogowski

Études Against AI

The titular piano études are no accident.

"The piano was something I really missed while I was traveling so much. I managed to get hold of a piano for a longer stretch of time. And it was like going back to practice playing — while at the same time bringing back memories of walking to school, listening to hip-hop. Those two things didn't fit together at all, so in fact almost every track grew out of a little miniature like that, which I'll definitely write down — I think we might even put out a little notebook of these études. In case someone wants to practice something on the piano that's a bit different emotionally — hip-hop for piano."

The record is unpolished, unrefined. You can hear a lot of back-and-forth between the artists — comments, discussions, whistling, interaction.

"These times really are very polished right now. Absolutely. This is a protest against that. So in that sense it's some kind of reaction, a rebellion. Maybe a few years ago I wouldn't have gone this far with it."

Jimek explains that this "rawness" is also a nod to traditional hip-hop skits.

"Skits used to be those little interludes between tracks that, back before streaming and view-counting existed, made up the whole atmosphere of an album. You'd listen to the whole LP, and all those interludes were often conversations in a shop, conversations in a car, conversations in the studio — the whole backstage. For me, artistically, that backstage of the piano, of the process in the studio, is exactly that skit — and often it happens right within a track itself."

"It used to be, maybe, kind of a men's sport, but today masculinity, being a guy, is a subject worth exploring," Radzimir "Jimek" Dębski tells Euronews, Hotel Polonia Palace. Paweł Głogowski

Manhood, Being a Guy, Sensitivity

There are no female rappers on the album. All twelve invited artists are men. Jimek explains to Euronews:

"It just happened on its own. At some point I noticed it and decided not to change it — quite the opposite, to turn it into an asset. Rap that's changing is also something we talk about a lot. It comes up in the lyrics. It used to be, maybe, kind of a men's sport, but today masculinity, being a guy, is a subject worth exploring. What does it even mean? We have different approaches to it. That sensitivity... how do you show it? That's a dilemma for a guy. Maybe in my generation there's this internal dialogue going on: what kind of man should I be, who should I become, what does the world need? Not long ago there was a mood in which traditional manhood was seen as passé. Now we're at a moment where maybe we're seeing again that it's needed."

The interview was conducted at the Hotel Polonia Palace in Warsaw.

World.title: Trump says he'd like to see Ireland 'reunified' as he meets Taoiseach Martin in two-day official visit
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic,” wading into a complex and politically charged subject during a two-day visit to a major tournament at his private Irish golf course.

 

At a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the UK’s Northern Ireland.

“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified," Trump offered when asked for his opinion on the issue by a reporter. "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.

“I think it would be a fantastic thing," he said, adding that "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.”

US President Donald Trump during a meeting with Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether it's Irish or British — drove decades of violence in Northern Ireland that left some 3,600 people dead. Previous US presidents have avoided commenting directly on the subject, even those, like Joe Biden, with strong ancestral and emotional ties to Ireland.

When Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbour Britain, became a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country a century ago, a six-county region in the north with a Protestant majority remained part of the United Kingdom.

Northern Ireland was split between two main communities, nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British.

Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles, unwinding three decades of violence involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.

A 1998 peace accord that Washington was instrumental in brokering largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved.

US President Donald Trump arrives for a meeting Ireland's President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

The peace accord allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it.

Newly-appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said point blank on Wednesday that there won’t be another referendum on reunification unless there is an evident desire for one.

“I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one,” said Burnham.

Trump also held talks Saturday in Dublin with his Irish counterpart Catherine Connolly and will address US and Irish business leaders at the US ambassador's official residence, before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open golf championship.

Connolly is a left-wing politician who was among those who protested when Trump visited Ireland in 2019, during his first term in office. She is now Ireland's elected head of state, which is a largely symbolic and ceremonial position.

A supporter of the Palestinian cause, she has in the past criticised US policy in the Middle East and called the Republican president a “bully” in his dealings with other states, pressuring of them and approach to foreign policy and bilateral relations.

Ireland's President Catherine Connolly greets US President Donald Trump during a meeting at Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

The Irish president met Trump at the end of a red carpet at her official residence in Dublin. They shook hands and chatted before going inside. He emerged alone a few minutes later and saluted as an Irish Defence Forces band played the US national anthem and inspected an Irish Army guard of honour.

Trump rebukes European allies

The US president also lashed out at European allies as he spoke in a joint press conference with Martin following the meeting, slamming them for what he says has been a notable decline in their societies.

"I hate to see what's happening with Europe. I hate to see what's happening on trade, energy, and immigration," he said. "Ooh... that immigration, what you're doing to yourselves, you're just killing yourselves."

He also criticised Washington's relationship with European allies as "disappointing" following many nations' unwillingness to help the Republican president with his Iran war efforts, and the chaos that ensued with the closure of a strategic waterway, the Strait of Hormuz.

The US president however said that his country is maintaining a working relationship with all its allies in the continent.

Donald Trump during a review of soldiers from the Guard of Honor during a visit with Irish President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.

Trump plays golf about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organising some of them in ways that benefit his family business.

His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.

The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump's golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.

Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire.

During that visit, he held talks with the then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss his controversial global ‘reciprocal’ tariff policy.

World.title: Drone attack on Leipzig: clues apparently point to Russian intelligence service
World.content:
Previously undisclosed investigative files have emerged in connection with the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport, reports the newspaper Welt. The information is based not only on the documents themselves, but also on details from security circles.

 

In the course of the investigation, the identities of the two suspects and details of their journeys to and from Germany apparently became known. The findings compiled in the process are said to have been crucial in prompting Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (CDU) and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) to publicly hold Russia responsible for the attack at a joint press conference around a week and a half ago.

At the centre of the investigation are the Russian citizen Oleg Le. and the Belarusian national Andrei Ka. While, according to German security authorities, Le. is believed to have organised the logistical preparations, Ka. is suspected of carrying out the drone attack.

Drone came to rest next to a Ukrainian aircraft

The incident took place on 4 August at Leipzig/Halle Airport. A drone fitted with explosives approached a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. The device was detected and later rendered harmless.

Two other drones are believed, according to current findings, to have failed or been destroyed even before the actual attack: investigators found corresponding debris in the vicinity of the airport.

What makes the attempted attack particularly explosive is the potential blast. According to information from the investigation, a total of around 1.8 kilograms of Semtex was to be used. At the time, the targeted Antonov is said to have been fuelled with around 25,000 litres of kerosene.

In the end, the explosive charge did not detonate, as the detonator apparently became detached, according to current findings. CCTV footage is said to show the drone coming to rest directly next to the aircraft.

DNA trace: possible link to sabotage cases across Europe

The Leipzig case is apparently not being viewed in isolation by European security authorities, Welt reports. Investigators are looking into possible links to other sabotage operations in which drones, explosives or so‑called disposable agents are thought to have been used.

In the investigators' view, a recurring pattern is that individuals with a criminal background are recruited for specific jobs, while the real masterminds remain in the background.

A DNA trace apparently plays a key role in the search for the suspected perpetrators. Investigators found remnants of a glove on an antenna construction that was presumably used to control a drone.

The traces secured there are said to match DNA data already known from Finland and Lithuania. This brought the Belarusian national Andrei Ka. into the focus of investigators.

Ka. is said to have already come to the attention of the authorities in both countries for ordinary criminal offences; in Finland he is reportedly linked, among other things, to property crimes.

Polish authorities are also said to have mentioned his name in connection with a fire at a DIY store in Łódź. The incident in the summer of 2024 is being investigated there as a possible act of sabotage.

Investigators suspect professional planning

The German authorities apparently assume that the attack was not carried out on the spur of the moment. Hints of multiple drones, possible hiding places for equipment and the use of different launch points all point, in the investigators' view, to a pre-planned operation.

Ten days after the attack, investigators reportedly came across another drone and a fire site in Kabelsketal, a municipality in Saxony-Anhalt not far from the airport. Specialists are said to have secured around 50 grams of Semtex there. Semtex is a powerful, malleable explosive developed, among other things, for military and industrial blasting operations.

Potential hiding places were also examined south of the airport: near Schkeuditz, investigators are said to have identified several locations where, in their view, material or explosives could have been stored.

The search was driven forward, among other things, by the analysis of a hire car believed to have been used by the suspects.

Russian intelligence service under scrutiny

Particular importance is attached to Oleg Le. According to German security authorities, he is associated with the Russian military intelligence service GRU and is believed to have been responsible for the logistical side of the operation.

Le. is said to have entered Germany via Turkey. He later left the country via Berlin-Brandenburg airport, initially travelling on to Serbia. According to the available information, he is now back in Russia.

In the investigators' assessment, the German authorities were already aware when he entered the country that he could be linked to the GRU environment. Nevertheless, he was apparently not placed under permanent surveillance.

Political fallout

The dispute has now also had concrete diplomatic repercussions. The federal government has already responded to the allegations and initiated measures against Russia. These include the decision to close the Russian consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. The Russian ambassador was also summoned to the Foreign Office. Further steps, including additional measures at European level, are being examined.

Moscow responded in turn with countermeasures, closing the German consulate general in St Petersburg and also announcing the closure of the Goethe-Institutes in Russia.

The Russian government holds Berlin responsible for the escalation and continues to reject the accusations in connection with the drone attack. From Moscow's perspective, there is insufficient evidence of direct involvement by Russian state bodies.

For the German security authorities, the priority now is to further substantiate the evidence gathered so far and clearly identify those responsible as well as any possible masterminds. If the suspicion of an operation orchestrated by Russian actors is confirmed, the case could have further consequences for German security policy and its policy towards Russia.

World.title: At least 11 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine as Kyiv strikes Russia's 'shadow fleet'
World.content:
At least 11 people were killed and 96 injured across Ukraine in overnight Russian attacks between 11 and 12 September.

 

The Odesa region was hit hardest, but strikes also targeted, among others, the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Sumy, Kharkiv and Kherson regions.

According to Ukraine's Air Force, Russia used 129 drones of various types, as well as Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, eight Kalibr cruise missiles and six guided Kh-59/69 missiles. Around half of the drones deployed were fitted with jet engines.

Ukraine's air defences destroyed or disrupted 110 aerial targets, including six Kalibr missiles, two Kh-59/69 missiles, one S-8000 Banderol cruise missile launched from a drone and 101 unmanned aerial vehicles.

Attack on Odesa

One of the main targets of the overnight attack was Odesa. At around 5.30 a.m., Ukraine's Air Force warned that Russian cruise missiles were heading towards the city from over the Black Sea.

A multi-storey residential building was damaged in the strike. "The enemy attacked the city. A multi-storey residential building has been damaged," said Odesa region governor Oleh Kiper.

The number of wounded in the Odesa region rose as more information came in about the aftermath of the attack. In the end, at least 35 people were injured, including a five-month-old baby and a 17-year-old. Some of the victims required hospitalisation.

A multi-storey residential building in Odesa was damaged in the strike, 12 September 2026. Odesa Regional State Administration

Russian attacks in the Dnipropetrovsk region

Russian forces also attacked the Dnipropetrovsk region. In Dnipro, drones, artillery and air-dropped bombs damaged an industrial facility, residential buildings, garages and vehicles. One person was killed and 19 were injured.

During the night another Russian strike hit an industrial plant in Kryvyi Rih. One person was killed and three were wounded. A 54-year-old man was taken to hospital in a serious condition.

In total, two people were killed and at least 22 wounded in the Dnipropetrovsk region, including a child, governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.

Russian attacks also hit the Zaporizhzhia region. Over the past 24 hours, Russian forces have carried out strikes on 45 towns and villages, including five missile attacks on Zaporizhzhia city. Two people were killed and 11 injured in the region.

In the Donetsk region, four people were killed and five wounded. Two people died in Sloviansk, one in Kramatorsk and another in Yasnohirka, governor Vadym Filashkin said.

In the Kyiv region, one person was killed and three were injured, including a child. Russian attack drones struck five districts: Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil and Vyshhorod. Fifteen facilities were damaged, including seven houses, vehicles, warehouses, hangars and a power line.

In the Sumy region, a 68-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone strike on the Myropillia community. In a separate attack on the Novoslobidske community, a 64-year-old man was wounded. Over the course of the day, Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks on 25 localities there, using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other unmanned aerial vehicles and guided air-dropped bombs.

In the Kharkiv region, a 32-year-old man was killed in an attack on Kharkiv, and a 19-year-old man was wounded elsewhere in the region. Russian forces struck Kharkiv and seven other localities, using guided air-dropped bombs and various types of drones.

In the Kherson region, 18 people were wounded. Russian attacks targeted residential areas as well as critical and social infrastructure. Fifteen residential buildings were damaged, along with shops, a petrol station, a service station, an ambulance and vehicles.

Attack on Russian plant

Ukraine's defence forces confirmed that during the night of 11 to 12 September they carried out a strike on the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara region. The factory supplies products used by the Russian military-industrial complex.

The attack sparked a fire on the plant's premises. "The scale of the damage is still being assessed," Ukraine's General Staff said.

The plant produces, among other things, synthetic rubber, monomers, fractions and additives for high-octane fuels. The Ukrainian military stresses that synthetic rubber is used, among other purposes, in the production of solid fuel for short-range missiles and ballistic rockets.

Earlier, "Ukrainska Pravda" reported a strike by Ukrainian forces on the Machine-Building Plant in Snizhne, located in Russian-occupied territory of the Donetsk region. The plant manufactures components for gas turbine engines, including compressor and turbine discs and blades.

Ukraine targets Russia's "shadow fleet"

As Russia was carrying out its overnight bombardment of Ukraine, Ukrainian forces continued operations aimed at the country's economic backbone.

On 12 September, Robert "Brovdi" Browdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, announced further attacks on Russia's so-called "shadow fleet", used to transport Russian oil in circumvention of some sanctions.

According to Browdi, since the operation began around ten weeks earlier, Ukrainian forces have attacked a total of 285 vessels belonging to Russia's "shadow fleet" operating in the Azov and Black Seas.

The highest number of attacks was recorded in July: 215. In August, a further 54 vessels were struck, and between 1 and 11 September another 16.

Browdi claims that the Ukrainian strikes have almost brought traffic by Russia's "shadow fleet" in the Sea of Azov and the Kerch Strait to a halt. He says the operation has also seriously impeded its activity in the northern and north-eastern parts of the Black Sea.

The commander released footage which, he said, shows an attack by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces on a sanctioned Russian tanker belonging to the "shadow fleet". The ship was reportedly being escorted by a Russian helicopter.

Browdi stressed that revenues from Russian oil exports are one of the sources of funding for the war against Ukraine. Attacks on vessels involved in transporting Russian oil are therefore intended as part of broader efforts to limit Moscow's financial capabilities.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Baghdad confirms attack on Saudi pipeline came from Iraq
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has said it will not relatiate and wants Iraq to "take the necessary measures." Baghdad is under pressure from the United States to rein in Iran-backed militias.

Iraq's government confirmed on Saturday that Friday night attacks on a key Saudi oil pipeline had been launched from Iraqi territory.

Saudi Arabia said that it shut down the pipeline on Friday, calling it a "precautionary measure" over a drone attack that occurred the previous day.

Riyadh said that it would not retaliate, stressing that it wanted to give Baghdad "an opportunity to take the necessary measures."

Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is behind the attacks on the Saudi pipeline?

No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks.

The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an alliance of Iran-backed Iraqi militias, denied any involvement.

The militias are formally part of Iraq's security forces, but some of the groups occasionally act independently.

Also on Saturday, US President Donald Trump said Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack, while also seemingly downplaying the US and Saudi Arabia's conflict with the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia that control swathes of Yemen.

"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."

The Houthis and some of the Iraqi Shiite armed groups are part of what Tehran dubs the "Axis of Resistance," a group of Iran-backed militias in the Middle East that oppose the United States and Israel.

The Yemeni armed group has imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia since July and seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha on Thursday.

The Houthis have previously targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, citing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza amid Israel's offensive in the territory, but have said they do not intend to do so as part of their recent advances along Yemen's coast.

The Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia group has said it will not comply with Baghdad's order to disarm by September 30 [FILE: September 2014] Image: dpa/picture alliance

Iraq under pressure to disband Iran-backed militias

Iraq has been under pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned Shiite armed groups, as some of the militias have hit US-linked targets in the region since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28.

While Baghdad has set a September 30 deadline for their disarmament, several militias have said they will not comply with the order,

The deadline coincides with the date set for the withdrawal of the remaining US-led coalition forces from Iraq.

One of the most influential militias, Kataib Hezbollah, has heavily criticized the disarmament plan and called for guarantees that US forces would never return and measures would be implemented to rid Iraq of US influence on political or economic decision-making.

World.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?
World.content:
The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fears about the reliability of the US, but equally important is the need to keep gold closer to home in the event of a crisis.

Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where about half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security.

To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the United States as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane.

The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move about 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis.

The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness."

France also removed its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although Bank of France Governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time that it was not politically motivated.

The Dutch have moved their gold to the Bank of England Image: Peter Nicholls/REUTERS

Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves, respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns about the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy toward the European Union, including threats to annex part of Greenland.

The gold rush

Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, told DW the outright seizure of assets is an "extremely remote risk" for European central banks. However, he said, there are growing concerns about ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty.

"The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he said.

In general, said Krishnan Gopaul, of the World Gold Council, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs.

A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-tonne average over the preceding decade.

Because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign-debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset, Gopaul said.

"As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he said.

The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the United States and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis.

Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location.

"Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximize resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," Tillett said.

Gopaul said reserve management had become "incredibly important" and that, while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure that the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub that moves fast.

He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the United Kingdom is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market."

"The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he said. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold."

The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion).

The US question

While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making.

Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries.

That decision seems to be driven by concern about US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors.

Tillett said gold remained sensitive to decisions by the US Federal Reserve and general concern about US financial markets meant that gold holders are looking to move their assets.

As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric about Greenland and continued veiled threats toward the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around.

US President Trump's threats against Greenland alarmed EU leaders Image: Federico Parra/Odd Andersen/AFP

Yet the United States, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan, in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved about 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017, it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the United States.

Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves."

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: Ukraine: Several killed in series of Russian strikes
World.content:
Local authorities said several civilians were killed and dozens more wounded across Ukraine by Russian strikes. Meanwhile, the Kremlin has rejected Volodymyr Zelenskyy's proposal to meet with the Russian leader in Miami.

Russia continued on Saturday its constant strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, killing at least four people and wounding dozens more.

According to Ukrainian officials, two people were killed in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, while steelmaker ArcelorMittal reported that two more people were killed at its plant in Kryvyi Rih, a city in the center of the country.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said that a Russian strike on an apartment building in Odesa wounded 37 people and that rescue teams are searching for two missing individuals.

The southern Ukrainian port city of Odesa is a frequent target of Russian attacks Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Odesa Region/Handout/REUTERS

He added that ten regions came under Russian attack last night and that Russian attack drones are still flying over many of them.

Ukraine retaliates by hitting chemical plants

In response to Russian attacks, Kyiv is fighting back. According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine has attacked "chemical enterprises" in the Perm region of the Urals and in the Samara region, which is located southwestern Russia.

The General Staff in Kyiv also reported a fire at a rubber factory in Togliatti, located in the Samara region. According to their statement, the company specializes in producing synthetic rubber important for tactical and ballistic missiles.

Togliatti Mayor, Ilya Sukhih, said that one person was hospitalized following a massive attack on the city. He added that several multi-story residential buildings were damaged.

Kremlin rebuffs Zelenskyy's meeting proposal

In an exclusive interview with DW, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he is willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit in Miami in December.

Zelenskyy backs Putin meeting at Miami G20: 'Results matter' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, on Saturday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow has yet to decide whether Putin will travel to the summit. "We don't know yet ​whether we'll be going to ​Miami," Peskov said, according to Russian media.

Commenting on Zelenskiy's proposal, Peskov reiterated Moscow's longstanding position that if the Ukrainian leader wants to meet with the Russian leader, he should come to Moscow.
