World.title: Zoe Bonafonte: “Hay que disfrutar cada proyecto como si fuera el último y gestionar bien  el dinero, por favor”
World.content:
En un momento de El 47, en uno de los picos emocionales del filme que triunfó en la taquilla y en los Premios Goya de 2025, Zoe Bonafonte (Barcelona, 22 años) canta a capela el tema antifranquista de Chicho Sánchez Ferlosio, Gallo rojo, gallo negro, y rompe a llorar. Para la actriz, que entonces tenía apenas 18 años, aquella era su primera película, y aquella fue la primera escena que le tocó grabar. “No había más remedio que empezar por ahí…”, le dijo Marcel Barrena, director de la película, al también director Daniel Monzón. “Me contó esa anécdota cuando vi su película en un pase antes del estreno oficial, le pregunté por Zoe, porque estaba buscando protagonista para mi siguiente filme, Ruega por nosotras, y me había gustado mucho. Me dijo que esa escena del canto fue la primera que hizo ella y se quedó con la primera toma porque era perfecta. Me dijo que no lo dudara”, explica Monzón, que no lo dudó. Tampoco Estel Díaz. Ni Óscar Pedraza. En los próximos días y meses, la actriz barcelonesa estrena tres películas, dos de ellas como protagonista. Primero llegará A fuego (en cines desde el 21 de agosto), donde junto a la cantante Ruslana reivindica el baile y lo colectivo; después vendrá Enfrentados: Marfil (en Prime Video el 9 de septiembre), primera parte del díptico basado en las novelas de Mercedes Ron en el que interpreta a la hermana pequeña de la protagonista, Ester Expósito, y le seguirá Ébano, en la que tendrá más protagonismo; y, ya en noviembre, tras su paso por el próximo Festival de San Sebastián, estrenará Ruega por nosotras, película basada en los testimonios de decenas de chicas caídas en desgracia o en riesgo de caer que pasaron por el Patronato de Protección a la Mujer durante la dictadura y hasta 1985 “con el fin de elevar su moralidad”.

Jersey de punto, falda midi con flores, calcetines hasta la rodilla y zapatos de piel, todo de PRADA. Santiago Belizón

El encuentro con Zoe tiene lugar a principios del mes de julio en Madrid, reservamos toda una mañana con ella para una sesión de fotos y una larga charla. Su concentración y dedicación quedó clara enseguida: acabando las fotos mucho antes de lo esperado, la charla se podía haber alargado mucho más. A pesar de su aún breve experiencia en el oficio y ante las fatigosas promociones, demuestra una confianza, saber estar y tranquilidad que no tienen nombres más veteranos. No hace ni dos años que descubríamos su nombre con El 47 (después de su paso por las series Amar es para siempre y Escándalo. Relato de una obsesión) y era nominada como actriz revelación en los Goya de 2025 y ya parece un nombre asentado. La pillamos justo cuando acaba de terminar el rodaje de La facultad y a punto de marcharse a Málaga, donde pasará el verano rodando Veleta, “la historia de la primera futbolista española, se cree, porque se hizo pasar por hombre durante muchos años”. Confiesa, además, que dijo que no a una película internacional por conflicto de agenda, aunque tiene claro que quiere trabajar fuera. ¿Cómo se hace para mantener los pies en la tierra y el equilibrio emocional en un cambio de vida y atención tan brusco? “Una de mis mejores amigas me dice siempre: ‘Zoe, ¿necesitas irte a un parque y darte cuenta de todo lo que te ha pasado?”, ríe. “Y es verdad que aún no me han caído muchas fichas. Voy disfrutando cada día, agradeciendo lo que tengo, pero soy consciente del hecho de que llevo sin cuatro años parar de trabajar. Voy tan en el presente que no miro para atrás porque me agobio… Cuando sí me ha pasado, que se me haga un mundo, me ha entrado demasiada ansiedad”. Desde sus primeras entrevistas, Bonafonte ha hablado con mucha honestidad de la importancia de la terapia para ella y, a lo largo de esta charla, menciona en más de una ocasión lo importantes que han sido y son sus amigas, su “red de apoyo”, su madre, su pareja, “la familia escogida…”. “Esta industria es muy puñetera porque, por una parte cuando estás trabajando, bien, pero también es un trabajo muy demandante, se te juntan rodajes en los que estás ahí todos los días 10 y 11 horas. Es muy agotador, pero mejor eso que no trabajar. Y luego cuando no estás rodando, pero estás de promo, es otra movida porque también agota. Te expones mucho y estás también interpretando un papel de alguna manera”, explica precisamente en una de esas mañanas de agotadora promoción. Toma aire y sonríe. “Pero luego tiene tantas cosas tan bonitas. Y sí, es literalmente aprender a gestionarlo, volver a ti, volver a tu red de apoyo, a tus amigas”.

Chaqueta 'denim' con cuello en uve y solapas maxi y pantalón vaquero, ambos de BALENCIAGA. Santiago Belizón

Curiosamente, las dos películas que estrena a continuación como protagonista tienen como corazón emocional la reivindicación de esa red, las amigas como refugio y salvavidas. “Siento que sí es un tema que me toca de forma muy personal en mi vida porque a los 15 me fui de casa y llegué aquí a Madrid a los 16. Entonces, al final he vivido muchos años alejada de mi familia. Y es verdad que ambas películas hablan de la familia escogida”. En A fuego, el grupo de bailarines callejeros que conoce en un lugar llamado El Búnker, en Barcelona, es quien salva a su personaje, Lola, de una espiral depresiva, quien le da respuestas ante la muerte de su hermano y le abre los ojos ante un mundo injusto —con crisis de vivienda, paro juvenil— y la necesidad de actuar como colectivo. En Ruega por nosotras es Ana, una adolescente en Madrid en 1974 que comete el crimen, según su familia, de salir por las noches y acostarse con su novio. Su padre decide ingresarla en el Patronato de Protección a la Mujer para que la enderecen y es enviada a un convento lejos de su casa. Entre horas de trabajos manuales (coser muñecos para Galerías Preciados, limpiar, planchar, cocinar…), rezos, castigos físicos y maltrato psicológico, las chicas allí encerradas encuentran entre ellas el único alivio.

Camisa de lamé, pantalón y cinturón, todo de Nº21 BY ALESSANDRO DELL’ACQUA. Santiago Belizón

Hablando de estas películas también aparece la idea de la responsabilidad como actriz, del micrófono que ahora tiene delante, a través de entrevistas y de los papeles que interpreta. A fuego habla de una Generación Z, a la que Zoe pertenece. “Creo que, al igual que hay una parte de la generación que ve mucho, hay otra que se niega a ver y vive un poco en el pasado, agarrados al que antes las cosas eran mejor”, reflexiona y ahí engancha con la relevancia de una película como Ruega por nosotras, que lleva a la gran pantalla la realidad silenciada que vivieron miles de mujeres durante años en el Patronato. Una realidad que parece distópica, pero que son experiencias reales de supervivientes de aquellos centros. El título, de hecho, Daniel Monzón y su coguionista Jorge Guerricaechevarría se lo pidieron prestado a Consuelo García del Cid de uno de los libros en los que denunció todo lo que ella y tantas como ella sufrieron durante años a espaldas de la sociedad, y en cuyos testimonios se ha basado la película, cortando algunos que “eran tan agresivos que no parecían reales”, cuenta el director. Preparándose para el papel, Bonafonte y sus compañeras de reparto no hablaron con ninguna de ellas, pero ahora está deseando que vean la película y conocerlas. “Aunque algunas no se sientan identificadas porque es una película ficcionada y no puedes abarcar todas las historias, espero que estén contentas y orgullosas con el trabajo que hemos hecho y de que el mundo conozca lo que les pasó”, explica la actriz que reconoce la idoneidad de la película ante un momento de auge de la ultraderecha, la violencia machista y los ataques al feminismo. “Suelo ser una persona bastante optimista, creo que nunca volveremos a algo así, pero es verdad que hay mucha gente que dice que con Franco se vivía mejor y eso es muy preocupante”, cuenta. “No creo que sea un comentario hecho desde la maldad, sino desde la ignorancia y desde el privilegio, sobre todo porque lo dicen personas que no han sido una mujer oprimida del siglo pasado, ni un hombre gay que paga las consecuencias por serlo, ni una persona que tiene una lengua cooficial que no se puede hablar… Yo intento no enfadarme, pero también es fuerte y asusta porque es gente muy joven y dices: ‘¿esto es el futuro o qué?”.

Vestido de punto de LOUIS VUITTON. Santiago Belizón

Para ella su responsabilidad como actriz empieza con formarse e informarse, más aún en películas sociales como las que ha protagonizado, El 47 o Ruega por nosotras —ambas se las ha tatuado en su cuerpo, por cierto—, historias reales a las que tiene que servir, pero sus ganas y capacidad de aprendizaje vienen de atrás. De forma desordenada, durante la entrevista van saliendo todos los campos que ha ido probando en su vida, siempre claramente enfilados hacia algo artístico. “Soy muy de empezar cursos y dejarlos”, admite. Hizo piano, batería, ballet… El saxofón es el único instrumento que ha seguido tocando y esa base de baile le sirvió para “mentir” en el casting de A fuego, diciendo que sabía contemporáneo; ahora da clases de canto porque protagonizar un musical sería su sueño —si le preguntas su película favorita, su actriz favorita: Meryl Streep en Mamma mia!—. “Me parece que un buen actor no tiene que saber hacerlo todo, pero tiene que tener la capacidad de aprenderlo todo, de sacrificio, de esfuerzo”, dice. “En ese sentido, estoy orgullosa de tener una buena capacidad de aprendizaje. A fuego, ¿tengo que bailar? Voy a aprender a bailar. Veleta, tengo que aprender a jugar a fútbol, yo no he tocado una pelota en mi vida, pero cuando llegue, sabré. Para Marfil y Ébano aprendí a montar a caballo”. Sus directores lo confirman. “Es una persona muy minuciosa, muy trabajadora, le echa muchísimas horas, se vuelca y llega muy tranquila al rodaje”, dice Estel Díaz, directora de A fuego. “Es una chica capaz de rodar en muchísimos idiomas y que, a diferencia de lo que nos cuentan de las nuevas generaciones, no tiene prisa, no vive instalada en el ahora, ahora mismo, sino que vive instalada en construir este ahora y un futuro. Es para mí un orgullo verla crecer y ver que no para de trabajar”, cuenta Marcel Barrena, que ve a la actriz como “el mayor descubrimiento” de su carrera.

Blusa y falda con botones y volantes, ambos de DIOR. Santiago Belizón

Después de estudiar un año de instituto en EE UU, decidió mudarse a Madrid para empezar a tomar clases de interpretación, la escuela real que le dio la televisión diaria de Amar es para siempre no tardó en llegar y, a día de hoy, sigue yendo a todos los cursos que puede, incluso mientras está rodando. Allí ha conocido a las amigas que tiene hoy, con las que comparte el sube y baja de esta profesión con el que prefiere no obsesionarse, pero que tiene muy presente. “Yo tengo, afortunadamente, varios proyectos ahora confirmados, pero no sé si la serie que tengo en noviembre será la última”, confiesa. “Hay que disfrutar cada proyecto como si fuera el último y gestionar bien el dinero, por favor. Eso no se habla y yo lo hablo mucho con mis amigas. Hay tantos actores que les ha empezado yendo bien y se han gastado todo en viajes y lujos… ¿Y no tienes un techo? Que te estás acostumbrando a un nivel de vida que no vas a sostener, ¡baja los pies a la tierra, por favor!”. ¿Ella tiene un techo? “Estoy en ello. Tengo el privilegio de haber trabajado mucho en estos cuatro años y he ahorrado mucho dinero, soy una obsesionada con eso del ahorro”.

Americana, pantalón y zapatos, todo de SAINT LAURENT X ANTHONY VACCARELLO. Santiago Belizón

La confianza que destila y esa capacidad de trabajo de la que puede presumir, dice haberlas heredado de su madre, que siempre la animó a hacer lo que quisiera. “Pero lo que hagas, lo haces muerte”, le decía, para que siempre dependiera de ella misma. Por eso quizá se creyó actriz en el momento en que empezó a estudiar el oficio. “El primer paso era confiar en mí misma y partía de llamarme actriz y presentarme al mundo como tal. Si no te lo crees tú, ¿quién va a creer en ti?”, afirma. “Luego hay mucho que no está en tu mano y puedes tener tus inseguridades, las tengo, pero al final del día confío en mi trabajo y confío en que yo soy buena trabajando y soy buena compañera y buena persona”.

Vestido de seda, collar bicolor y zapatos de piel, todo de CHANEL. Santiago Belizón

Tens of thousands of people marched through Amsterdam on Saturday to call on the government to end its reliance on fossil fuels, three days before the cabinet presents its annual budget plan.

Organisers the Klimaatcrisis Coalitie, an alliance of Greenpeace, Milieudefensie, Extinction Rebellion and around 200 other groups, said more than 40,000 people took part.

The 2.5 kilometre route ran from the Dam to Museumplein, with 43 organised blocs including a youth bloc, a tech bloc and one from trade union federation FNV.

ANP reported many placards had the word “klimaatdrammer” – the “climate nag” label prime minister Rob Jetten adopted as a badge of honour after a VVD MP used it against him in 2019.

The coalition wants the government to end fossil fuel subsidies and speed up the switch to wind and solar rather than nuclear. Spokeswoman Merel Fiets said early reports on the leaked budget were “not encouraging” and that current policy would not meet the climate targets.

Organisers said climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven was handed their demands at a press conference before the march but announced no new measures.

World.title: Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent
World.content:
Employers will no longer be allowed to deduct rent from foreign workers’ minimum wage from July 2028, social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has told parliament.

Under current rules, employers and agencies can withhold up to 25% of the minimum wage – around €144 a week – to cover accommodation, provided the housing is certified.

The scheme is used mainly for the estimated 600,000 to 900,000 foreign workers in the Netherlands, most of them from Poland, Romania, Hungary and Ukraine, who work in meat processing, distribution centres and greenhouses.

Research by the ministry found employers regularly deduct the full 25% even when the quality of the housing does not justify it, Vijlbrief wrote in a letter to parliament on Thursday.

He said employers are using the deductions as a “business model” and told Nieuwsuur that too many people are being exploited.

Employers will still be able to provide housing, but will have to charge for it separately and at a fair price, the minister said. Ending deductions will also make it easier for inspectors to check whether workers are actually being paid minimum wage, he said.

The decision is the cabinet’s third on the issue in little over a year. Eddy van Hijum, former social affairs minister, proposed phasing out the deductions from January 2026, but his successor Mariëlle Paul of the VVD reversed that decision, arguing that workers would struggle to find housing without employer involvement.

Trade union federation FNV called the move a “perverse profit model at the expense of migrant workers”, and parliament has twice voted for the deductions to go.

Vijlbrief acknowledged that the ban will mean foreign workers will have to find their own accommodation amid the housing crisis. As a result, the ban will come with a rent protection bill, which has yet to reach parliament. Both are scheduled for July 1, 2028.

The measure is part of a wider package to tackle the exploitation of foreign workers, including a ban on temp agency staff in the meat industry, also from mid-2028. A long-delayed licensing system for staffing agencies is set to take effect in 2027.

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The government has backed an EU-wide minimum age for social media, ahead of proposals from Brussels expected next week.

The Netherlands and Spain have sent joint proposals to the European Commission calling for a single minimum age across the bloc, with privacy-friendly age checks.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is expected to outline how the bloc can can limit social media by children in her annual State of the Union speech to the European Parliament next Wednesday.

“In the physical world we do not accept that products are unsafe for children,” junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts (D66) said in a statement. “The same standard must apply online.”

D66, VVD and CDA agreed in their coalition agreement to push for an enforceable European minimum age of 15. The joint paper with Spain does not name an age, but Aerdts told broadcaster NOS that 15 remains the Dutch position.

Australia became the first country in the world to bar under-16s from platforms such as Facebook and Instagram in December 2025. France’s ban on under-15s took effect this month, and the UK has announced a ban on under-16s from 2027.

The proposal faces criticism, including from privacy advocates worried about how age verification would work in practice.

Brussels unveiled an age-check app in April, but a security researcher demonstrated a way to bypass it within hours of the launch, and the commission had to issue a patch.

World.title: Feyenoord bans 47 fans over Cambuur fireworks barrage
World.content:
Feyenoord has banned 47 supporters from De Kuip stadium over the fireworks barrage that injured seven Cambuur fans during last month’s match in Leeuwarden, the club said on Friday.

The 47 have also had their away-match cards blocked and have been reported to football association KNVB for a nationwide stadium ban.

The bans follow several weeks of investigation, including video footage analysis. They include the people who set off the fireworks and those who are accused of coordinating the attacks. Many reportedly held up banners or hid beneath them to avoid the cameras.

“It cannot be ruled out that criminal proceedings will follow in due course,” the club said. Any further action on a national ban would then be decided by the KNVB on the basis of information from the public prosecution department.

Seven home supporters suffered burns, eye injuries and hearing damage when fireworks were fired from the away section towards the pitch and the home stands in the 12th minute of the August 23 game, which Feyenoord went on to win 5-2 after a 20-minute stoppage.

Feyenoord general manager Robert Eenhoorn described the incident as “simply terrible”. The club did not take supporters to its subsequent away games at NEC Nijmegen and PEC Zwolle, and Cambuur barred visiting fans for its home match against FC Twente before lifting the restriction.

World.title: Horse meat fraud: three arrested, seven Dutch premises raided
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Belgian police have arrested three suspects in an ongoing investigation into an international horse meat fraud ring, and carried out raids at 24 locations, including seven in the Netherlands.

According to the Belgian Federal Police, a horse trader in East Flanders was at the centre of a ring which faked passport and microchip information to export horses used in racing for slaughter.

European regulations stipulate that animals destined for a slaughterhouse must be fitted with a microchip that tracks, among other things, whether or not they have been treated with medication.

An investigation by Belgian authorities revealed a large number of horses exported from Ireland to mainland Europe had modified or manipulated microchips.

During the raids, more than 1,000 horses were checked and many were seized. Police also confiscated electronics and more than €100,000 in cash.

The operation was carried out with the assistance of Europol, together with Dutch, French and Irish authorities.

In 2013, the Netherlands was embroiled in a horse meat scandal after it was found in products said to be 100% beef in Britain, Sweden, Ireland and Poland. The Netherlands is a major processor of horse meat imported from abroad.

World.title: Van Weel accused of neo-colonialism in Bolle Jos extradition row
World.content:
Sierra Leone’s chief minister has accused Dutch justice minister David van Weel of “neo-colonialism” after he appeared on a national television show to demand the extradition of fugitive drugs lord Jos “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers.

Van Weel spoke by video link from The Hague on broadcaster AYV’s State of the Nation programme on Wednesday, saying that the Netherlands had lodged a formal extradition request more than a year ago but no progress had been made.

Leijdekkers is suspected of hiding in Sierra Leone after footage of him at a church service with the president surfaced online last year. It’s alleged he is in a relationship with the president’s daughter and has a child with her.

Major drug shipments passing through West African ports are also suspected to be orchestrated by Leijdekkers’ organisation, including the biggest cocaine shipment ever seized earlier this year, and last week a 4,000 tonne seizure in France that had sailed from Ghana.

“Show the pictures”

Sierra Leonean minister David Moinina Sengeh, the president’s most senior official, responded on the same programme, saying the pressure the Netherlands was putting on the country was “scandalous” and amounted to “neo-colonialism.”

Sierra Leone is an independent country, he said, and Van Weel should stop appearing on television and threatening to cut EU aid – adding that the country did not live on European money, Nieuwsuur reported.

“Hand on heart, our security intelligence does not know where Leijdekkers is,” Sengeh said. “We cannot go by what these guys are saying or what some people are using others to say. If they know, show the pictures.”

Sengeh also accused the Netherlands of double standards, saying Freetown had twice asked The Hague to extradite a political activist and social media commentator known as Adebayor, who lives in the Netherlands and whom Sierra Leone accuses of inciting violence during riots there in 2022.

“We sent the attorney-general there. We sent the foreign affairs minister there,” he said. “They refused extradition. Have they given us that due respect to come?”

Van Weel: “ridiculous”

Van Weel told Nieuwsuur in Dutch that the neo-colonialism accusation was “ridiculous” and that the fierce reaction showed his strategy was working. He said he had not yet received a call from Freetown indicating any acceleration of the extradition process.

The interview is the latest step in a pressure campaign that has escalated since the spring. In June, Van Weel asked the EU to halt development aid to Sierra Leone, worth €352 million for the 2021 to 2027 period, though the request has so far failed to win support from other member states. In July he travelled to Ghana to build a coalition of West African countries to lean on Freetown.

Leijdekkers has been sentenced in absentia in the Netherlands and Belgium to terms Van Weel says total around 80 years.

World.title: Cardiologists in Amsterdam and Nijmegen raided over corruption
World.content:
National fraud investigation service FIOD has raided the homes of six cardiologists in Amsterdam and Nijmegen on suspicion of corruption, and property worth at least €1.5 million has been seized, current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported on Friday.

The FIOD believes the doctors took money from medical supply companies, under the guise of research funding, in exchange for giving those suppliers better deals. The money may have been pocketed by the doctors and funnelled through holding companies, the FIOD said.

The raids were announced on Thursday but no details were given as to which hospitals were involved, only that they were in Noord-Holland and Gelderland. Eight addresses were searched but nobody was arrested.

Nieuwsuur and research platform Investico identified the doctors through land registry records. Two work at the OLVG hospital in Amsterdam; the other four were, until recently, at the CWZ hospital in Nijmegen.

Long-running row

The Nijmegen doctors were sacked by the CWZ last year after a dispute over money. The hospital said in May 2025 they had taken €2.7 million in “sponsorship” from medical suppliers over five years, at a time when it was buying equipment from the same companies.

The FIOD has not said whether that dispute is connected to its investigation.

Zwolle

In 2022 the FIOD raided the homes of five cardiologists at the Isala hospital in Zwolle who were suspected of taking €3.2 million from a German pacemaker maker. Waiting lists there more than doubled after two of the doctors were suspended. That case has still not come to court.

Later that year Nieuwsuur found dozens of cardiologists were taking millions from device makers without their hospitals knowing. The FIOD says tips from within the medical sector and media reports prompted the new investigation.

Neither hospital had responded to a request for comment on Friday.

World.title: Poland issued EU’s third most residence permits to immigrants in 2025
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland issued first residence permits to almost half a million immigrants in 2025, which was the third-highest figure in the European Union, behind Spain and Germany but ahead of Italy and France. However, the number of permits issued by Poland fell for the fourth year running, as the country continued to tighten its migration rules. Previously, between 2017 and 2022, Poland had led the EU figures for six years running, reaching a peak of almost one million permits in 2021. The new data, released on Friday by Eurostat, the EU’s statistical agency, show that Poland issued 467,314 first residence permits to immigrants from outside the EU in 2025. Like last year, Spain (635,438) issued the most, followed by Germany (605,292). Poland was then followed by Italy (433,099) and France (377,462). However, whereas in those four other countries the number of permits rose in 2025 (by 13.1% in Spain, 11.1% in Germany, 25.0% in Italy and 9.2% in France), in Poland the figure fell by 4.4%. That decline has come amid a tougher new migration strategy by the current government, a coalition that ranges from left to centre right, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Ahead of elections in 2023, Tusk, then in opposition, accused the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which had ruled Poland since 2015, of allowing “uncontrolled” migration, including through widespread abuses of the visa system. Shortly after coming to power in those elections, Tusk, a former president of the European Council, declared that the “survival of Western civilisation” depends upon preventing mass migration. His government has since introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students, suspended asylum rights for migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus, and stepped up deportations of immigrants who have committed crimes or entered the country unlawfully. Poland has introduced tougher new rules regulating the entry of foreign students and immigrant workers. “This is another step towards regaining control over migration and increasing the safety of Poles," says the government https://t.co/gYdikpc6pL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2025 The new 2025 data show that, in relative terms (the number of permits issued in relation to countries’ populations), Poland was only ninth in the EU (12.8 permits per 1,000 people), behind Malta (56.9), Cyprus (46.7), Portugal (27.3), Lithuania (18.5), Ireland (13.4), Croatia (13.2), Luxembourg (13.1) and Spain (12.9). That marks a significant decline since 2021, when Poland issued 967,345 permits, which was the highest in the EU in absolute terms but also second-highest in relation to population. In 2025, as in previous years, Poland issued the most first residence permits to Ukrainians (241,126, 51.6% of the total), who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. They were followed by Belarusians (128,468, 27.5%), Georgians (10,249, 2.2%), Indians (9,230, 2%) and Turks (7,533, 1.6%) – the same top five nationalities as in 2024. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Following a decade of unprecedented mass migration, the number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland this year passed two million for the first time, making up just over 5% of the country’s population. Around 1.5 million of those are Ukrainians. In June, the number of foreigners working in Poland reached 1.14 million, making up almost 7% of the workforce. While Ukrainians constitute two thirds of the total, the fastest-growing nationalities are Colombians and Indians, who are now the third- and fourth-largest groups of foreign workers. The rise in migration has come as Poland’s economy has boomed but the country has also faced a demographic crisis, with a shrinking, ageing population and one of the lowest birth rates in the world. In 2023, the state Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) calculated that, in order to maintain its ratio of working-age population to retirees, Poland would need to attract almost two million immigrant workers over the following decade. However, it admitted that that target was “unrealistic”. World.title: Poland and other V4 countries will block EU climate policies that raise energy costs, warns Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. Związek Zawodowy Maszynistów Kolejowych mówi "dość" i ogłasza ogólnokrajowy protest po tragicznej katastrofie w Sokolnikach Suchych. W piątek, 11 września, pociągi w całej Polsce będą zwalniać na przejazdach kolejowych do zaledwie 20 km/h. Więcej o tym: https://t.co/jj6jKm40X2 pic.twitter.com/ThqfLx3dEc — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) September 10, 2026 The union chief said that Wednesday’s accident “was not a surprise to us, considering that statistically we have an accident at a railway crossing every two days”. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. This would include “very tough” punishments “for those who, unfortunately, quite systematically drive onto railway crossings despite barriers and red lights”. Infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak later confirmed that they were working on “radical” measures to toughen penalties for those who violate the rules at rail crossings. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek… — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026 On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade. “Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.” “We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation, including DiNanno, was in Poland this week to discuss potential locations for the base. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
