World.title: Bolick redeems self, Ahanmisi catches fire as Gilas Pilipinas rips Kazakhstan in Asian Games
World.content:
Robert Bolick and Jerrick Ahanmisi spearhead Gilas Pilipinas' scoring spree from three-point range as the defending champions earn their first win in the Asian Games and boost their chances of advancing to the quarterfinals

MANILA, Philippines – Robert Bolick rebounded from a scoreless outing, while Jerrick Ahanmisi shot the lights out as Gilas Pilipinas claimed its first win in the Asian Games, dealing Kazakhstan a 109-78 beating at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday, September 12.

Held scoreless in a narrow 89-85 loss to Bahrain the day prior, Bolick fired 20 points in just a little over 15 minutes to help the defending champion Philippines improve to an even 1-1 record in Group C and boost its chances of advancing to the quarterfinals.

Ahanmisi, meanwhile, erupted for a game-high 22 points on a 7-of-11 clip from beyond the arc, torching the Kazakhs in a fourth-quarter scoring spree that allowed the Filipinos to break the game wide open.

Gilas Pilipinas held a slim 18-15 lead at the end of the opening period before Bolick took charge and scattered 13 points in the second frame as it mounted a 50-37 halftime advantage.

Ahanmisi then picked up where Bolick left off, knocking down five three-pointers in the fourth quarter and singlehandedly outscoring the entire Kazakhstan team, which managed just 12 points in the final period of the 31-point blowout.

Calvin Oftana, who erupted for 31 points in the loss to the Bahrainis, still made his presence felt with 12 points, while Sedrick Barefield contributed 11 points, 5 assists, and 4 rebounds as he redeemed himself after going scoreless last game.

Zavier Lucero also delivered a near double-double outing of 10 points and 9 rebounds in the win, which saw the Filipinos sink 16 of their 29 attempts from long range for a healthy 55% shooting.

Bolick and Barefield, who both went 0-of-5 from three-point land against Bahrain, made 4 and 3 triples, respectively, this time around.

One of the few bright spots last game before he tweaked his right ankle late in the fourth quarter, Adrian Nocum played just a little under 16 minutes against the Kazakhs, contributing 4 points and 3 assists.

Anton Bykov produced 15 points and 10 rebounds to show the way for Kazakhstan, which fell to 0-2 after also absorbing a 38-point drubbing from China.

Given a one-day break, the Philippines turns its attention to unbeaten China in its last game of the group stage on Monday, September 14, with a win sending the Filipinos to the quarterfinals.

Only the top two teams from each of the three groups and the two best third-place teams will reach the knockout rounds.

The Scores

Philippines 109 – Ahanmisi 22, Bolick 20, Oftana 12, Barefield 11, Lucero 10, Baltazar 6, Arana 6, Abarrientos 6, Trollano 5, Nocum 4, Ganuelas-Rosser 4, Bates 3.

Kazakhstan 78 – Bykov 15, Marat 12, Maydekin 12, Neff 11, Rabchenyuk 9, Murzagaliyev 8, Fedchenko 7, Ivanov 2, Sakhipov 2, Severgin 0, Marchuk 0, Kuanov 0.

Quarters: 18-15, 50-37, 82-66, 109-78.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Multi-sport athlete Chino Sy finds Olympic calling in judo
World.content:
DREAMS. Filipino judoka Chino Sy hopes to make it to the grandest stage in sports: the Olympics.

Also a standout athlete in sambo and wrestling, Chino Sy has shifted his focus to judo as he pursues an Olympic berth that would fulfill not only his dream, but also that of his family

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino judoka Chino Sy learned at an early age to make the most of every opportunity.

Hailing from Davao City, Sy developed a sense of responsibility to perform whenever he and his family traveled to Manila for combat sports competitions, knowing that they invested not only time and effort, but also money, just to be there.

As he embarks on his biggest challenge yet to make the Olympics, Sy is taking that same approach.

“I feel like those experiences shaped how I compete today and my mentality towards sports. Even when we were young, we were told that we couldn’t come home with a loss. For one, we already spent money on plane tickets. We also paid entry fees and covered all other expenses,” said Sy in a mix of Filipino and English.

Sy, 25, grew up immersed in combat disciplines.

His father, Paolo Tancontian, represented the Philippines in judo, winning medals in international competitions including the Southeast Asian Games and the Arafura Games, and now serves as the president of the Pilipinas Sambo Federation.

Sy’s older sister, Sydney, is currently the fifth-ranked sambo athlete in the world in the women’s +80kg division and has won medals in the last three Asia and Oceania Sambo Championships, including gold in 2025.

With martial arts deeply rooted in his family, it comes as little surprise that Sy found success in the field that he captured medals in three different sports in the SEA Games.

At 18 years old, Sy delivered a sambo gold when the country hosted the biennial showpiece in 2019. Four years later, he earned a wrestling silver in the 2023 edition in Cambodia.

But Sy has shifted his focus on judo, the sport in which he dominated the UAAP by winning gold medals in four seasons at UST and earning two MVP awards, as he sets his sights on qualifying for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

And he showed promise in that pursuit by striking a judo gold in the men’s -100kg division in the 2025 SEA Games in Thailand.

“Every athlete’s dream is the highest stage, the Olympics,” said Sy. “I feel like I’m at the peak of my career as an athlete. I’ll grab this opportunity and I’ll do everything I can to make it to the Olympics.”

Sy is not pursuing the Olympic dream for himself alone, but also for his family, revealing that his father once dreamed of competing in the 2000 Sydney Olympics — hence his sister’s name.

“This is not just my dream, it’s also my family’s dream. Papa may not have made it to the Olympics, but he’s doing everything he can to help me achieve our dream,” said Sy.

“If all goes well, this will truly be a milestone for our family.”

And with an Olympic dream in sight, Sy knows his belief in himself has to match his ambition as he eyes a rare judo medal in the upcoming Asian Games, which will be hosted in Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4.

The Philippines has won only one judo medal in Asian Games history courtesy of Kiyomi Watanabe, who bagged the women’s 63kg silver in the 2018 edition in Indonesia.

“My target is to win. I know it will be difficult, but I’m doing everything I can in training and preparation,” said Sy.

Sy also looks to Watanabe, who represented the Philippines in the 2020 Tokyo and 2024 Paris Games, for inspiration, hoping to learn from someone with Olympic experience as they team up in the Asian Games.

“[Kiyomi] has been competing for a long time and I’m looking forward to seeing how an Olympian thinks, how she prepares, and how she approaches every match,” Sy said.

And just as he did in his early years, Sy is determined to live up to the trust placed in him — this time, not only by his family but the entire country.

“I never want to let our country down, myself, or everyone who has put their trust in me,” said Sy. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kilyab’s Karl Ramirez turns Bicol pop into call for good governance
World.content:
By putting Bicol music at the center of his work, this musician inspires a new generation of artists to celebrate their roots and use their craft to push for change

ALBAY, Philippines – From the dimly lit corners of local bars and cafes in Naga City, Karl Ramirez and his band, Kilyab, quietly listen to the stories of their community. They transform these local narratives, heritage, and aspirations to reinvent Bicol pop — giving voice to the region’s call for change.

Now, the movement is helping the younger generation of musicians to do the same.

Ramirez, a music industry veteran, returned to Bicol during the pandemic. As a founding member of Musika Publiko, a nationwide network of artists dedicated to advance socially relevant music, he sought to localize the group’s advocacy.

KILYAB. Karl Ramirez and his band perform at Pista Nin Teatro 2026, introducing the Bicol pop movement to a nationwide audience. Photo courtesy of The Mariners Collegian

Starting without financial backing in an unfamiliar base, Ramirez and his band brought together local musicians from across Camarines Sur to create a platform for original Bicol music. Initially, they had to persuade reluctant bar and cafe owners to grant them a stage to perform. Soon, those same venues were inviting them back, fueling the community’s rapid growth and popularity.

“We were surprised when more and more bars and cafes opened their doors to Bicol pop. It was challenging at first because every venue has its own specific brand, but through their support, our movement grew larger and reached more listeners,” Ramirez said.

By rooting their songs in community struggles, the movement transformed Bicol pop into a platform for local causes. To sustain this momentum, the organization eventually formed Pagsibol, an initiative that trains aspiring musicians, particularly the youth, to write songs about their local experiences in their native language while using music as a driver for social advocacy.

“We decided to form Pagsibol to expand our reach and prepare younger musicians to lead and advance the movement. We realized we needed to grow our ranks,” Ramirez said.

He explained that the organization not only expanded its footprint, but also created a more open environment for continuous growth: “We wanted to encourage the youth to create fresh work that directly serves their communities and generation.”

Pagsibol now functions as a structured platform for training enthusiasts in songwriting and music production. Beyond developing artists, the group focuses on empowering broader communities through local skills training.

PAGSIBOL. Aspiring young musicians participate in a Pagsibol songwriting workshop aimed at advancing socially relevant original Bicol music. Contributed photo/Verna Abalyan-Velasco

Local support

In Naga City, the group has leveraged music to reinforce good governance, placing “active listening” at its core. Partnering with the local government, they have reached more students while advancing advocacy for Musikong Nagueño, a collective pushing for local government support and funding for community musicians and cultural workers.

“We invited Mayor Leni Robredo to a concert held in 2024 at the Jesse M. Robredo Coliseum, where we presented her with a Bicol pop roadmap and policy proposals for the Naga City music industry,” Ramirez recalled.

“Following her election, our movement established a collaborative partnership with the local government, placing active listening at the center of the city’s good governance agenda.”

He noted that if such a partnership can thrive in Naga, there is immense potential for other local government units to provide genuine backing for artists working to preserve and promote their local heritage.

HERITAGE. The cast of ‘Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical’ performs 17 original songs composed by Karl Ramirez in collaboration with the local theater collective Sining Banwa. Reinnard Balonzo/Rappler

In August 2026, Ramirez also served as the lead composer and music producer for Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical, writing and producing 17 original songs in just 17 days. The production was funded by the City Government of Legazpi.

“With this play, the original Bicol music we produced, and state support, we proved that local artists and collectives deserve greater investment if we want to advance regional talent and heritage,” Ramirez said. “Ibalong Z stands as a testament that with proper support, local artists can rival mainstream productions.”

Hyperlocal to mainstream

Speaking on the shift to mainstream media, Ramirez said that Pagsibol students are fully supported if they choose to pursue mainstream careers. For him, Bicol pop serves as a springboard — helping emerging artists introduce their work to broader audiences and share regional stories with the national music scene.

“We encourage our musicians to seize opportunities to go mainstream and bring Bicol pop to more listeners. Our hope is that wherever their success takes them, they carry the movement with them,” Ramirez said.

ARTISTIC SUPPORT. In partnership with the City Government of Naga, Bicol pop launched its SongLab initiative for Pagsibol students. Contributed photo/Verna Abalyan-Velasco

Through this hyperlocal music movement, artists gain a solid community to rely on a network that offers support wherever their careers lead. Ultimately, the movement aims to empower budding musicians by giving them greater leverage in their creative expression and stronger control over their career trajectories.

“What we teach the youth goes beyond writing lyrics. We focus on how we, as a community, can support one another in artistic growth and management while advocating for artists’ rights and welfare,” Ramirez shared. “We also guide them as they navigate the music industry and hone their talent.”

For now, Ramirez and Kilyab continue to mentor Pagsibol’s emerging artists by immersing them in local communities. This hands-on approach ensures that every lyric accurately reflects the real issues, places, and people they write and sing about. – Rappler.com

World.title: What the settlement left out: Meta can still collect data from kids
World.content:
ZUCKERBERG. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026

In August 2026, Meta agreed to one of the largest consumer protection settlements in American history. The settlement resolves claims from 47 states alleging that Meta intentionally designed its Facebook and Instagram platforms to be addictive to young users and harmful to youth mental health.

As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.1 billion — approximately 20% of Meta’s 2025 pretax profits — in penalties over the next 10 years. Meta also agreed to implement changes to its platforms for young users, including daily time limits, access restrictions during school hours and late nights, and “productivity breaks” that interrupt scrolling every 60 minutes.

The $17.1 billion penalty and promised changes to the platforms have grabbed the headlines. But, as a law professor who studies social media regulation, I believe that what the settlement does not include will prove more important to youth safety in the long run. The settlement does not restrict Meta from continuing to collect data from young users, from using that data to sell its targeted ads, or from serving those targeted ads to young users.

In short, while Meta agreed to some limited changes to safeguard young users, it also succeeded in protecting its surveillance-based business model.

How Meta makes money

Meta’s core business is advertising. It is the world’s second-largest digital advertising company by revenue and will soon overtake Google to claim first place. Last year, Meta generated over $200 billion in revenue, up 22% over the prior year.

Meta’s growing revenue comes from delivering more ads to platform users and charging advertisers more for those ads. For Meta, maximizing the amount of time that users spend on its platforms is critical to revenue growth. The more time users spend on Meta’s platforms, the more ads Meta can serve to those users and, consequently, the more money Meta makes.

Meta’s ad business operates on a surveillance model that gives advertisers the ability to serve personalized ads to the users who are most likely to purchase the advertiser’s goods or services. Meta does this by collecting a large amount of data about platform users. This data includes users’ friends, followers and other connections; the websites they visit, the apps they use, the games they play and the purchases they make; their demographics, including education level; the ads they see and how they interact with them; and how they use third parties’ products and services, online or in person.

The more time a user spends on Meta’s platforms, the more Meta learns about that user and the more effective its targeted ads become. This means Meta has a strong incentive to keep users scrolling on its platforms and to collect as much data as possible from those users. The recent settlement does not change that incentive structure.

A history of breached settlements

This is not the first time that Meta has settled with the government and agreed to change its platforms to improve user safety. In 2012, Meta, then Facebook, Inc., settled with the Federal Trade Commission to resolve claims that it deceptively designed its privacy settings and collected data from users without their knowledge.

Then, in 2019, the FTC again sued Facebook, alleging that it violated the terms of the 2012 agreement by continuing to collect user data without consent. Again, the company settled, agreeing to pay a $5 billion penalty and again promising to stop its deceptive data collection practices.

Based on Meta’s prior conduct violating the terms of its settlements, many observers questioned whether the $5 billion penalty would deter Meta from continuing its data collection practices. It did not take long to get an answer.

In 2023, the FTC brought yet another action against Meta, alleging that it had violated the terms of the 2019 settlement. As a result of this violation, the FTC sought to restrict Meta from collecting and monetizing the data of young users.

Meta responded by challenging the FTC’s authority to impose those restrictions. Litigation in that case is ongoing.

Meta’s incentives remain the same

In 2026, Meta has again settled with the government, again paid a penalty and again promised changes. And again, those promises do not restrict it from collecting data and monetizing young users, nor does the settlement restrict Meta from continuing to serve young users targeted ads.

Youth safety advocates and legislators have long fought to stop social media platforms from collecting data from young users and targeting ads to them. They have argued that doing so would remove social media companies’ incentive to design platforms that addict young people. By not including data collection and targeting restrictions in the settlement, I believe that the states missed an opportunity to change this incentive structure.

Repeatedly violating the terms of its settlements with the government seems to be an effective strategy for Meta. The company has learned that penalties for doing so are small in comparison with the profits gained through its conduct. This recent settlement looks like more of the same. With this pattern in mind, it is fair to ask whether the settlement will provide meaningful protection for young social media users or just allow Meta to continue with business as usual.

As former FTC Commissioner Rohit Chopra stated when dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, “When companies can violate the law, pay big penalties and still turn a profit while keeping their business model intact, enforcement agencies cannot claim victory.”

I believe this most recent settlement repeats the patterns of the past and continues to leave young users vulnerable on Meta’s platforms. – Rappler.com

This article originally appeared on The Conversation.

Randolph A Robinson II, Associate Professor of Law, University of Illinois Chicago

World.title: New rules, new season: What to know about UAAP 2026-2027
World.content:
READY FOR ACTION. The UAAP holds a press conference for its Season 89 basketball tournament on Tuesday, September 8.

With what is already shaping up to be an interesting UAAP Season 89, here are the new rules fans can expect to see as the games officially begin

The 89th season of the University Athletic Association of the Philippines (UAAP) has officially opened.

The Far Eastern University (FEU) is the host for the 2026 to 2027 games — taking on the theme “For Everyone, UAAP,” which aims to recognize not just the efforts of student-athletes and coaches, but all the people who work on the sidelines to make play possible.

FEU last hosted the UAAP in Season 80.

Heading into the collegiate league’s basketball tournament, the La Salle Green Archers vie to defend the men’s championship without standout center Mike Phillips. Meanwhile, all eyes are on the Ateneo Blue Eagles, who are coming into the season led by new head coach Louie Alas, just months after the deaths of players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili and the subsequent resignation of Tab Baldwin.

With what is already shaping up to be an interesting season, here are the new rules fans can expect to see take effect as the games officially begin.

On fielding foreign student-athletes

Come Season 89, each team is now allowed to have two foreign student-athletes (FSAs), compared to past seasons where teams were limited to just one active FSA.

Teams are still only allowed to field one FSA on the actual court, but may switch from one FSA to another so long as they declare it at least an hour before the game starts.

This rule only applies to team sports outside of 3×3 basketball.

‘One-and-done’ phenomenon

Among the issues the UAAP board aims to address is the “one-and-done” phenomenon, where players who have already graduated from a different university pursue a master’s degree to play for just one year in a UAAP team.

According to UAAP executive director Rebo Saguisag, this rule was already legislated some time last year, but will be “prospective in nature.”

Student-athletes who graduated from a non-UAAP school are currently allowed to enroll and immediately compete in the league as long as they meet the other eligibility criteria. But under this new reform, which will take effect in Season 90, players will have to undergo a year of residency with their new school before being allowed to play.

“The rationale is the board wanted somehow for the student-athletes to inculcate the culture of their respective schools before they compete,” Saguisag explained. “They should know what Igma Kadima of UE means. Or what it means to be a ‘klasmeyt’ at Adamson. Or for FEU, what it means to be actually brave. So they’ll sit out one year, get inculcated in the culture, and play next year.”

In Season 88, the Ateneo Blue Eagles were led by their own one-and-done Fil-Am trio of Jaden Lazo, Kymani Ladi, and Dom Escobar.

The new rule applies to all sports in the UAAP.

Stricter FIBA-style officiating, new suspension system

The UAAP had recently undergone a referee’s refresher course administered by FIBA officials last July — and learned that bench decorum was something the collegiate league had to work on and monitor more closely.

“We had two FIBA officials come to the Philippines and observe our games, and what they both observed was that bench decorum has to be aligned further in FIBA. So coaches, there may be more technical fouls this year, so please keep your benches in control,” said UAAP commissioner Jai Reyes during the league’s basketball press conference.

According to Reyes, these new rules were set to ensure that once the student-athletes, coaches, and officials step off the UAAP court, they’ll be equipped with the necessary knowledge and etiquette fit for the world stage.

With this, the UAAP will be implementing a new suspension system when its basketball tournament begins. When a student-athlete is suspended, they will still automatically be disqualified from receiving any post-season awards.

How will the new system work?

Two unsportsmanlike fouls will merit suspension for a player, depending on the severity of the infraction they committed.

Meanwhile, a player will get suspended once they reach their third technical foul. From there, every two additional technical fouls they get will lead to suspension. The same format applies for head coaches, who will now also be bearing the brunt of bench technical fouls.

The count of these fouls, however, resets during the playoffs. – Rappler.com

World.title: Add these cozy places in your next Kapitolyo cafe crawl
World.content:
If you’re in the mood for some winding down or sense of wonder, hang out with us at Loop, The Beachhouse, and Pancho Cafe

After being strangers, I’m officially acquainted with Kapitolyo.

To be honest, I didn’t feel this years ago, when I was a teenager who occasionally attended events in this unassuming neighborhood’s creative spaces. I didn’t feel this last year either, when I started working at Rappler, making the Pasig barangay an accessible post-shift hangout hub.

What changed things for me is the decision to finally check out one of its charms: Its cafe community. Kapitolyo’s cafes have become third spaces, offering a smooth wrap-up, however your entire day went – and I’d have to thank their distinct coziness for pulling me in.

Interestingly, we discovered these cafes the way our ancestors intended: Walking around or asking our friends for some recommendations. In our quest for discovery, we made three stops – here’s why they all passed the coziness test.

If you’re a cool-down connoisseur: Loop Kapitolyo

“A good cup of matcha is rooted in intention, and that always starts with our baristas. We ensure that each and every customer experiences that intention in every cup at Loop,” owner Luis Padilla tells Rappler.

While matcha is popularly known as Loop’s magnum opus, Padilla said they originally didn’t intend for the cafe to be a matcha place. People just assumed it was because of its color, but they eventually maximized the happy accident.

Among their matcha drinks is the Sea Salt Matcha. It’s light and sweet, initially giving you an intriguingly unique salty kick. Fun fact: They use asin tibuok, a rare artisanal sea salt made from a lengthy and traditional process in Bohol.

Meanwhile, the Coconut Espresso is a strong surprise with its toasty goodness, and the Honey Shaken Oat Latte will lure you to lock in.

Loop’s ambiance is perfect for deep focus. Apart from it being well-decorated but not visually overwhelming, the cafe has an abundance of power sockets, and even features an upper floor that’s frequently used for meetings.

But productivity isn’t the only language here, as cool down-ready runners and bikers flock during early weekend mornings. It sounds full-circle, as the Loop’s name (as in “run loop” or “bike loop”) and logo (the double o’s resemble pedals) are meant to reflect Padilla’s fitness background.

Cooling down also means being relaxed in conversations, as different age groups gather inside. There are even children’s books for the youngest customers.

“The community in Kapitolyo is vastly diverse. From the cafes, restaurants, and people, we’re consistently innovating and improving. I like how wherever you go in Kapitolyo, it always feels very homey and inclusive,” Padilla said.

📍: 3 San Rafael St., Brgy. Kapitolyo, Pasig City

🕰️: 8 am to 7 pm (weekdays), 7 am to 7 pm (weekends)

If you’re a maximalist cat lover: The Beachhouse

Stepping inside The Beachhouse will make you rethink your initial agenda: Am I taking a quick cafe visit, or barging into someone’s giant bedroom?

(Well, it’s both. But you’ll likely extend your “quick” stay.)

One minute you’re staring at strangers’ Polaroid photos, the next you’re flipping through a cool mini calendar. Posters, stickers, CDs. An eccentric restroom. Remnants of a film club. A summer-ready shop.

Co-founder Jelito de Leon uses the term “dopamine decor”.

“Actually, I first heard this from Kenneth and Sarah, my partners in Beachhouse! They actually did most of the decorating and made sure every corner was filled with things we loved and enjoyed,” he told Rappler.

But of course, the experience wouldn’t be complete without their interesting roster of drinks. Although my first bias off the menu was the Coffee Morning Crunch (which tastes like carefree childhood), my bias wrecker became their signature Kamote Cold Brew, which spotlights the unlikely duo of sweet potato and coffee, leaving a refreshingly sweet result. Their Coconut Cream Matcha also has a memorable texture and harmony of flavors.

Composed of three floors, the Beachhouse can cater to various comfort levels: A couch area for lively group catch-ups, and more intimately spaced rooms for solemn alone time, or even a creative brainstorming session. There’s CC, the resident cat, if you need an additional member.

The sense of community is very much alive, with artists getting a platform for their livelihood, too.

“The best thing about the [Kapitolyo] community is how friendly it is. Some regulars of the cafe are actually from the neighborhood and have become friends with our baristas!” de Leon said.

📍: 11C East Capitol Drive, Kapitolyo, Pasig City

🕰️: 9 am to 9 pm daily

If you’re a sidequest master: Pancho Cafe

You can stay in Pancho Cafe for 24 hours, not only because you’re allowed to – but also because this Italian-inspired haven has so much in store.

There’s a photo booth that can fit 10 people, a gorgeous flower shop, and an abundance of artwork. While some food spots are designed not to make you linger for too long, Pancho offers enough space and a variety of chairs for you to stay comfortable in moving around for the rest of the day.

You’ll also never run out of things to try.

Among their offerings are their devour-worthy lasagna that oozes with creamy cheese, and quick bites like their croissant. In true Italian fashion, you can also get a scoop (or two) of gelato.

Or you can start with their generous serving of coffee – and they do not disappoint. Enjoy the Caramel Macchiato’s thick blend of creaminess and sweetness that’s not off-putting for the non-sweet tooth.

And while the Cafe con Leche (the Spanish Latte equivalent) isn’t that strong, its striking milky aftertaste will make you want to gradually finish the glass, just to enjoy a little longer. According to their staff, more customers come in between 9 pm to 3 am, so it’s up to you if you’re game to join the pack – or delight in the quiet morning with Pancho’s equally relaxing playlist.

📍: 50 West Capitol Drive corner United Street, The Vantage at Kapitolyo, Pasig City

🕰️: Open 24 hours

We want to hear from you!

Expecting to see your go-to spot here but didn’t? Share it away and we might just pay a visit. – Rappler.com

World.title: Q&A: Could AI really kill off humanity within the decade?
World.content:
ANTHROPIC. The Anthropic logo, a keyboard, and a robotic hand are shown in this illustration created on June 5, 2026.

Amid looming IPOs, professor Kate Devlin says, 'Let’s remember that [these AI companies] are constantly looking for investment and, in return, they promise the most powerful and dominant models. What could be more powerful than a model that threatens our very existence?'

Artificial intelligence (AI) could wipe out humanity this decade, according to three researchers from the US company Anthropic. One of the employees, Jacob Coxon, has quit the AI firm.

His predictions were backed by two other current Anthropic researchers in posts on social media. On X, Coxon claimed: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”

It’s not the first time AI researchers and companies have issued such assessments. Here, Kate Devlin, professor of artificial intelligence & society, explains what is behind them and whether there’s anything different about the latest warning.

The latest claims about AI have come from a researcher who resigned from Anthropic. What is your general view on what has happened here?

To give this a sense of perspective, we should remember that it’s one AI company ex-employee posting on a platform known for grandiose claims, which was then quoted by a current AI company employee who put a figure on the risk of human extinction at greater than 10%.

So, it’s another doom-laden narrative about the supposed threat from AI. There is some dialling back from this in a follow up tweet from current Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger that read: “I think the risk from present models is low. What I’m worried about is superintelligence”.

These tweets have gained huge coverage because these kinds of things always do. It taps into our very primal fears — and our decades of watching dystopian sci-fi.

The claims from Jacob Coxon were backed by current employees of Anthropic. Why do you think AI companies are happy to support these kinds of claims in public?

It’s likely that these men believe what they’re saying, but we’ve heard warnings like this for years. It does seem odd that AI companies are okay with these kinds of claims.

Let’s remember that they are constantly looking for investment and, in return, they promise the most powerful and dominant models. What could be more powerful than a model that threatens our very existence?

One theory for doom-mongering by AI companies is that they want to avoid regulation. Do you think outside regulation of AI companies is inevitable?

It has been incredibly difficult to regulate AI, certainly at an international level. There has been little appetite for AI to be regulated in the US because there’s a view that regulation might stifle innovation.

The UK doesn’t have any AI-specific laws either, just existing laws that might apply in some cases. China began to introduce national-level laws but has now replaced that with technical standards and sector regulation. The EU remains the only place where there is dedicated AI regulation.

However, it looks like this has kicked off yet another call for better regulation, and we’re seeing that at present in US Congress and in the Houses of Parliament in the UK.

There is another angle, in that industry might be on board with regulation, as big tech companies would have the money to comply, but it could knock out their competitors with smaller budgets, so it would leave the leaders in dominant positions.

How far away are we from the kind of superintelligent AI mentioned in the latest warnings?

We don’t have superintelligence. I’m reluctant to put a time frame on that. Often people say “5-10 years” but that’s happened a lot in AI and 5-10 years pass without anything arising. It also depends on what is meant by superintelligence. Something that is conscious and thinks for itself? That might never happen.

In this case, it doesn’t really matter, as there are other harms already happening from AI, and there are other ways things can go wrong, though probably not at the existential level that’s being suggested here.

For example, AI is energy-hungry. It needs water to cool data centers. It has a damaging environmental impact. There are also issues around the content generated by AI, anything from a lack of plurality in the models’ outputs (meaning that the information it returns is homogenized, converging on particular viewpoints) to the spread of misinformation and disinformation.

We also know there is hidden labour in the AI supply chain: there are people working in terrible conditions to deliver the technology. And we know that it’s having an impact on people’s lives in terms of how it’s changing the workplace.

What are the potential practical ways in which AI could actually wipe out humans?

“Wiping out” is a bit extreme but there are some dangerous threats. There are the “bad actor” scenarios where AI is used destructively, like creating weapons or deadly viruses.

More mundane, but potentially very destructive, are AI agents let loose due to human carelessness or incompetence, hacking or taking control of insecure systems.

A survey we recently ran at King’s College London found that the UK public are feeling increasingly negative about AI, and that 42% of people are deliberately limiting their AI use. With claims from tech companies that it poses a direct threat to our existence, it will be unsurprising if public opinion dips even further. – Rappler.com

This story originally appeared on The Conversation.

Kate Devlin, Professor of Artificial Intelligence & Society, Department of Digital Humanities, King’s College London

World.title: Palawan ferry fire death toll climbs to 76 as identification process begins
World.content:
Philippine Coast Guard personnel in protective suit unload body bags of victims of a ferry fire blaze at the port of Borac in Coron, Palawan province on September 12, 2026. The bodies of passengers killed in a ferry fire off the Philippines arrived at a port near the resort town of Coron, Palawan on September 12. (AFP)

CORON, Philippines – The death toll from a Philippine ferry fire jumped to 76 on Saturday after the coast guard confirmed the discovery of 41 more bodies aboard the burnt-out vessel.

The remains will be transported to a port in Coron, Palawan, coast guard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said in a statement.

AFP watched hours earlier as disaster agency workers carried coffins to a cemetery in the resort town, intended for the temporary burial of victims of the fire that tore through the M/V June Aster on Wednesday.

Article continues after this 

The first 30 bodies arrived by sea earlier on Saturday as forensic specialists began the painstaking process of identifying the remains.

The confirmed death toll now stands at 76, including five bodies recovered in the immediate wake of the incident. The ship sits grounded about 7.5 kilometres (4.5 miles) off the coast.

One-metre (three-feet) deep graves have been dug to hold the victims’ remains until DNA testing is completed, Kristine Ablana, a tourism official serving as an official spokesperson, told reporters on Saturday.

Relatives will be brought to identify personal items that may have belonged to family members.

“Once someone is able to verify… that this photo or these belongings are indeed those of their relative, they will be asked to provide a DNA sample,” Ablana said.

Article continues after this 

Thirty passengers, including two Chilean nationals, and 13 crew have been rescued, according to the coast guard. Around a dozen people are believed to remain unaccounted for.

‘Happened in seconds’

Cayabyab said in a radio interview that the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.

Article continues after this 

“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly,” she said of survivors’ accounts.

“Everything happened in seconds,” she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on life jackets.

Near the pier where the bodies were to be returned, an emotional Josenit Mayo, 40, told AFP her daughter had been aboard the ferry, returning from the capital Manila for a family visit.

“She told me ‘Mom, I want to go home as I’m missing my siblings,'” Mayo said. “She insisted she was lonely.”

Myra Cabilan told AFP she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.

“His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter,” Cabilan said, fighting back tears.

“At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he’s still missing. I have lost hope.”

Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.

The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.

Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country’s more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.

In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.

World.title: Legarda puts literacy at center of learning recovery on Int’l Literacy Day
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Senator Loren Legarda placed literacy at the center of the country’s learning recovery efforts as we mark International Literacy Day, stressing that reading with understanding remains one of the strongest foundations of a child’s education and future opportunities.

“Nagsisimula sa pagbasa ang pagkatuto. Kapag nauunawaan ng isang bata ang kanyang binabasa, mas kaya niyang sumabay sa mga aralin at matuto nang mag-isa. Kaya dapat malinaw ang ating prayoridad: tiyaking marunong bumasa at umunawa ang bawat batang Pilipino,” Legarda said.

Recent data from the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II) show both significant improvement in reading proficiency, but also underscore the scale of the challenge that remains.

Article continues after this 

At the beginning of School Year 2025–2026, an average of 40 percent of learners from Grades 1 to 10 were classified as struggling readers.

By March 2026, the share of Grade Level Ready or independent readers had risen from 19 percent to 48 percent, a 29-percentage-point improvement.

Despite the gains, one in every two learners remained below grade-level reading proficiency by the end of the school year.

Legarda, who currently serves as an EDCOM II commissioner and previously served as its co-chairperson, said the figures demonstrate that targeted interventions can improve learning outcomes, but these gains must reach more learners and be sustained as they advance through the education system.

“Malaki ang naitulong ng ating mga guro at paaralan, at nakikita natin ang pag-angat ng reading levels ng mga bata. Pero hindi sapat na kalahati lamang ang umaabot sa antas na inaasahan sa kanilang baitang. Dapat matiyak na mas maraming bata ang marunong nang bumasa at umunawa sa mga unang taon pa lamang ng kanilang pag-aaral,” she said.

Article continues after this 

EDCOM II also found that the challenge remains especially pronounced in the higher grades.

In DepEd’s pilot Senior High School Literacy and Numeracy Assessment, only 12.58 percent of Grade 11 learners were classified as independent readers.

Article continues after this 

This means that nearly 9 in 10 Grade 11 learners, or about 87 percent, were not able to read independently, with 58.9 percent at the frustration level and 28.5 percent at the instructional level.

“Hindi dapat umabot sa senior high school ang isang bata na hirap pa ring umunawa sa kanyang binabasa. Dapat matibay na ang pundasyon niya sa pagbasa bago pa man maging mas komplikado ang mga aralin. Kaya kailangang matukoy at matugunan nang maaga ang kanyang pangangailangan, at maipagpatuloy ang suporta habang siya ay nag-aaral.” Legarda said.

Legarda has pushed for reforms across the education system, including stronger support during the foundational years. Among the measures she has filed is Senate Bill No. 1853, or the K to 3 Foundational Learning and Nurturing Care Act, which seeks to strengthen early language, literacy, and numeracy from Kindergarten to Grade 3 while aligning classroom learning with nutrition, health, social and emotional development, and responsive caregiving.

She stressed that addressing literacy gaps in the early years is critical to preventing learners from falling further behind as they move to higher grade levels and eventually prepare for college, technical-vocational training, employment, and other opportunities.

“Hindi sapat na mabasa lang ang mga salita. Dapat naiintindihan ng bata ang mensahe at nagagamit niya ang kanyang binabasa upang matuto at makapag-isip. Iyan ang literacy na kailangan natin, iyong nagbibigay sa bata ng kakayahang matuto, pumili, at magkaroon ng mas maraming oportunidad sa buhay,” Legarda said.

International Literacy Day is observed every September 8. This year marks its 60th anniversary, under the UNESCO theme “Literacy for people, the planet and prosperity,” highlighting the role of literacy in learning, inclusion, livelihoods, and wider opportunities.

World.title: San Juan City LSB OKs funding for security equipment in public schools
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The San Juan City Local School Board (LSB), chaired by Mayor Francis Zamora, approved a resolution authorizing the allocation of funds for the procurement of walk-through metal detectors and additional handheld metal detectors for the city’s public schools.

Zamora presided over the LSB meeting where the measure was discussed and approved, highlighting the importance of strengthening existing security protocols in public schools.

The additional security equipment are intended to support schools in conducting more effective screening and monitoring of individuals entering school premises.

Article continues after this 

The walk-through metal detectors would provide an additional layer of security at school entrances, while the handheld units would allow security personnel and designated school personnel to conduct supplementary screening when necessary.

The equipment would be deployed to help schools enhance their existing safety and security measures.

Following the board’s approval, the procurement process is set to begin in accordance with applicable government procurement rules and procedures.

The measure underscored San Juan City’s continuing efforts to strengthen school safety and provide students, teachers, and non-teaching personnel with a more secure environment conducive to learning and teaching.

World.title: Calleja: VP conviction vote threshold could drop to 13 with 20 senators
World.content:
(INQUIRER file photo / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA)

MANILA, Philippines – The number of votes needed to convict Vice President Sara Z. Duterte could fall to 13 if only 20 senators are legally able to function and participate as senator-judges when the impeachment court renders judgment, according to one interpretation of the Constitution being advanced outside the prosecution panel.

“We are applying two-thirds kasi tignan po natin ang batas, concurrence of two-thirds of all members. Hindi sinabing 16, hindi sinabing 24. So, movable po yung number ng two-thirds, movable din yung number ng all members,” lawyer Howard Calleja stressed during the Saturday News Forum at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City.

Calleja argued that the denominator should change when senators are legally or practically unable to function as members of the impeachment court, rather than automatically treating the full 24-member Senate as the base.

Article continues after this 

“So, tatlo na po yan. So, 21 so, ano ho ang two-thirds ng 21? So, doon po tayo titingin kung 13 po yan o 14,” Calleja explained.

He proceeded to calculate the requirement based on only 20 senators participating in the court.

“So, kung yan ay 20, I think at 20 is 13 na po,” Calleja stressed.

The House prosecution’s present position remains that 16 votes are required for conviction, consistent with the initial ruling of the impeachment court’s presiding officer, while the Senate is preparing to hear constitutional experts before reconsidering the issue.

The court has invited former Supreme Court (SC) justices to discuss the constitutional phrase requiring concurrence of two-thirds of all members of the Senate before senator-judges take up oral arguments on the disputed threshold.

Article continues after this 

“So ang aking bilang po diyan is depende po kung sino ang present and functional senators na makakapag-participate doon po sa impeachment court,” Calleja explained.

He stressed that his interpretation treats the constitutionally required fraction as variable according to the number of senators actually capable of exercising their functions when judgment is rendered.

Article continues after this 

“So ganoon po yung bilang po dyan. So it’s a moving number kasi as I said, hindi naman nilagay ng Constitution 16, hindi naman nilagay ng Constitution 24,” Calleja maintained.

The Senate impeachment court will ultimately determine whether to retain the present 16-vote rule or adopt another interpretation before Duterte’s case reaches a final vote.

World.title: Ridon cites relevance of VP Sara’s husband in unexplained wealth charge
World.content:
Rep. Terry Ridon (INQUIRER file photo / Grig C. Montegrande)

MANILA, Philippines – Lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio is highly relevant to the unexplained wealth charge against his wife, Vice President Sara Z. Duterte, because what he owns also bears on her wealth, House impeachment prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said Saturday.

“Very relevant po ’yung asawa po ng Pangalawang Pangulo dahil, siyempre, basically kung ano po ’yung pag-aari ni Atty. Carpio ay pag-aari din po ng ating Pangalawang Pangulo,” Ridon said during the Saturday News Forum in Quezon City.

Ridon, who co-leads the prosecution of Article II with Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno, said questioning Carpio could help establish the actual extent of the couple’s properties, wealth and business interests.

Article continues after this 

“So I think very relevant po ’yung mga pagtatanong patungkol doon sa mga actual na extent ng kanilang mga ari-arian, ’yun pong actual na extent ng kanilang mga kayamanan at kanilang mga kumpanya,” he said.

Ridon said the prosecution is therefore keeping open the option of calling Carpio as a hostile witness as it begins presenting evidence on the unexplained wealth charge Monday.

“So as it is, asking him to be a hostile witness for the prosecution today remains on the table,” he said.

The Senate impeachment court earlier allowed subpoenas for bank and tax records involving Duterte, Carpio and their companies.

Prosecutors have since received copies of the documents for use in Article II.

Article continues after this 

Ridon also expressed the view that Carpio could not necessarily invoke the same right against self-incrimination that Duterte might assert if she were called to testify.

“So if the Vice President, for example, will insist on her right against self-incrimination, I don’t think Atty. Carpio can actually raise that same particular point,” Ridon said.

Article continues after this 

Any invocation of the constitutional protection against self-incrimination would have to be resolved in relation to the particular questions posed before the impeachment court.

Prosecutors are reviewing more than 1,800 financial documents for Article II, including bank and tax records involving Duterte, Carpio and their companies.

World.title: Mindanao first to host 2 LegisHear legs as House brings consultations to Cotabato
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Mindanao became the first major island group to host two LegisHear consultations as Senior Deputy Speaker and South Cotabato 2nd District Rep. Ferdinand “Dinand” Hernandez on Saturday welcomed the House of Representatives’ public consultation program to the province and thanked Speaker Faustino G. Dy III for bringing the legislative process closer to the people.

Dy said LegisHear brings Congress directly to communities because residents themselves best understand what their localities need to achieve greater progress.

“Anumang sanga o anumang katayuan natin sa ating lipunan, kailangang naririnig natin ang tinig at lalong-lalo na, pinag-uusapan natin kung ano ang makakabuti sa atin pong mga lugar,” Dy said.

Article continues after this 

“Sapagkat kayo lamang po ang nakakaalam kung ano ang mga kailangan at kung ano po ang dapat nating gawin para lalo pong umunlad at maging progresibo ang inyo pong sinasakupang lugar,” he added.

Hernandez underscored that the consultations are a serious congressional undertaking aimed at ensuring that legislation reflects the concerns and aspirations of ordinary Filipinos.

“Ang LegisHear ay seryosong programa ng Kongreso. Ang batas ay hindi nabubuo kung hindi kami makikinig sa mga taumbayan—kung ano ang daing nila, ano ang gusto nila. Kailangang mag-umpisa sa inyo iyong batas na ipinapasa namin sa Kongreso,” Hernandez said at the South Cotabato Gymnasium and Cultural Center.

“This is a brilliant project na ang Kongreso ay bumaba na mismo sa ground para makinig kung ano pa ang gusto ninyo, ano pa ang kulang, para kami na mga mambabatas ang gagawa ng batas na base sa sentimyento ng mga tao, lalong-lalo na ang mga masa, mga farmers natin, at ang marginalized sectors,” he added.

The Koronadal City event followed the first Mindanao LegisHear held in Butuan City in August. The program was also previously conducted in Isabela for Luzon and Dumaguete City for the Visayas.

Article continues after this 

Hernandez, the main host of the South Cotabato leg, welcomed the House delegation and recognized the regional directors of national government agencies, local officials, Tulong Dunong beneficiaries, and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority scholars who joined the consultation.

South Cotabato Gov. Reynaldo Tamayo Jr. likewise thanked the House for choosing the province as the latest LegisHear venue, describing it as one of the most important programs initiated by Dy.

Article continues after this 

“Napakaswerte natin na dito gaganapin ang isa sa pinakaimportanteng programa ng ating Speaker,” Tamayo said in his welcome remarks.

“Gaganapin ngayon ang isang town hall meeting kung saan papakinggan ang boses ng ating mga kababayan,” he added.

Tamayo said the consultation embodies the principles of direct democracy and participatory governance being advanced under Dy by allowing citizens to take an active role in shaping measures that affect their communities.

During the program, Dy updated participants on two Hernandez-authored measures of particular importance to South Cotabato that have already been approved by the House on third and final reading and are now awaiting action in the Senate.

House Bill No. 8342 seeks to rename the SOCCSKSARGEN General Hospital as the SOCCSKSARGEN Regional and Medical Center and increase its authorized bed capacity from 75 to 1,500 beds.

The proposed expansion is intended to improve access to hospital and specialty services for patients across South Cotabato and neighboring communities.

House Bill No. 8627, on the other hand, seeks to convert the South Cotabato State College in Surallah into the South Cotabato State University. The proposal aims to widen access to higher education and strengthen the institution’s capacity to serve students in the province.

The South Cotabato LegisHear featured an orientation on how a bill becomes a law, followed by discussions on the two local measures and proposals addressing electricity costs.

Residents and sectoral representatives were given opportunities to raise questions, share their experiences, and submit recommendations directly to lawmakers and government officials.
