World.title: Twin study asks if immune systems are shaped by our genes or our lives
World.content:
Identical twins Nicole and Amanda Campbell may look and sound alike, but that's where the similarities end.

"Amanda and I have very different personalities," Nicole says.

"We process information differently. We see the world differently."

And there's another difference between the Campbell twins, now in their 40s, which scientists want to learn more about: their immune responses.

Nicole and Amanda Campbell are in remission after supporting each other through significant health challenges. (Supplied: Nicole and Amanda Campbell)

Nicole and Amanda are in remission from separate chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory diseases.

Nicole was diagnosed with Crohn's disease, a long-term condition that causes swelling and irritation in the digestive tract, when she was about 11.

And Amanda was 24 when she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune disease that disrupts the flow of information between the brain and the rest of the body.

Both conditions have a genetic link.

They may look alike, but Nicole and Amanda Campbell have always had very different personalities. (Supplied: Nicole and Amanda Campbell)

Scientists have long been fascinated by what drives the body's immune response.

Is it primarily the genes we are born with, or the environment we live in?

A new Australian-led twin study aims to learn more about why two genetically similar people, like Amanda and Nicole, may respond differently to infections, diseases and treatments.

Understanding the immune system

Immune systems are complex networks that protect the body against infection.

White blood cells, or memory cells, recognise when a known germ reinfects the body and remember how to fight it off.

Your immune system at work It's cold and flu season, so your immune system is likely getting a thorough workout. But exactly how is it fighting off these infections?

Vaccines work by mimicking a virus or bacteria, teaching the body to make antibodies against the real thing.

But different people's immune systems can respond differently to vaccines or infections.

Some of this is due to genetics, but some is due to environmental exposures, like diet, lifestyle, past infections and stress.

Jason Tye-Din, director of the Snow Centre for Immune Health, which is running the study, says researchers plan to use blood samples from 100 healthy sets of twins to monitor how their immune system cells respond under certain laboratory conditions.

Jason Tye-Din (right) says twin studies give scientists a rare opportunity to control for genetic influence. (Supplied: Snow Centre for Immune Health)

Professor Tye-Din says this will help them understand how the immune system works on "a very fundamental level", including more about how immune cells divide, survive and die off.

"This shapes very much how we as people respond to vaccines or infections or why we might be at risk of developing certain diseases or how we respond differently to different treatments," he says.

Using twins for this research, Professor Tye-Din says, allows scientists to control for the genetic influence, so they can narrow in on environmental factors.

MS, twins and genetics

This isn't the first study to put twins under the microscope.

One of the first known classical twin studies was in 1922, led by German ophthalmologist Walter Jablonski, who examined the eyes of 52 pairs of identical and non-identical twins to understand more about the genetics of a common visual impairment called refractive error.

Florian Ingelfinger, immunologist at the German Cancer Consortium's Freiburg site, says twin studies give scientists the "unique opportunity" to separate genetic from environmental influences.

"That distinction really matters: environmental risks may point towards prevention, while genetic risks can reveal new therapeutic targets," he says.

Twin studies give scientists a chance to answer questions about human health that are extremely difficult to address in any other way. (Pexels: Muhammed Eratilgan)

Dr Ingelfinger led a separate study, published in Nature in 2022, examining 61 pairs of identical twins — one with MS and one without — looking at immune differences between each pair on a cellular level.

His team wanted to learn more about why one twin remained healthy while the other's immune system attacked its own central nervous system.

Dr Ingelfinger says they found some specific differences.

"The strongest difference was in a cell type we did not expect at all: a very early, naive-like T helper cell," he says.

T helper cells alert other cells to fight infection.

In twins with MS, these cells showed "altered communication", potentially making them more sensitive to inflammation.

Florian Ingelfinger (left) says studying identical twins can help scientists understand why genetically similar people can have different disease outcomes. (Supplied: Maryna Stamatova)

Dr Ingelfinger says the findings suggest that while genetics may create a "susceptibility" to MS, "something else during life is needed to turn that susceptibility into disease".

"This is highly relevant because every one of us has a very unique immune system," he says.

"Everything we do, including sports, nutrition, smoking, alcohol and previous infections, can shape how our immune system behaves.

"At the same time, our genes also have a massive influence."

Healthy twins key to findings

Unlike Dr Ingelfinger's study, Australian researchers are recruiting sets of healthy twins.

This was an important variable in a study led by Petter Brodin, professor of paediatric immunology at Stockholm's Karolinska Institute and published in Cell in 2015.

"Healthy twins strip away disease as a confounder," he says.

"If we'd studied sick people, we couldn't tell whether differences were cause or consequence of illness."

Studying twins across different life stages led to some interesting conclusions for Petter Brodin's team. (Pexels: Kaboompics)

Professor Brodin's study looked at 105 healthy twins and measured how each person's immune cells responded to germs and their antibody levels against vaccinations.

They found the "single biggest driver" of someone's immune response was past infection history, specifically prior infection with cytomegalovirus, a common virus most people encounter at some point without symptoms.

Professor Brodin says this finding has significant implications for long-held assumptions about nature versus nurture.

"[The immune system] is built to be shaped by what you're actually exposed to over a lifetime, not primarily by what you inherited," he says.

"That makes biological sense: the immune system's entire job is to respond to a changing external world of pathogens, so it would be a poor design if it were rigidly hardwired by genetics before any of those exposures occurred."

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

Professor Brodin's study, which included twins aged 8 to 82, found the age of each twin pair was also significant and suggested heritability wasn't "fixed" but "eroded with time".

Back in Australia, Professor Tye-Din hopes his study, still in a very early phase with registration still open, will help scientists learn more about how the immune system works.

They aim to complete their work within 12 to 18 months.

World.title: Theatre audiences still show up. So why do so many shows fail to make money?
World.content:
Recent cancellations of major musical theatre productions, including Waitress and Beetlejuice, have raised an obvious question: has Australian theatre become too expensive?

It's tempting to blame the audience. As people contend with higher mortgages, rent and bills, a night at the theatre seems easy to cut. But that doesn't mean everyone has.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics' 2025 General Social Survey found 22.8 per cent of Australians aged 15 and over had attended a theatre performance in the 12 months prior. That's more than 5 million people.

So if people are still going to the theatre, why is it getting harder to make the numbers work?

Growing audiences aren't enough

We reviewed the 2024 and 2025 financial statements of major theatre companies, and found a striking pattern. Even though more money is coming through the door, companies are still struggling to break even.

Queensland Theatre grew its mainstage audience by 5.6 per cent in 2025 and box-office revenue by 42 per cent, compared with 2024 figures — yet recorded a $989,000 deficit in 2025.

Belvoir in 2027 Belvoir St Theatre's season for next year includes a new adaptation of dystopian novel a Clockwork Orange and a one-woman show starring Noni Hazlehurst.

Bell Shakespeare increased its income from $10.96 million to $11.47 million over the same period, but expenses rose faster — from $10.99 million to $12.87 million.

Sydney Theatre Company, operating at a much larger scale, generated $28.75 million in revenue from continuing operations in 2025 — but still had an underlying operational deficit of $8.76 million. One-off funding and increased fundraising ultimately helped turn this into a $786,418 comprehensive surplus.

Even if a company can get a considerable amount of people through its doors, this doesn't guarantee it'll turn a profit.

Theatre companies also fund work beyond the stage. Queensland Theatre's Scene Project takes scripts into regional communities for young people to explore acting, directing and storytelling. The project, funded by the Rekindle Foundation, reached almost 4,000 students in 2025.

This demonstrates how grants and philanthropy can also support education and artist development in a way the box office alone cannot.

What a ticket price doesn't tell you

A $100 ticket doesn't buy $100 worth of theatre.

Take a professional company production with 11 actors (a rare luxury for publicly funded theatre companies), four weeks of rehearsals and a four-week season. How much might this cost?

Based on minimum wage conditions laid out in the Media Entertainment & Arts Alliance's (MEAA) Performers' Collective Agreement 2026, paying the performers alone would set the company back at least $154,400. That's before they have paid the director, stage manager, designers, technicians and crew.

Independent theatres innovate to survive While multi-million-dollar musical theatre productions are closing mid-tour, smaller companies are finding ways to thrive on local stages.

Then there are other costs that audiences rarely see. Venue hire, performance rights, insurance, workers' compensation, sets, storage, transport, accommodation and marketing all add to the bill — often before anyone knows whether enough people will buy tickets.

Theatre producer Suzanne Jones said the latest Australian production of The Book of Mormon cost $11.5 million just to reach opening night.

Why don't the numbers add up?

In 1966, economists William Baumol and William Bowen identified a key driver behind theatre's ongoing financial woes.

Over time, most sectors have leveraged manufacturing and technology to raise productivity. Live theatre can't do this.

For instance, automation has dramatically reduced the labour required to manufacture a car, without changing what a car does. Theatre can't replicate this.

Australian theatre calls for lifeline The local theatre industry hopes a live performance incentive modelled on a successful UK scheme will provide salvation.

A company could, in theory, "increase productivity" by casting six actors instead of eleven, or trimming a two-hour play down to 90 minutes. But that doesn't make the same production more efficient; it makes a different production.

The cost of wages, venues and materials keep rising with the rest of the economy, while the product of theatre stays stubbornly human. This is what Baumol calls the "cost disease". Any gain in efficiency comes at the cost of the thing itself.

Companies can use smaller casts and simpler productions, such as Sydney Theatre Company's recent one-man production of An Iliad. But there is a limit to this. Eventually, cutting costs means losing the very thing we're trying to save.

So who should pay?

Companies can cut costs, but only so far. Ticket prices can be increased, but that eventually turns the cost problem into an audience problem. And public funding alone is unlikely to solve theatre's structural economic issues.

The realistic solution is a combination of all three.

Producers are calling on the Australian government for an equivalent of the United Kingdom's theatre tax-relief scheme. This scheme allows UK theatre companies to claim close to 50 per cent in tax deductions for theatre productions.

That's worth taking seriously, even if a conventional tax deduction does little for companies that are charities or not-for-profits (with little taxable profit).

Another option could be a refundable theatre production incentive. Australia already provides 30–40 per cent offsets for eligible screen production expenditure.

A similar incentive for theatre would allow small and not-for-profit companies to benefit, even when they have little or no tax to pay. An incentive set at 30 per cent of eligible expenditure, for example, could return $30,000 on a $100,000 production. Having a cap in place would ensure it isn't swallowed by the biggest commercial shows.

On the audience side, the MEAA has proposed a government-funded cultural pass for young people, to the value of up to $200, to help boost theatre attendance.

Philanthropy also has a role to play, as Queensland Theatre's Scene Project demonstrates.

None of this removes the need for public funding, and none of it alone solves the problem. But spreading the load is more realistic than expecting theatre companies to simply keep cutting costs. Ultimately, there still needs to be an actor, on a stage, before an audience.

Sixty years since Baumol identified the "cost disease", we still haven't found a more efficient way to produce theatre without turning it into something it's not.

Linda Merewyn Lorenza is a senior lecturer and Robert Vanderburg is a lecturer CQUniversity. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

World.title: Ten of the best waterfalls in Victoria now enjoying winter flows
World.content:
Regional Victoria's winsome waterfalls may lack the sheer size and grandeur of those of the Congo River, the Zambezi, or the Niagara.

But each of more than 100 charismatic cascades has its own rugged appeal and, thanks to record-breaking August rainfall across the state, they are currently putting on a show.

ABC listeners from across the state flooded the Regional Victoria Saturday Breakfast program with photos and reports demonstrating the power and beauty of falls across the Southern Grampians, the Otway Ranges, South Gippsland and the Victorian high country.

But the prospect of a warm, dry spring means they are best explored now, before the torrent inevitably slows to a trickle.

Wannon Falls at Hamilton in Victoria's west after heavy rains. (ABC News: Peter Corbett)

Waterfall season

Federation University's professor of water resources engineering, Andrew Barton, said this spectacle would not last more than a few months before what is forecast to be a strong El Niño takes effect.

"It's a question a lot of tourism operators, farmers and landowners are all interested in — what's going to happen with our farm dams, our water supplies and our waterfalls?" Professor Barton said.

"We've had quite a good inflow season, with a good rainfall month, lots of inflows through our reservoirs, creeks and rivers, which are flowing nicely.

"But with this Bureau of Meteorology advice of a pending El Niño and perhaps one of the strongest El Niños we've seen, we're all waiting and watching for when those inflows will start drying up, and the rainfall will disappear."

Hilda Falls, near Loch in south Gippsland, cascades over a series of ledges for about 10 metres. (Supplied: David from Leongatha)

Professor Barton said existing rainfall and inflows should carry these waterfalls until October.

However, November will likely see the countryside start to dry out, which will inevitably reduce flows down rivers and creeks that feed these falls.

Pam Baker in front of the seasonal and aptly named Silverband Falls in the Grampians National Park. (Supplied: Pam Baker)

"I would expect waterfalls to some greater or lesser extent will be around up until October at least," he said.

"If we get some continued rain, we could maybe push on into November or December, but that's about it.

" Depending how hard the El Niño hits us, a lot of these waterfalls may dry up very quickly. "

Victoria's charismatic cascades

Travel guide Undiscovered Victoria has catalogued 50 of Victoria's more than 100 named and documented waterfalls that can be accessed by walking track.

Co-author and publisher Jay Dillon said much of their appeal was in their variety.

Jay Dillon says the appeal of waterfalls in Victoria is in their variety. (Supplied: Jay Dillon)

"I think we're very blessed in Victoria to have a whole range of different types of waterfalls in different environments to discover and explore," Dillon said.

"They represent a wonderful destination to put on your map and head towards because — especially this time of the year — you will experience a visual delight when you arrive.

" The other thing is there are often those little spaces and nooks along the way that add to the journey. "

MacKenzie Falls in the Grampians is a popular destination for hikers. (Supplied: Nick Esser, Parks Victoria)

Millennia in the making

In a geological sense, many smaller waterfalls are fleeting, created and then undone by erosion.

However, many of Victoria's memorable waterfalls formed over periods of time measured in tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of years.

Some are a million years old and more.

Professor Barton said that when fast-flowing water interacted with a combination of hard and soft material in the earth, such as basalt and sandy loam, it scours away the softer material to create a fall.

Andrew Barton expects waterfalls to flow until at least October. (supplied: Federation University)

"Their origin story starts with the fact that all water, when there's enough of it, and it flows fast enough, is very effective at eroding and scouring out dirt and earth," he said.

"When a river or a creek runs across a landscape where some of the soil will be soft and easy to scour out, and other parts will be quite hard, it's [the harder area] where it forms the top of a waterfall.

"Over time, you get this effect of hard geology upstream, softer geology downstream, and you start getting this elevation difference as that water flows over the top.

" Over years, over centuries, over millennia, that can make quite a dramatic impact on the landscape. "

Ten to fall in love with

There are scores of waterfalls to discover around Victoria. These are some of Mr Dillon's favourites:

MacKenzie Falls

The largest of about a dozen named waterfalls in the Grampians/Gariwerd National Park in western Victoria.

It is the largest waterfall in Victoria by water volume, with a drop of about 35 metres.

Nigretta Falls

Nigretta Falls near Hamilton in south-west Victoria in October 2020. (ABC News: Daniel Miles)

One of two major waterfalls along the Wannon River (the other is Wannon Falls), which flows from the Southern Grampians region.

Wannon Falls features a large, single plunge, while Nigretta Falls spills into several falls.

Lal Lal Falls

Lal Lal Falls is a short drive south east of Ballarat. (ABC News: Gavin McGrath)

A short drive from Ballarat, Lal Lal has a 30-metre drop over volcanic basalt into a deep gorge. It features a viewing platform for spectacular photographs.

Hopkins Falls

Hopkins Falls on the Hopkins River in Victoria's Western District. (Supplied: Debbie Taylor)

One of Victoria's widest falls with multiple cascades through layers of hexagonal volcanic basalt columns which can be seen from the banks of the Hopkins River.

Situated a short drive from Warrnambool on the Victorian south-west coast.

Stephenson Falls

Stephenson Falls is an easy to access waterfall in the Otway Ranges. (ABC News: Jeremy Lee)

There are numerous spectacular waterfalls in the Great Otway National Park, including Erskine Falls, Beauchamp Falls and Triplet Falls.

Stephenson Falls drops more than 20 metres into the Gellibrand River.

Narracan Falls

Narracan Falls, near Trafalgar in Gippsland, is a popular tourist destination. (Supplied: Graeme Edwards)

An elegant little fall in the Latrobe Valley that is wider than it is tall, with an eight-metre drop into the Narracan Creek.

Agnes Falls

Agnes Falls is in Gippsland's Strzelecki Ranges. (Supplied: Stan Crossley)

Cascading nearly 60 metres into a gorge in South Gippsland's Strzelecki Ranges.

Situated a 12-minute drive from Toora on the South Gippsland Highway.

Woolshed Falls

Woolshed Falls, just north of Beechworth, in full flow. (Supplied: Glenys McGrath)

Located in the Chiltern-Mount Pilot National Park, close to Beechworth in north-east Victoria, where Reedy Creek plunges about 15 metres over granite into a pool.

Ladies Bath Falls

Ladies Baths Falls is along the equally delightfully named Crystal Brook near Mt Buffalo. (Supplied: Parks Victoria)

Ladies Bath Falls and Eurobin Falls near Bright are a short walk from each other, offering a two-for-one deal for hikers in the Mount Buffalo National Park.

Trentham Falls

Tretham Falls cascades more than 30 metres into a pond. (Supplied: Glenys McGrath)

A single-drop waterfall within a short distance from Trentham in central Victoria. The Coliban River falls about 32 metres over columns of basalt.

Due to instability caused by erosion, it cannot be accessed directly but can be viewed from a platform.

World.title: Housing with benefits: Why co-housing could be the new Australian dream
World.content:
It was a conversation with their son who put words to something Ross and Paula Wade had always felt: the desire to live a little differently. They wanted to share a garden and were happy to live in a modest home in exchange for community. They just didn’t think realising this dream would come with a $200,000 premium. Members of the Brougham Street Collective in Eltham (from left): Suzanne Hurley, Shaun McLeod, Ann Cox, Pam Wade, Ross Wade, Mae Donaldson and Emily Donaldson. Ruby Alexander The Wades, a couple in their 70s, are part of a group of like-minded prospective home owners who want to live as part of a co-housing development. Recent moves by the federal government to make property more affordable for younger people, such as restricting tax breaks for negative gearing to new builds, has opened the door to thinking about residential property in ways other than an investment. For Australians less concerned about asset price growth and more with building community, the changes signal a new way of living is possible.



Still under construction, the Brougham Street Collective in Eltham in Melbourne’s leafy north-east is already a collection of buildings surrounded by heritage-listed structures of various sizes. It’s planned to have no fences for privacy, no individual driveways and smaller houses. It is set to have 20 homes, of two, three and four bedrooms, a shared garden, babysitting on-site, access to eco-friendly power, communal cooking and good friends of all ages. The Brougham Street Collective is still under construction. Ruby Alexander “It’s magic, staying connected, not only within your own family but with a whole group of people who have become friends,” says Paula. But there is no blueprint for such magic, as the group found out.



Council approval was a sticking point. Brougham Street failed to secure a permit because “planners just don’t have a model for this kind of development”, Ross says. Related Article Housing affordability What was the Great Australian Dream? “It’s just a tick-box process [for the council]. We say we have a common house, they say, well, what’s a common house? I can’t see a box to tick for that.” Brougham Street was forced to go to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to overturn the council’s decision, adding about $200,000 in costs. Ross says while the collective was not thrilled about the cost, the only other option was to abandon the project and sell the land.



“The whole community agreed that it was worth it to secure our dream of living in an intentional community together,” Ross says. The cohousing development in Eltham is set to have 20 homes, of two, three and four bedrooms. Ruby Alexander The co-housing model is more common in Europe, and originated in Denmark in the 1960s. The developments are generally small-scale communities of up to 50 households: resident-governed and -planned, rather than developer-led. Some have communal areas, although each community decides its format. Caitlin McGee, UTS Institute for Sustainable Futures research director, says the motivation for co-housing participation was “largely around social connection”, as family structures change and people seek intergenerational support. “I feel like there’s definitely a connection between the kind of rise in social isolation and this kind of renewed desire for co-housing,” she says. “It’s just this idea that people help each other out a bit more in an informal way and live as a community.”



The number of shared households has risen over recent years. Census data for 2021 shows about 848,000 people lived in group households, with about 19 per cent of these aged 55 and above. Related Article Housing affordability What the Great Australian Dream looks like today The at-cost housing project development in Eltham was spearheaded by Tim Riley, developer and founder of Property Collectives, his tenth project of this type. It is a joint venture where collective members get a vote on the management committee, where decisions are made. “These groups are intentional about creating a certain type of community – every project is different and dependent on the land,” he says. Co-housing remains an anomaly in Australia, where the desire for standalone houses on large blocks dominates the property market.



There are 28 completed co-housing developments around the country, including seven finished in the past three years, according to peak body CoHousing Australia. More than 12 other groups are looking for co-housing opportunities. Teresa Dominik, CoHousing Australia’s planning policy working group convenor and a Brougham Street member, says those numbers aren’t precise. Some co-housing communities have had staged construction, with the new stage a new community group. “Also, increasingly, people are doing more informal types of co-housing – often more like co-living but with many of the elements of co-housing. These aren’t listed but go to people looking at alternative and more affordable housing options.” The myth of the quarter-acre block, says Michael Fotheringham, former managing director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, lives on because “the development industry leans into it, as building detached houses on greenfields is the cheapest model”.



Urban spread, fuelled by a preference for detached housing, means Australia’s suburbs are among the lowest-density in the world. “We still build about six detached houses for every apartment,” Fotheringham says. But not everyone wants to live in a traditional detached home. Vincent Murray, 72, became interested in co-housing after being inspired by communities he had seen in France, where homes surround a village square with shared activities and spaces. He and his partner had long maintained separate residences but wanted another housing option as they aged. Vincent Murray thinks that co-housing provides a transition to life after work. Kate Geraghty “A lot of people have their work community but when you retire you lose all of that, so you need to have something else to put in its place. And so the village concept seems perfect for transitioning to a different sort of life after work,” says Murray, a retired academic.



When a flyer from a group called Agency Cohousing and Community – a development for over-50s in inner Sydney’s Balmain – landed in his mailbox, Murray thought he’d found the perfect solution. “I went along to the meeting and became more involved in it,” he says. He later became president of Agency. Related Article Housing affordability Melissa moved into a share house in her 50s. More people are doing the same “Before COVID a lot of people were very enthusiastic about it. We had these meetings with hundreds of people. And then COVID … Because we couldn’t meet because we’re more at the older end of the age spectrum … people became much more fearful about coming out and meeting people.” Dominik says co-housing had traditionally attracted older people. But recent moves to create more intergenerational communities has piqued the interest of younger people and families as housing affordability plummets and loneliness rises.



“The greatest saving is more that you can actually have a smaller house,” Dominik says, noting there can be communal facilities like guest rooms or shared dining rooms. McGee says “conceptually”, co-housing should deliver affordability benefits. “But in places where we have such a housing crisis and land so expensive, that doesn’t end up as the main driver, the main driver is really about the community-building,” she says. At Brougham Street, to ensure the community is diverse, the older members decided to lower the deposit for younger members. Emily Donaldson and her children will be younger members of the co-housing development. Ruby Alexander



“The collective is definitely age-weighted – it’s a bit of a Boomer paradise currently because of the cost,” says Emily Donaldson, 45, a married mother of three girls. Related Article Exclusive

Housing affordability Where first home buyers have been getting into the market this year The houses, while modest, are not exactly affordable, spanning $875,000 to $1,475,000, with an average cost across the 20 homes of $1.06 million. Setting up co-housing developments in Australia is not simple. Challenges include finding suitable land to build and land costs, as well as getting bank financing. Balmain’s Agency, for example, faced a range of challenges in its attempt to set up its community, and has now wound up after about 10 years.



The high cost of land and development building costs, and inability to borrow via conventional banking mechanisms, were some of the roadblocks. “When you’re in a community group with diverse backgrounds and abilities, some have difficulty, first of all, to visualise what it might look like, and also the financial side of it,” Murray says. Murray outside a site in Sydney’s inner west that was considered by Agency Cohousing and Community as an option for their co-housing development. Kate Geraghty Adam Russell, a partner of creative practice Saltbush Projects, which has worked with prospective co-housing dwellers, says from a legal perspective they can be complicated to set up, with roadblocks including approvals, loans and insurance. “Co-housing is, as a mindset, is establishing a habitat where people live in that sort of way, permanently,” he says.



“And legally it’s also a bit complex because the types of buildings that get customised or custom-designed for co-housing don’t have a very clear pathway or definition under planning codes.” Related Article Exclusive

Construction How Zac Efron is turning an Aussie bush block into his forever home Brougham Street faced this and other complications. The upfront costs were nothing to sneeze at. As their co-housing model operates in the private market, groups only have access to commercial debt funding and their own capital. The group also met resistance from locals. But it was the council’s reluctance to issue a building permit for a development they had not seen before that was the major issue.



Riley expected this, and factored VCAT costs into the project. However, the spend went beyond what he’d imagined. “We spent about $200,000 on additional architectural fees to alter our design to make it VCAT-proof, on lawyer fees and expert witnesses – we called traffic, planning and urban design witnesses. There were also the construction cost escalations,” Riley says. This masthead contacted Nillumbik Shire Council but did not receive a reply. VCAT took only 1½ weeks to rule in favour of the collective. It said this was the type of project that “could and should have been supported and fast-tracked”, an “exemplar of an innovative approach” to addressing the housing crisis. Ann Cox at Brougham Street, which is still under development. Ruby Alexander



The Victorian government has introduced a new planning pathway for apartments and townhouses that demonstrate great design. The Great Design Fast Track is available for apartment and townhouse proposals two to eight storeys in height, with eight or more homes. Related Article Housing affordability Cassandra grew up in a large family home. Then she found something better Projects are assessed against the design principles of being neighbourly, welcoming, landscaped, sustainable, healthy, adaptable and good value. “If you get a permit through the process, there is no chance of going to VCAT,” Riley says. In New South Wales, the NSW Housing Pattern Book and fast-track assessment pathways are not designed specifically for co-living developments, but may be applicable depending on the type of proposal.



“In NSW, co-living development proposals are assessed through existing planning approval pathways, depending on the type of housing proposed and the planning controls that apply to the site,” says a spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure. At Brougham Street as of June, all 20 homes on the about-7000-square-metre block have been purchased and are expected to be completed at the end of the year. Brougham Street members at the site of what will be their new homes. Ruby Alexander “We first heard about the collective over coffee at a cafe, and came to an information day,” says Shaun McLeod. He and his wife Suzanne are future residents of the Eltham development. “We were a little unsure at first but the more we read about it, the more we became convinced it was a great idea.”



For Murray, while Agency has closed down, the experience remains valuable. He has made new friends, some of whom are considering buying into a new development in Rozelle. Murray and his partner have purchased side-by-side units off the plan there. Those who still want to continue to meet up. The group also provides assistance to former Agency members in need. “There’s a group of us that meet once a month for dinner and we rotate it around people’s houses … So we’re still continuing on, in a more informal basis.”

World.title: Can travelling with a toddler be relaxing? I visited Australia’s happiest town to test the theory
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsBallarat Can travelling with a toddler be relaxing? I visited Australia’s happiest town to test the theory Julia Naughton September 13, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 13 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Planning a holiday that’s enjoyable for both adults and toddlers requires prodigious skill. The mental gymnastics of nap navigation, finding accommodation with ample (safe) outdoor space and close-ish proximity to family-friendly attractions alone requires careful consideration. It goes without saying that for this season of parenting, my proclivity for uncomplicated logistics means long-haul flights are on hold and road trips of more than three hours are off the table. A long weekend in regional Victoria, though, meets all of these requirements. The boutique wineries, famous local produce and contemporary dining options promise some adult fun, too. Fresh air, rolling hills and this sunset welcomed us on the first evening. Julia Naughton Skipping city traffic is a plus (we’ve chosen to fly into Avalon airport, rather than Melbourne’s Tullamarine, from Sydney), as is the offer by our hire car company to install the car seat – a skill my husband and I are yet to master (see also: tantrum-free placement of toddler in said car seat). We’re headed for the tiny town of Scotsburn, population 244 according to the 2021 census. It’s just an hour’s drive from the airport but, more importantly, only 20 minutes south of Ballarat – a charming city in Victoria’s Central Highlands that was recently named Australia’s happiest city and our base for the long weekend.



Upon learning that “Ballarat” comes from the Wadawurrung words balla and arat, meaning “resting place” I ponder the advice more experienced parents steadfastly offer that “holidays are just parenting in a different location”. In other words, rest they are not. Victoria’s 1851 gold rush attracted plenty of migrants – Chinese, Irish, Scottish, European and North American – who originally set up shanty towns. Today, Ballarat Central, the city’s commercial hub, is set out as a grid pattern on a bluestone plateau overlooking Ballarat East and the surrounding goldfields once home to those transient settlers. The perfect spot to settle in for the night at Mingara Park Cottage. Tara C Moore We arrive at our accommodation, Mingara Park Cottage, to find a loaf of freshly baked bread and a herd of goats and gaggle of geese visible through the floor-to-ceiling windows. The combination forces me to catch my breath; almost instantly, I am enchanted by the rhythm of country life and its promise of rejuvenation. Originally a log cabin, the four-bedroom homestead has been reimagined for city folk in search of fresh air and a morning alarm clock of laughing kookaburras. Owners Wayne and Robyn purchased the cottage derelict and kept only the stone fireplace. The new interior is farmhouse-cosy, with a palette of warm whites, caramels and natural wood that complements the theatre of the surrounding countryside.



Two gates must be opened and closed to enter the property. At home, this would be a nuisance. Here, it feels almost satisfying. I’m no longer on a treadmill and have the time to complete simple tasks. Life is easier. Slower. Sweeter. That layer of worry synonymous with a big city – where the search for free time is futile – begins to lift, allowing me the space to think thoughts beyond the childcare pick-up, next meal or work deadline. The next morning, at Ballarat cafe Johnny Alloo, there is an unshowy conviviality as off-duty nurses and doctors from the neighbouring hospital await their takeaway coffees and unhurried parents with prams grab tables for brunch. I order the French toast – brioche, spiced chai maple syrup, mascarpone, salted pecans and rhubarb (the latter is usually grilled peach, “but we’re trying something new with the rhubarb” the waiter tells me with equal parts pride and passion). The scrambled eggs on sourdough with crispy soft-shell crab and lime and chilli jam is also tempting. Related Article Sunday Life I’m not a hiker, but I walked the Camino de Santiago with ease. This is how I did it Fully caffeinated, we head to Lake Wendouree adventure playground, next to the Ballarat Botanical Gardens. Its fenced play area is appreciated for affording us the unique experience of consuming lunch slowly. Pat’s Sandwiches lives up to the hype and I suggest ordering the chicken schnitzel with dill mayo for yourself, grilled cheese on thick sourdough for the kids, and finishing with their excellent coffee or matcha while the kids play or take a tram ride around the gardens. The next day brings an unusually exotic promise: meeting Kai, the 10-year-old Sumatran-Siberian tiger at Ballarat Wildlife Park. The weather is crisp yet gloriously sunny and the 160-kilogram cat spends most of the afternoon sunbathing majestically on a high vantage point.



We also meet Pearl, the seven-year-old koala who, not unlike my toddler, refuses to sit still during the encounter, preferring to climb her handlers rather than munch on gum leaves, as instructed. But the most relaxed animals must be the free-roaming kangaroos who lie unbothered on the grass as visitors approach them. A trip to Ballarat would not be complete without a visit to Sovereign Hill. In this “open-air museum”, an extra sense of nostalgia is added as I reminisce about coming here as a child with my parents. While the educational offerings are lost on little kids (a trip down one mine lasts roughly 45 minutes and sounds particularly hellish with a toddler), the candy shop, horse-carriage ride, bowling alley and gold panning provide low-effort fun. Finish at the cafe which overlooks a playground featuring a giant ship, a slide and plenty of photo opportunities at the “Bank of Australia”. Our last stop is the Buninyong Hotel, a classic country pub that reopened last year after a major spruce-up by the former host of The Project, Gorgi Coghlan, and her husband Simon. We enjoy some of Buninyong’s best chardonnay and pinot noir in the sun-drenched beer garden and natter to locals gathered for a 70th birthday party. “We love it here in Buninyong,” says the woman throwing the soirée, her friends nodding in unison. With the afternoon sun on my back and wine in hand, a gear shift has most certainly taken place. Rather than simply “parenting in a different location”, rest is upon us. Don’t miss Eat and drink: Go to Pancho in Ballarat for the South American-inspired decor and stay for the ceviche, tacos and margaritas. A spot of history: Creswick Woollen Mills is Australia’s last remaining coloured woollen spinning mill. Check out its exhibition and pat the baby lambs and alpacas. Stock up: Visit the Meredith Farm Store to see where its famous marinated goat’s cheese is made and stock up on goodies for the trip home. World.title: Before his mum died, Josh Pyke was able to share an important career moment with her
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Before his mum died, Josh Pyke was able to share an important career moment with her Jane Rocca September 13, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 13 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Musician Josh Pyke is best known for winning four ARIA Awards. Ahead, the 48-year-old talks about his close relationship with his mother – and losing her to Alzheimer’s – and how an encounter in a record store led to him marrying his wife, Sarah Tran. Joh Pyke: “When I was a kid, [Mum] was like a magical being to me, a beautiful singer who could play guitar and piano, and a great storyteller.” Michelle Pitiris My maternal grandmother, Madeline, and I were very close. I’d spend the night at her house in Strathfield, Sydney, with my sisters; she’d always make us hamburgers between white bread and we’d watch Young Talent Time before we went to bed. She was from a wealthy Queensland family and married my grandfather, Lew – an American GI who became an artist and writer. Together, they ran a screen-printing business. She was strict and firm, but very loving and very close to Mum. Mum, who was born Catherine but went by the name Kate, sadly passed away 22 months ago. She had a long, awful battle with Alzheimer’s. When I was a kid, she was like a magical being to me, a beautiful singer who could play guitar and piano, and a great storyteller. She worked as a primary school teacher and then an ESL teacher later in life. Mum was the first person I’d play my songs to in my early days, when I was living at home. On my recent album, the song Magic is a tribute to her.



Just before Mum passed, I played at the re-opening of the Balmain Power Station. In my childhood, it was an abandoned building that loomed large, just 200 metres from the house I grew up in. By the time it opened Mum was non-verbal, but was able to come in a wheelchair. It was amazing to have her there. I was terrible with girls during high school. I was shy, nervous and had no confidence. JOSH PYKE Mum met my dad, Jon, at a party in Bondi in the 1970s. He’s from England and at the time he was working and figuring what to do with his life, so he stayed in Australia after they met. I have two sisters – Emma, 51, and Zoe, 47. We learnt how to sing rounds together with Mum, and often sang Red, Red Robin while doing the dishes. As a teenager, I had a big crush on actress Claire Danes in the 1990s TV drama My So-Called Life. I also liked the main character from another TV show, The Press Gang. She was played by Julia Sawalha, who went on to be the daughter [Saffy] in Absolutely Fabulous. I had a great teacher at Balmain Public School called Miss Northey, who I adored. She saw something in my creativity and told Mum I was really good at storytelling and tapping into my emotions. I still see her occasionally.



Another primary teacher, Miss Zavotosky, put me forward to be a character in the Schools Spectacular when I was in year 3. It was a really seminal moment, but I’d completely forgotten about until I was cleaning out my studio and came across some old school reports. She said my communication skills were really good. I was terrible with girls during high school. I was shy, nervous and had no confidence. It was only after high school and at university that I started dating. There were a couple of really formative relationships that I learnt a lot from, but by the time I met my wife I’d been single for over a year. I was 26 when I met my wife, Sarah Tran, in 2004. I was a struggling musician working in a record store and she was managing the bookstore across the road. She came in one day and ordered a Tom Waits CD. I recognised her because we’d been at the same high school, but she was a few years below me. One night, we happened to be at the same party and I knew I needed to put myself out there. I felt there was something between us that I had to pursue. We dated for five years before we got married. Sarah has influenced every single song I’ve written since we met. She is from a close-knit Vietnamese family; her mum is a strong matriarch, as are her sisters. We are all close. Sarah and I have two sons, aged 16 and 13.



Related Article Sunday Life Michelle Lim Davidson dated a fellow actor for 10 years. Now she’s happily single Justine Clarke is one of the greatest women I’ve ever met, incredibly hard-working and an inspiration to me. We met as ambassadors for the Indigenous Literacy Foundation [ILF], wrote a song for the ILF together, and then did songs for a TV show. She’s a huge source of compassion and empathy. My sons had only ever seen Justine on Play School, and when she was working in my studio they couldn’t compute that the person from the television was at our house in real life. Josh Pyke’s new album, Kingdom Within, is out now. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: When women like Julie win at this sport, some men still accuse them of ‘getting lucky’
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life When women like Julie win at this sport, some men still accuse them of ‘getting lucky’ Paul Kalina September 13, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 13 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

The first thing you’ll notice if you attend a chess tournament is how few women there are. It’s not uncommon for men to outnumber women by as many as 20 to one, often more, at these events. Chess remains stubbornly dominated by men, especially among adults. At elite and professional levels, the bias is glaring. Globally, women make up only 2 per cent of Grand Masters, the Everest of achievements in the ferociously competitive chess world. Despite the success Australia has enjoyed in women’s sports domestically and internationally — cricket, rugby league, Australian rules, soccer, to name a few — when it comes to chess Australia is placed 108th of 119 nations for gender equality, which is measured by participation, rating performance and progression at international tournaments. That’s according to a report published in March by the University of Queensland and FIDE, the worldwide governing body of chess. But chess is not the only sport that skews heavily towards men for participation, prize money, achievements and stigma. Men outnumber women in cue sports (billiards, snooker, eight-ball, pool) and darts, which have long been associated with cultures and settings where women don’t feel welcome, or been barred from playing. The paradox is there are no physical, biological or financial barriers to playing these games, be that at a social or even professional level. Gender is a raw nerve at the heart of these sports. Here,

three champions reveal how they are hoping to boost female participation.



Julie Watson, 53, Australian Women’s Billiard Champion 2023 Not just lucky: Julie Watson is a billiards champion, but some men in the sport still doubt her ability.

”I started playing billiards as a teenager, then pool in my 20s. It was social, with loud music, drinking, partying. When I got into my 50s, it was the same environment but I didn’t like it anymore. In 2022 I returned to playing billiards and snooker, and I’ve won 10 state and national titles in the past four years. Historically, women weren’t allowed in billiard rooms. It was a place men could go and be themselves, smoke cigars, drink cognac. It was for the upper class. It was a men’s sport.



The biggest problem now is that men don’t see women as their equal in snooker; even if we beat a man in snooker, it will be their belief that we got lucky. Quite often even if I win, my [male] opponent will tell me what I could have done better, what I should have done better. That happens in billiards as well but not as much. It’s not as attacking as snooker. There tends to be less ego in it. Funding is an issue for promoting women’s competitions, because if there are seven women for every 500 men in the sport, the focus will be on the men. That’s driven us to incorporate the Women’s Billiards and Snooker Network, which is solely devoted to promoting and developing women’s cue sports. We have no objections to men being on the board, and we have no objections to men being involved, but the network is purely to encourage women to play the sport. Women get scrutinised. We’ll be told, ‘She looks good bending over the table’ – really sexist remarks like that. Weight, whether we look good in our clothes … they’re things that come up regularly. When I play in open events, I’m often the only female playing. I don’t have an issue with that, but initially it was very difficult. Any new women who come in will be scrutinised. I don’t know what the answer is. You just have to get a thicker skin. You can’t be too sensitive if you’re coming into the sport.



Cue sports are huge in China, which has developed a new variant. It’s called Heyball and there’s massive money in it. One of our Australian girls just won the under-19 world championship. I find the discrimination is more of a generational thing. Younger players are more accepting of women being part of the field. The 50-year-old to 70-year-old generation is very old-school. I was a firefighter for the Country Fire Authority and it was the same thing. I ended up leaving.” Chloe Fan, 19, Australian Under-18 Girls Chess Champion 2023 Chloe Fan: “Sexism [in chess] today looks quite different to a couple of decades ago, when Russian grandmaster Garry Kasparov said women were weaker fighters. It’s more covert and hidden.” “I didn’t really notice it until I was 13, but it was really common for me to be the only female chess player among 50 or 100 boys. After I won the girl’s title, I felt it was a better learning experience to play in open events than in women’s. It wasn’t about gender, there was simply better competition.



Chess is a social game, so as a young girl I would watch the boys bunch together and make friends more easily than I did. There were a couple of incidents that made me feel on edge or more vigilant. Sexism today looks quite different to a couple of decades ago, when Russian grandmaster Garry Kasparov said women were weaker fighters. It’s more covert and hidden [today]. If I win against a boy, he will complain to his friends that he lost to a girl. I have witnessed boys making unwarranted observations about girls’ physical appearance. I had close friends in chess when I was younger, but a lot of them dropped off because their passion was not worth the treatment and uncomfortableness. CHLOE FAN For a long time, I didn’t realise these comments were offensive. They were disguised as humour, jokes, trivialised. As I’ve got older, I’ve felt more confident to stand up for myself and for other girls. There definitely needs to be work in supporting girls who speak up because there are so many boys involved, both explicitly and as bystanders. There needs to be support from the whole community. I had a lot of close friends in chess when I was younger, but a lot of them dropped off because their passion was not worth the treatment and uncomfortableness they felt. But things like more prize money and women’s titles mean women are willing to stay and compete compared to previously.



There are no physical reasons women can’t play a board game like chess. The gaps between men’s and women’s participation and achievement comes down to the number of men/women taking part and socialisation.” Joanne Hadley, 65, Darts Pacific Masters Women’s Winner 2025 Joanne Hadley: “The stigma [in darts] is not there as much as it used to be. We’ve had to fight hard to get where we are.” “Darts is not just a pub game, which is what it’s thought of. When I was in my early 20s, there were no other women there. That environment of it being just a bloke’s game doesn’t exist any more. A lot of women are playing. People like [three-time women’s world champion] Beau Greaves inspire young players because she’s only 22 and younger girls look up to her. And then you have the Luke Littler effect, as we call it, who has inspired younger kids to play. [In 2025, aged 17, Littler became the youngest ever world darts champion.]



Related Article Sunday Life Jo was brutally assaulted in her 20s. Finding fishing ‘saved her life’ There are a lot more tournaments for women and teenagers today. The stigma is not there as much as it used to be. We’ve had to fight hard to get where we are. A lot of women are getting the respect they deserve. It’s just a matter of having a go. It doesn’t matter if you’re male or female. There’s still some people out there who don’t think women are as good, but we’re just as competitive and we’ve earned our spot. Once you start beating blokes, you get respect. They know I can play, so they don’t take me lightly. Prize money is weighted towards the men because they get more entries. I get annoyed because we are taking off the same amount of time to be away from work or our families as the men are. [Women’s events] don’t always get the same number of entries. I understand why [women’s prizes are less] but I don’t have to like it.



I tend to say [darts] is 95 per cent mental, 5 per cent body. Playing darts all day takes a lot. The concentration, standing up, you’re just exhausted at the end of the day. It can be physically exhausting.” Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Oat lattes taste good, but they fail to get a dietitian’s tick unless they contain this
World.content:
6.30am When I wake up, I have a glass of water and give myself an hour to feed the horses, get some fresh air and get into the day.

6.45pm Home for a dinner of oven-baked salmon with chilli oil, coriander and freshly squeezed lemon with a side of steamed greens.

1pm I am in the warehouse today, so I am having a packed lunch of homemade roast chicken with a tomato and cucumber salad dressed with lemon myrtle olive oil and some goat’s cheese.

Top marks for… The salmon, vegetables and avocado eaten throughout the day give you a terrific mix of healthy fats, including omega-3s, plus potassium and phytonutrients. And I love the use of Australian native ingredients – many are exceptionally rich in antioxidant plant compounds. That’s a beautifully nutrient-dense lunch and dinner.

If you keep eating like this you’ll… Risk missing out on fibre diversity and possibly calcium. At 50, protecting bone density is increasingly important, and unless those oat lattes are made with calcium-fortified milk, goat’s cheese alone is unlikely to get you close to your needs. It looks as if you are avoiding foods containing carbohydrates, but risk throwing out the good with the bad in the process.

Why don’t you try… Not just thinking “carbs”, but considering carbohydrate quality. Add fibre-rich foods such as wholegrains, legumes, fruit, nuts and seeds to your day, Together, these foods bring resistant starch, prebiotic fibres, magnesium and polyphenols that eggs, fish and vegetables alone simply can’t provide.

Sharon Winsor is founder of Indigiearth and the Australian Native Food Festival at Carriageworks, Sydney, September 26-27.
